As a result, plethodontids are especially vulnerable to changes in climate, as respiration through skin limits the temperatures and moisture levels at which individuals can be successful. Due to a particularly high biomass in the northeastern United States, Plethodon cinereus (Red-Backed Salamander) has been extensively studied for decades and is often used as a model system for how plethodontid populations may be changing. To examine how plethodontid populations are impacted by climate change, we compare P. cinereus populations across a ten-year span. We use six coverboard arrays (50 boards each) of different ages in the same forest in Ithaca, NY for spatial capture-recapture (SCR) surveys. Four sites were established in 2014 and we established two additional arrays in 2023. Because many of these boards were degraded, we replaced approximately 50% of boards at 2014 arrays in 2024. Using these sets of sites we examine coverboard preference, salamander life span, and changing population structure. We predict that salamanders will prefer older boards in the 2014 arrays, and that different demographics of salamanders will be found under the old and new boards. We also expect to find a significant population of salamanders that have remained in the old arrays for the last ten years. Lastly, while we do not expect to observe a change in salamander density, we predict a difference in salamander surface activity between 2014 and 2024. Preliminary data supports that P. cinereus prefers older coverboards, and shows that approximately 7% of salamanders caught in 2024 were initially caught and tagged in the 2014 CMR surveys. We also observe a shift detection probability, indicating a shift in peak surface activity, between 2014 and 2024. Additional work will examine how range size and movement patterns have changed since 2014.
2552: A population of the blue spotted salamanders (Ambystoma laterale) and their hybrid has been protected by a road closure in Marquette, MI since 2020 as a result of prior documented vehicle mortality. The population has been studied by students at Northern Michigan University as a community service project with the scientific goals of understanding migration timing and its association with environmental variables. Annual counts at a standardized time as well as hourly through the day night cycle were made. Results show that the migration typically occurs over about two weeks, but that outliers can be found moving as much as two weeks in advance or following the main migration, depending on environmental conditions. Movements are tightly tied to dark hours with salamander activities starting at just after sunset (about 21:00) and concluding at sunrise, with relatively consistent movements throughout the night. As expected, highest counts occur on rainy nights, but we have seen movements in warm and dry weather in recent years. Ongoing work seeks to characterize the different timing of movements of sexes and genetic morphs.
2553: Many woodland salamanders have narrow ranges restricted to higher elevations, whereas related species are widespread across both elevational and latitudinal gradients. Despite many decades of research, the processes that determine range sizes in woodland salamanders are poorly understood. Because higher temperatures should lead to increased metabolic rates, range limits could occur where endemic species are unable to meet their caloric requirement for growth and fat deposition. If this is the case, widespread species should be better able to grow and store fat in warmer environments as compared to related high-elevation species. I studied a high-elevation endemic salamander (Plethodon sherando) and its widespread congener (Plethodon cinereus) across elevational gradients in a region of Virginia where both species occur. I hypothesized that body size and condition would decline more steeply with decreasing elevation for the endemic species than for the widespread species. As is typically the case, my hypothesis was entirely incorrect. I did find some evidence that salamanders had reduced body size and condition at lower elevations, but this was more apparent with the widespread species than with the endemic species. Furthermore, for both species, body size and condition varied more among sites at similar elevations than it varied across elevations. Body condition tended to be correlated with soil temperature at the time of the survey (rather than elevation), suggesting that body condition may change over relatively short time intervals in response to seasonal changes in temperatures. I conclude that woodland salamanders are mysterious creatures, at least to me.
2554: Rough-skinned newts (Taricha granulosa) occur along the Pacific coast from central California to southwestern Alaska at elevations from zero to 2,800 m. Adults breed and larvae hatch during spring, larvae spend summer in breeding ponds, then transform into terrestrial juveniles in the fall, with variation in timing based on elevation. Using minnow-trap and dip net surveys at nine sites in northern Humboldt County, California, we observed differences in timing of breeding and length of larval period within a small geographic range. All sites were lentic and at elevations between 400 and 1,000 m. We detected overwintering larvae at five (56%) sites, but the proportion of the population that was overwintering was highly variable between sites. At two sites, larvae hatched in August and persisted through the winter and spring, while at another two sites, most larvae hatched in June and transformed by October, leaving < 4% of the larval population at those sites to overwinter. At four sites, larvae began transforming at snout-to-vent lengths (SVL) of 21-23 mm, whereas at other sites larvae did not start transforming until 30 mm SVL. Based on visual surveys of amplecting pairs, timing of breeding was variable among ponds, with some populations breeding from fall to spring, and others breeding from spring through the summer. We have yet to find an association between environmental factors and larval period, overwintering, or timing of breeding, suggesting these aspects of newt reproductive biology are plastic and influenced by a complex interaction between multiple environmental cues.
2555: The increasing global temperature, with an average increase of 1.8°C in the last century, is anticipated to induce significant alterations in wildlife habitats and populations around the world. Particularly, ectothermic organisms like reptiles, which rely on external temperatures for thermoregulation, are projected to be disproportionately affected by these climatic shifts. This research aims to explore the impacts of climate change and habitat loss on freshwater turtles in New Mexico, focusing on their dietary patterns. Employing stable isotope analysis (δ15N and δ13C), we studied the dietary habits of turtle populations across four distinct sites, correlating these with varied habitat and environmental conditions. We also conducted a temporal dietary comparison between present-day isotopic values of Western Painted Turtles (Chrysemys picta bellii) and those from the 1960s-1980s using museum specimens. The site-to-site analysis showed differences in isotopic values between species at Elephant Butte State Park and the Rio Grande Nature Center State Park. The historical comparison of Chrysemys picta bellii showed differences in isotopic values between present and historical turtles at the Sevilleta National Wildlife Refuge and the Rio Grande Nature Center State Park. Next season, we will assess the genetic structure of the turtle populations across the Rio Grande. Genetic data will allow us to calculate the effective population size, connectivity between populations and hybridization between the native Big Bend Slider (Trachemys gaigeae) and the Invasive Red-ear slider (Trachemys scripta elegans).
2556: Climate change is a primary driver of the worldwide decline in amphibians, whose functioning is highly dependent on local climate. In salamanders, temperature influences many physiological processes, including embryo development rate. This effect has been studied in many salamanders in the genus Ambystoma, but not in the ringed salamander (Ambystoma annulatum), a species of conservation concern in Missouri, USA. Determining A. annulatum’s response to rising egg incubation temperatures is crucial to conservation and management efforts and contributes to the scientific literature on this understudied species. We determined the effect of incubation temperature on survival, larval size, and egg incubation period in A. annulatum. A. annulatum eggs were collected from three wild populations in the St. Louis, Missouri, USA area, subjected to three different incubation temperature treatments, and monitored for five months after hatching. We predict that survival, larval size, and egg incubation period will be reduced at greater incubation temperatures.
2557: Understanding a species’ conservation status requires evaluating its ecological relationships, contemporary distribution, and vulnerability to future environmental change. Species distribution models (SDMs) are widely used for these purposes, but regional-scale applications often suffer from extrapolation and niche truncation, reducing model accuracy and transferability. Spatially-nested hierarchical SDMs, which integrate data across multiple spatial scales, offer a promising solution but remain underutilized in regional conservation research. Crawfish frogs (Rana areolata) are a cryptic grassland species reliant on crayfish burrows that have experienced declines across their range and are data deficient in Oklahoma. This study combines field surveys with hierarchical SDMs to determine the species’ current distribution in Oklahoma, assess environmental factors influencing habitat suitability, and predict future range shifts under climate and land use change. Additionally, we compared the accuracy of spatially-nested hierarchical SDMs to regional-only SDMs. We documented R. areolata at 303 survey locations and found no evidence of historical county-level declines. Our models suggest large amounts of suitable habitat exist in eastern Oklahoma. Our traditional regional-only SDM suffered from extreme extrapolation and niche truncation, leading to predictions of significant habitat loss under future conditions. In contrast, our  hierarchical SDMs mitigated these issues and projected an increase in future habitat suitability. Our findings highlight the advantages of hierarchical SDMs for improving model accuracy and informing conservation assessments. We advocate for the broader adoption of this approach in regional-scale studies to enhance model accuracy, improve predictions of species responses to environmental change, and more effectively assess species status at a regional level.
2558: Habitat loss through land conversion and fragmentation is the single greatest threat to biodiversity and the persistence of species in the 21st century. Decreases in carrying capacity and population size from habitat loss simultaneously increase the probability of inbreeding and inbreeding depression. Combined, these factors synergistically increase extinction risk. The Eastern Massasauga (Sistrurus catenatus) rattlesnake is federally listed as threatened in the United States and Canada, and population declines associated with loss of habitat were cited as key factors for its listing. We used a 15-year capture-recapture dataset, targeted genomic sequencing, and capture locations from >1000 individuals from two populations of Eastern Massasaugas in Michigan to estimate inbreeding (Fgrm) and the effects of inbreeding on fitness. Using capture locations, we found evidence of spatial kinship structure, and limited dispersal ability, as a mechanism driving inbreeding within populations. We assessed the effects of inbreeding on fitness by combining reconstructed multi-generational pedigrees with capture-recapture data to estimate reproductive output and size- and site- specific annual survival probabilities. Both fitness metrics showed evidence of inbreeding depression: the 5% most inbred individuals had 11.6% lower annual survival probabilities and were 13.5% less likely to have surviving offspring compared to less inbred individuals. Our results demonstrate the mechanisms that give rise to spatial structure, inbreeding, and reduced fitness via inbreeding depression and may be used to inform future conservation efforts on Eastern Massasaugas and other vulnerable species with low vagility and slow life histories.
2559: Despite consisting of over 1,500 species and representing almost four percent of described amniote diversity, skinks (Order: Squamata; Family: Scincidae) are poorly represented in the genomic era. Despite this, the scincid lizards harbor an exemplary opportunity to investigate the genomic processes underlying ecological and morphological diversification across a global radiation. Here, we highlight this disparity as well as present a chromosome-level, annotated reference genome for the common five-lined skink (Plestiodon fasciatus) and newly assembled genomes for a majority of the Plestiodon genus.
2560: The level and distribution of genetic variation in populations provides key information for conservation assessment and actions for imperiled species. Blanding’s Turtle (Emydoidea blandingii) and Spotted Turtle (Clemmys guttata) are imperiled and have overlapping geographic ranges in the Great Lakes region. As part of project to assess the status of the species in Michigan, Indiana, and Ohio, we used microsatellite allelic variation to characterize within and among population genetic structure. A total of 833 individuals from 92 localities were genotyped across 16 loci for Blanding’s Turtle, and 600 individuals from 42 localities across 16 loci for Spotted Turtle. Overall patterns were quite similar for both species. Population genetic structure among localities was limited and showed isolation by distance. Levels of genetic variation within localities were moderate in most localities and comparable to other regions within their geographic ranges. We found populations have low effective population sizes and there was evidence of inbreeding in four Spotted Turtle populations. We modeled future genetic variation in representative populations of each species and found that they are expected to lose 50% of alleles over the next 200 years. These results suggest that translocation of individuals will likely be necessary for long-term viability of populations from a genetic perspective, but doing so is not likely to cause outbreeding depression within the region.
2561: Blanding’s Turtles (Emydoidea blandingii) are Midwestern freshwater turtle species that is declining across most of their range due to habitat loss and fragmentation. The species is currently petitioned to be listed as threatened under the Endangered Species Act. Maintaining landscapes of connected wetlands and upland nesting habitat is crucial for Blanding’s Turtle survival. In this study, we are investigating the movement of Blanding’s Turtles across a mixed landscape of high-quality habitat and developed land in Northern Michigan. We attached GPS data loggers to individuals across the landscape to gather movement and habitat use data. Habitat selection was then evaluated across multiple scales, via Euclidean distance analysis. Turtles selected for wetland habitats at the local range scale, and did not show selection against any habitats at the local or home range scale. This habitat selection data was then used to create a circuit theory habitat connectivity model of the site to provide information about potential corridors and barriers of movement to land managers of the site.
2562: The genus Micrixalus, commonly known as dancing frogs, is fifth on the list of the top ten threatened amphibian genera of the world. These foot-flagging frogs are endemic to the Western Ghats of India, a biodiversity hotspot. Out of 24 species in the genus, 22 species (92%) are categorised as 'Threatened' according to IUCN’23 red-list-assessment. One of the members, Micrixalus kottigeharensis was formerly an Evolutionary-Distinct-and-Globally-Endangered (EDGE) species. Following our work, it was down-listed to ‘Vulnerable’. Through this study, and my ongoing project called the Dancing-Frogs-Project-of-India (https://dancingfrogs.in), I present the habitat association, distribution modelling and anthropogenic threats to M. kottigeharensis. Through field surveys, we assessed the distribution using ensemble species modelling approach while gaining additional insights on the ecology and habitat association, including threats. The study shows that M. kottigeharensis prefers fast to slow-flowing streams with an average stream depth of 19±17.02 cm and width of 368±193 cm along with a canopy cover of >70%. Regression modelling shows a positive association of species presence to atmospheric humidity (Z= 3.46, p=0.00). The models also show a significant negative association with drizzle (Z= -3.24, p=0.00), intermittent rain (Z= -2.65, p=0.01) and rock temperature (Z= -2.71, p=0.01) within the streams. Our habitat suitability map for four different climate and anthropogenic scenarios shows that the species is restricted to mid-elevation, moist evergreen forests of the central Western Ghats and habitat suitability-area increase with future climate scenarios implying association with increased rainfall patters. This is the first detailed study on M. kottigeharensis highlighting the need for a conservation-action-plan.
2563: Animals continually balance the rewards of activity against the risk of predation. While sensory systems are essential for detecting predators, their role in mediating behavioral trade-offs remains underexplored. For nocturnal species, moonlight—a key driver of predation risk—varies cyclically, offering a unique opportunity to study how sensory capacity influences activity. We examined four species of Neotropical electric fish inhabiting clearwater Amazon streams where visually oriented nocturnal predators are common. These species are similar in size and diet but differ in body mass-adjusted eye size—a proxy for visual acuity. Using custom loggers to detect their continuous, species-specific electric signals, we monitored foraging activity across a lunar cycle, alongside moonlight illuminance measurements. The two species with the smallest eyes exhibited strong lunar phobia, hiding during moonlit periods and sacrificing ~25% of their foraging time. In contrast, the species with the largest eyes foraged continuously, likely using vision to detect and evade predators. A fourth species with intermediate eye size showed a canopy-dependent response, hiding only under closed canopy. Active electroreception allows these fish to forage in darkness but is ineffective for predator detection beyond ~10 cm. Our findings suggest that species with large eyes adopt a “vigilance” strategy, relying on visual monitoring, while those with small eyes adopt a “hiding” strategy. These alternative responses impose distinct energetic costs: reduced foraging versus the energetic costs of maintaining larger eyes. Overall, our results highlight how sensory adaptations influence critical trade-offs between foraging and predation risk across spatial and temporal landscapes of fear.
2564: Maintenance of genetic diversity is critical for preserving adaptive potential and avoiding inbreeding depression and further population decline.  As populations become smaller and more isolated, they are more likely to become inbred, which can lead to inbreeding depression, erosion of genetic diversity, and further population decline.  Eastern box turtles and spotted turtles co-occur in remnant oak savanna landscapes in Ohio and Michigan, and while both species have experienced substantial population decline due to habitat loss and fragmentation, remaining spotted turtle populations in the region are smaller and more isolated than are box turtle populations; thus, spotted turtles may be more vulnerable to inbreeding depression than eastern box turtles.  To test this prediction, we estimated population size, measured total area occupied, quantified home range size, measured baseline physiological stress levels, and calculated inbreeding coefficients in three populations of both species.  We used egg-hatching success and hatchling survival to overwintering as potential evidence of inbreeding depression.  Spotted turtles had smaller population sizes, occupied smaller geographic areas, had smaller home ranges, and had higher baseline physiological stress levels than box turtles.  Box turtle populations had higher inbreeding coefficients and lower rates of egg-hatching success and hatchling survival to overwintering compared to spotted turtles, suggesting that the box turtle populations are experiencing inbreeding depression. A top priority for conserving these vulnerable turtle species should be the preservation of intact tracts of habitat, restoring connectivity among sub-populations, and preventing further fragmentation of occupied habitat by roads in order to promote gene flow and random mating.
2565: The conservation and management of exploited marine fishes requires a thorough understanding of their population structure and connectivity. In the U.S. Atlantic and Gulf of Mexico, red grouper (Epinephelus morio) support one of the more economically important fisheries, but previous assessments of genetic population structure have been inconclusive. Thus, reduced representation DNA sequencing (ddRAD) and a landscape genomics approach were used to characterize patterns of genetic variation in red grouper across 6,756 SNP-containing loci. Spatial and environmental analyses detected 43 loci putatively under selection, enabling separate assessments of neutral and non-neutral structure. Results from analyses of neutral data indicate the presence of genetic heterogeneity, whereby red grouper from Cuba are differentiated from all other regions, while red grouper in the U.S. Atlantic and eastern Gulf of Mexico are differentiated from those in the central and southern Gulf of Mexico. In addition, redundancy analyses using Moran Eigenvector Maps based on physical distance suggest a potential genetic discontinuity along the West Florida Shelf, in an area previously identified as a potential break by differences in age-and-growth. Heterogeneity was also observed among non-neutral loci, and was associated primarily with sea surface salinity, suggesting local adaptation to environmental conditions. Overall, the results have important implications for stock delineation and management of red grouper, and demonstrate the utility of landscape genomic approaches for identifying stock structure in seemingly continuously distributed marine species.
2566: In the face of increasing urbanization, urban green spaces provide resources and habitat for free-living urban wildlife. However, the impact of different types of urban green spaces on the free-living organisms that inhabit them has not been widely studied. The amphibian skin microbiome, which is shaped in part by the host’s environment, has been identified to play a critical role in immune health and pathogen defense. In the context of significant amphibian decline due to the synergistic effects of anthropogenic change, it is imperative to understand the effect that urban spaces with different levels of protection have on amphibian skin microbiome. This knowledge will offer insight into the susceptibility of urban wildlife populations to infection depending on the habitat disturbance. We compared the effect that the Memphis Zoo, an urban dog park, and the protected Meeman-Shelby Forest State Park, had on the skin microbiome of wild Anaxyrus fowleri (Fowler’s toad). We performed metagenomic sequencing of the 16s region V3/V4 for 71 individuals at the three sites. We found that the alpha diversity and microbial abundance was higher in the toads living in the dog park, followed by the state park and the zoo. The microbial community structure was not significantly different among sites, but there was greater variation in community composition among the zoo population. As the first study to assess the skin microbiome of free-living amphibians within zoos, our results offer novel insights into the impact of urban green spaces on native wildlife.
2567: Morphometrics is a crucial component of analysis of size and shape. The data for morphometric analysis, traditionally, is gathered through manual landmark annotation. This results in a significant bottleneck for the production and assessment of morphometric data. In this study, we propose a Machine Learning based high-throughput workflow to collect landmarks of biological features from 2D, lateral views of fish specimen images from a digitized collection of fish specimen images.The analysis is based on 48 morphologically similar species belonging to genus Notropis and other American minnows. 24 landmarks were identified to from scientific publications as demarking important body features, 217 images were manually annotated to form a training set, and a separate set of 250 images comprised the test dataset. The model was trained using the DLIB Machine Learning Library. We calculated the accuracy of the produced landmarks by measuring the Euclidean distances between the manually generated and ML produced landmarks. The results show that the model works with 95.8% to 85.3% accuracy for 0.02 and 0.01 error thresholds respectively. The accuracy varies among the landmarks. Landmarks on the outline of the fish were found to be highly accurate while accuracy of landmarks in the inner parts were relatively low, except eye location. We found a 34.03% difference between the species with lowest accuracy (Notropis buchanani, 65.97%) and highest accuracy (Notropis chalybaeus,100%) accuracies calculated for 0.02 error threshold. The results suggest that the DLIB model is a powerful tool for extracting landmarks from images of fish specimens.
Artificial intelligence in ichthyology and herpetology (SSAR)
2568:
Machine Learning is one of the most applied data analysis methods for image datasets. Even though the variety and abundance of openly accessible biological data, researchers still spend up to 80% of their time preparing data into a usable, AI-ready format. For this reason, we have built a system, FishAIR, for managing and analyzing image data, particularly of fish, using ML techniques, focusing on AI-readiness, FAIR principles, and reproducibility, data provenance, with a modular and accessible approach. The workflow prioritizes making the data and metadata AI-ready, meaning it's structured and annotated in a way that facilitates ML analysis. FishAIR curates images and their associated metadata, ensuring quality and relevance for ML tasks.

Here, we present the components of FishAIR cyberinfrastructure and a feature extraction workflow to generate metadata, that are necessary for the preprocessing. For this purpose, we used fish images from iDigBio and classify these images to generate metadata. The main problem with the museum images is the lack of metadata, wrong categorization, or poor image quality. We describe how to overcome these by using AI. In this work, we trained a model for different objects in the images (scalebar, label, specimen, color-scale etc.) and classification model for the specimens (complete fish, drawing/painting, cleared/stained, X-ray, CT scan, skeleton/bones etc.). The object detection model has yielded an average accuracy of 98.4%. The classification model, on the other hand, reached to an accuracy score of 92.57% so far and improving by the addition of training data.
Artificial intelligence in ichthyology and herpetology (SSAR)
2569: It is well established that computational models such as neural networks can be trained to extract data from many types of digit images much faster and more accurately than humans can — a subfield of Artificial Intelligence, called Machine Learning (ML). In this presentation we describe ML methods we are using to train computer models to extract trait data from images of fish specimens, and how we are using the extracted data to distinguish different groups of fishes, from ordinal to species levels, a method we call the method Morphological Barcoding. We describe the Morphological Barcoding method, the different kinds of data we are training computer algorithms to extract from images of fish specimens, and how the method performs distinguish different groups of fishes.
Artificial intelligence in ichthyology and herpetology (SSAR)
2570: Computer vision could play a role in high-speed, low-cost snake identification and snakebite epidemiology, particularly when combined with information about geographic location and input from human experts. We developed a computer vision model trained on a global snake photo dataset covering 198 venomous and 574 non-venomous snake species (~20% of all described species). The model macro-averaged F1 score is 92.2%, but there are several limitations. Species with fewer training images are often mistaken for those with more images. Species complexes that have been recently delineated using molecular methods are not identified with high accuracy, probably due to a combination of training image mislabeling and extensive morphological overlap among putative species. Many diverse genera were represented in our training data by only one species, so performance is likely to worsen as more species are included. Species coverage is subject to the same geographic bias toward developed countries as all global datasets. Highlights included good ability to distinguish non-venomous mimics from venomous models in some cases. In follow-up experiments, we showed that adding geographic metadata improves performance, that uneven error costs (penalizing mistaking venomous snakes for non-venomous snakes more than confusion among non-venomous species) might have potential, and that stringent hardware limitations necessary to run such algorithms on mobile devices in the field reduce performance. We hope to set a foundation for developing global, regional and national snake identification systems for herpetologists, epidemiologists and healthcare providers, and the general public.
Artificial intelligence in ichthyology and herpetology (SSAR)
2571: Recent advancements in computational power and algorithm development have enabled objective classification and quantification of color patterns. Leveraging these innovations, we designed a framework integrating Java-based image processing software with computer vision techniques to systematically analyze dorsal color patterns in Anolis lizards, with plans for expansion into sharks (Selachimorpha). Our approach begins with the development of a custom macro, "ShapeShifter," within ImageJ, which automates the image segmentation and preprocessing pipeline. This macro allows for the selection of a region of interest (ROI), which is then isolated, converted to grayscale, and contrast-enhanced. Images are standardized through center-cropping and padding to produce square formats for uniform analysis. To diversify our dataset, we applied data augmentation by generating three variants of each image, enriching the dataset while preserving structural features. We then utilized DINOv2, a self-supervised vision transformer model, to extract robust feature vectors that encapsulate essential color and structural features of the lizards. This model, trained on unlabeled data, provides a 384-dimensional representation of each image, allowing for a comprehensive analysis of color pattern variation. The transformer’s ability to model long-range dependencies across patches makes it particularly suitable at recognizing complex patterns. This case study illustrates how computer vision techniques can quantify biodiversity in lizards and lays the groundwork for expanding this methodology to the study of sharks, offering new insights into the evolution of color and pattern diversity across species.
Symposium: Artificial intelligence in ichthyology and herpetology (SSAR)
2572: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has been applied to conservation and wildlife research in a variety of capacities to identify and monitor diverse taxa and ecosystems through non-invasive imaging techniques. Furthermore, the use of AI in combination with easy to use infrastructures accessible to citizen scientists have greatly expanded our understanding of both a geographic and taxonomic diversity that exists in the natural world. The goal of this project is to develop a deep learning AI system that is capable of identifying over 15 shark species that are commonly found in the Caribbean, Gulf of Mexico, and Florida coasts. Using Convolutional Neural Networks, our model aims to process and sift through pictures and provide a user with species identification and information. By analyzing distinct morphologies and skin patterns on a shark, the AI model can identify the species present with great accuracy while minimizing stress and disruption to the sharks and the ecosystem. This program is designed to be highly accessible to the public, which will allow for citizen scientists to further grow and train the model. This would enable researchers to increase their data collection, benefitting conservation efforts. We anticipate that the resulting datasets produced by the AI model would assist the scientific community by detailing the location and frequency of species, which can then be used to improve species specific conservation strategies. By creating this model, we are contributing to conservation on a broader level that also benefits biodiversity and the marine environment.
Symposium: Artificial intelligence in ichthyology and herpetology (SSAR)
2573: Artificial intelligence (AI) and Large Language Models (LLMs) promise to revolutionize science and society. Here we investigate to what extent ChatGPT can read, understand, and analyze species descriptions. We asked ChatGPT questions about reptile genera and species and analyzed the output. Depending on the specific taxon OpenAI has an estimated 0% to 80% of the information that we would expect from the literature. We also supplied ChatGPT with species descriptions and had it extract contents from it and organize it in character tables. From a sample of 120 species descriptions it was able to create correct character tables for about 50% (after manual verification) with the other half having more or less serious errors. Finally, we review the literature about other taxonomists' experience with LLMs and how they can be used in biology and taxonomy, with some practical examples. This study is an expansion to our initial analysis:  Uetz, P.; Darko, Y.A.; Voss, O. (2023) Towards digital descriptions of all extant reptile species. Megataxa 010 (1): 027–042, https://doi.org/10.11646/megataxa.10.1.6.
Artificial intelligence in ichthyology and herpetology (SSAR)
2574: iNaturalist is the largest nature community in the world, with over 4 million users per month. The platform is currently generating the most biodiversity data for the most species according to the Global Biodiversity Information Facility. To date, the iNaturalist community has made over 230,000,000 observations, representing nearly 25% of all named species. From these data, we train and deploy monthly AI models into the platform. The iNaturalist Computer Vision Model, trained on users' photos and identifications, takes an image as input and returns the most likely species based on visual similarity as an output. The iNaturalist Geomodel, trained on the same set of taxa plus elevation, takes a location as input and returns the most likely species at that location as an output. The Computer Vision Model and Geomodel currently include over 100,000 taxa with 1-2,000 species added each month, and together they provide accurate (90%), automated taxon identification suggestions for iNaturalist observations. This talk will dive deeper into these two iNaturalist models, and will highlight recent innovations based on this work.
Artificial intelligence in ichthyology and herpetology (SSAR)
2575: The blacknose shark, Carcharhinus acronotus, is a small coastal species found in the western Atlantic Ocean from Virginia to Brazil, including the Gulf of America (GoA). Historically, blacknose sharks, like many coastal sharks in the western Atlantic Ocean, experienced intense fishing pressure in the 1970s and 1980s. While the current status of the GoA blacknose shark stock remains unknown, research suggests that blacknose sharks have not exhibited signs of recovery, largely due to vulnerability as bycatch. Although studies have evaluated the age, growth, and maturity of blacknose sharks throughout their range, updated data are needed to better understand the current population dynamics of the GoA stock. Therefore, the objectives of this study are to determine the sex-specific and overall growth parameters, and size and age at maturity, of GoA blacknose sharks. From 2010 to 2024, blacknose sharks (n=201) were collected from the northern GoA via bottom longline and gillnet surveys and aged using vertebrae. Blacknose sharks ranged in size from 36-114 cm fork length, with females significantly larger than males (p=0.005). The male-to-female ratio was 1:0.69 and significantly differed from a 1:1 ratio (X2=6.45, df=1, p=0.011). Growth was analyzed using a multimodel framework incorporating the von Bertalanffy, Gompertz, and logistic growth models, while maturity was estimated using a logistic model. This evaluation of the GoA blacknose shark stock is necessary for informing effective management measures that ensure population sustainability.
2576: Elasmobranchs are important in shaping ecosystem functioning through their interactions, among the most obvious is predator prey relationships. One of the most common means of examining trophic interactions is by quantifying their diet based on stomach contents. Diet is typically expressed as number of individual prey items, frequency of stomachs containing individual prey or weight of individual prey items. Because each of the indices have shortcomings for appropriately expressing the contribution of prey, cumulative indices such as Index of Relative Importance (IRI) are often used to express diet. Since the major function of prey consumption is to acquire sufficient energy to meet their metabolic needs, the energetic contribution of prey may represent the most ecologically relevant expression of diet. To investigate the utility of quantifying diet on the basis of energy content of prey, we estimated the energy content of prey items consumed by a pelagic, demersal and benthic species of elasmobranch. The expression of diet as in energy was most similar to weight and the contribution of different prey on the basis of energy varied among maturity states, geographical location and sex. Quantifying diet in terms of the amount of energy contributed by different prey adds insight into trophic relations of elasmobranchs and for comparing feeding ecology of different species, age classes and sexes.
2577: Since November 2023, an abnormal fish behavior and mortality event has been ongoing in the Florida Keys involving more than 70 species including teleosts (n=61) and elasmobranchs (excluding sawfish; n=11).  Clinical signs include lethargy, erratic swimming patterns, and spinning at the surface.   Prominently among the affected species was critically endangered smalltooth sawfish (Pristis pectinata), with the first affected specimens reported by the public in January of 2024. As of March 19, 2025, 89 sawfish strandings and mortalities have been reported and 43 specimens have been necropsied, including 32  that were known to have exhibited clinical signs prior to death. Histopathology (hematoxylin and eosin; H&E) revealed that 15 specimens were in good postmortem condition for evaluation including brain tissue (Luxol fast blue H&E). The consistent gross necropsy finding across sawfish was an empty gastrointestinal tract. Sawfish were otherwise in good body condition with ample hepatic lipid stores.  Within the brain and specifically the cerebellum, histologic findings included swelling, vacuolation, loss of axonal myelin sheaths, and suspect areas of neuronal degeneration (n=11). Other notable histological findings included gill microvascular thrombi (n=9), renal tubular degeneration (n=25), and exocrine pancreatic lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates associated with atrophy (n=9).   Gambierdiscus sp. microalgae were found in the local environment at increased levels during the sampling period compared with historical records.  Links between the histologic lesions, microalgal toxins, and other undetermined etiologic factors lesions are under active investigation. Ongoing work includes the use of special stains and examination of tissues with transmission electron microscopy.
2578: Fuvahmulah, Maldives, hosts the world’s largest documented aggregation of tiger sharks (Galeocerdo cuvier), yet key aspects of their population structure, residency, and reproduction remain unexamined. Over an eight-year period, 268 individual tiger sharks were identified using photo identification and laser photogrammetry, with a female-biased sex ratio (84.5%). Residency analyses indicate that adult females exhibit strong site fidelity, spending an average of 60.7 ± 7.5 days in the area. Underwater ultrasonography of 28 adult females revealed that 93% were pregnant, with two distinct embryonic size groups suggesting a biennial or asynchronous reproductive cycle. The high proportion of pregnant females and extended residency suggest Fuvahmulah functions as an important gestation site within the central Indian Ocean. These findings provide novel insights into the ecology and reproductive biology of tiger sharks and highlight the significance of long-term monitoring at aggregation sites.
2579: Sharks swim using their caudal fin and body to produce a traveling wave. The wavelengths of the fastest swimming fishes are found most posteriorly near the caudal fin and faster animals have stiffer bodies. Shark cartilaginous vertebral columns are the main body axis contributing to whole body stiffness. The shortfin mako, Isurus oxyrinchus, is one of the fastest fish in the ocean. We previously hypothesized that shortfin mako vertebrae would be stiffer than other species to facilitate the body stiffness needed for fast swimming. Our hypothesis was not supported in previous data sets, where shortfin mako vertebrae were less stiff than other species. We did find that shortfin mako vertebrae had significantly different mechanical properties in the anterior body compared to the posterior body, where we hypothesize that stiffer vertebrae posteriorly will support thunniform swimming. Here, we examined the mechanical properties of vertebrae by quantifying stiffness (ability to resist compression) and toughness (ability to absorb energy) from I. oxyrinchus over a range of sizes (100-300 cm fork length) and body positions (anterior, middle, and posterior). We hypothesized that larger sharks would have stiffer and tougher vertebrae because they have more mineralized structures within the cartilage compared to younger sharks. Also, we predicted that stiffness and toughness would increase in vertebrae posteriorly because that is where the forces to generate swimming would be the largest. We found that stiffness was greatest in the middle region, followed by the posterior region. Toughness increased anterior to posterior, and toughness significantly decreased as sharks increased in size.
2580: Cartilaginous fishes (sharks, batoids, chimaerids) can experience indeterminate growth, where body and brain continue to grow throughout their lifetime. Thus, brain size and brain organization can change over ontogeny, potentially providing insight into sensory or behavioral shifts. However, very limited data are available on intraspecific variation in the brain between males and females at key life stages, especially at or around sexual maturity. This study assessed brain size and brain organization, or the relative size of seven major brain regions (olfactory bulbs, telencephalon, diencephalon, optic tectum, tegmentum, cerebellum, and medulla oblongata) in 22 individuals (9 males, 13 females) of the smooth butterfly ray, Gymnura micrura, in late ontogeny. The brain continues to increase significantly with body mass after sexual maturity in G. micrura, but male rays show a significantly higher intercept (ANCOVA, F1,18 = 8.157, p = 0.01), suggesting that mature males are more encephalized than mature females. Patterns of brain region scaling similarly show continued growth of all brain regions in both males and females. However, there are significant differences in the relative size (residuals) of major brain regions between the sexes. Mature males have significantly larger olfactory bulbs and telencephalons, while mature females have significantly larger diencephalons, cerebellums, and medullas. These differences may reflect sensory or behavioral specializations and/or differences in reproductive investment in males versus female rays after sexual maturity.
2581: Elasmobranchs often occupy important roles in marine ecosystems, exerting strong regulatory controls. However, given their diversity (e.g., habitat preferences, foraging ecology, life history strategies), a generalizable understanding of their ecosystem impact is not possible. Even within a species, foraging ecology can vary across time, space and ontogeny. For example, as an endothermic apex predator with high metabolic demands, the salmon shark (Lamna ditropis) likely have a strong impact on prey populations. However, previous studies noted broad differences in habitat and dietary preferences used among sexes and life stages (i.e. class), suggesting differential regulatory roles. Therefore, to comprehensively understand salmon shark ecosystem impacts, determining finer-scale patterns of their foraging ecology across class is needed. We integrated DNA metabarcoding of stomach contents with fatty acid analysis of muscle and liver tissues from salmon sharks to capture fine-scale, short-term shifts in foraging behavior across class. Our findings indicate distinct diets, dietary specializations, and habitat use among these groups. Ultimately, this study enhances our understanding of the ecosystem role of salmon sharks and provides crucial insights for ecosystem-based management of the Northeast Pacific.
2582:
A longstanding ecological debate has questioned whether sharks are ecosystem engineers for reefs – controlling fish abundances which ensures balance and thus healthy coral – or merely beneficiaries of already-healthy systems managed by the coral and algae themselves.




Using a dataset of 2,017 baited remote video station (BRUVS) deployments and 120 underwater visual censuses (UVC) taken across 24 coral reefs in French Polynesia from 2016-2017 for FinPrint, we discovered sharks modulate reefs through top-down processes, controlling predation pressure on small teleosts like grazers and stabilising reef health, but only when shark abundance is sufficient (maxn > ~3.25). Below that threshold, reef health dictates food availability and thus diversity and abundance of small teleosts, which in turn control predatory teleost and shark abundances, i.e. a bottom-up system.




Analyses were done on BRUV and UVC- plus remote data, using boosted regression trees to expound the relationship shapes and importance of environmental and human variables on coral health and fish abundances. We subsequently designed Directed Acyclic Graphs to model the study environment as either a top-down or bottom-up system, then used Structural Causal Modelling (featuring Bayesian Gaussian linear models) to elucidate the direction and strength of each link of the top-down and bottom-up model. Comparing statistical support per link and overall model, we found more top-down support on the shark-abundant atolls, but more bottom-up support on high islands, which had modest shark abundances.




Ongoing work in Florida promises to contextualise these findings to a more human-impacted environment, approaching a baseline shark abundance for top-down control.
2583: Lemon sharks (Negaprion brevirostris) are an abundant species in a variety of nearshore marine ecosystems in the Western Atlantic Ocean. Although studies on the diet of juvenile lemon sharks are common, little information on the diet of mature lemon sharks has been reported. To investigate the diet of mature lemon sharks we analyzed stomach contents of 67 lemon sharks (179 to 270 cm fork length) collected between 2011 and 2018 in the South Atlantic and Gulf of Mexico. Of the 67 stomachs examined, 53 (79.1%) contained prey. Diet was quantified as the number of individual prey (N), weight of each prey item (W) and the number of stomachs that contained a prey item, referred to as frequency of occurrence (O). Diet was summarized as Index of Relative Importance (IRI), a cumulative index derived as O(N + W) and as %IRI for individual prey. Based on %IRI, mature lemon sharks sampled fed primarily on fish (44.38%) and mollusks (48.79%), predominantly octopus (47.99%). The most common teleost prey were Lutjanus campechanus and Caranx hippos. The next most common prey besides fish and mollusks was elasmobranchs (6.28%).  The diet of mature lemon sharks in our study differs from the diet of young lemon sharks, which consists of nearly all fish and crustaceans, indicating that these sharks demonstrate ontogenetic shifts in their diet. The broader diet of mature lemon sharks, including various species of fish, mollusks and elasmobranchs, likely reflects more expansive movement, occupancy of more variable environments and more frequent encounters with more diverse prey as they age and increase in size. Ontogenetic changes within animals that demonstrate a broad range of sizes and that occupy a variety of habitats highlights the importance of considering ecological interactions of individuals across the size range of a species and within multiple habitats occupied.
2584: The whitespotted eagle ray (Aetobatus narinari) offers a unique perspective into coastal ecosystem dynamics as a large, mobile, benthopelagic predator that links inshore and offshore habitats. With a diet primarily dominated by hard-shelled mollusks, the species’ consumption behaviors are audible and can be logged to underwater recording devices (i.e., hydrophone). To better capture the whitespotted eagle ray’s foraging ecology we developed a customized multi-sensor tag (i.e., CATS-CAMs) and deployed it on 16 wild rays in Bermuda and Florida.  The tags recorded continuous accelerometry, gyroscopy, magnetometry (50 Hz), depth, temperature (10 Hz), and intermittent audio (22 kHz) and video (30 fps). With deployments of up to 60 hours we observed a wide range of ray movements and behaviors in the video and audio recordings and correlated them with data streams from the tag. Using these relationships, we developed models to predict behavior based on motion data, and found pitch-based signals to be extremely useful for distinguishing between foraging and other behaviors. Additionally, we report on unique intra- and inter-species interactions captured on video that are poorly documented in the scientific literature. Our study provides a foundation for future studies on the ecology and behavior of this species and related taxa.
2585: Largetooth sawfish (Pristis pristis) are a large, critically endangered ray with a toothed rostrum nearly 1/3 of their body length. Population declines have hampered our understanding of many aspects of basic life-history, including movement patterns and habitat associations, that are important for conservation planning. The rostral teeth of sawfish grow throughout their life and rostra are also frequently preserved, providing a potential archive of life-history data that may be difficult or impossible to recover from studies of extant fish. Our work has shown they record chemical changes that correlate with movements across salinity in much the same way otoliths store life-history information in bony fishes. However, the structure and morphology of sawfish rostral teeth has not been used extensively to inform our understanding of life-history despite prior studies indicating they contain repeated patterns in their internal structure or morphology. In this study 121 archived sawfish rostra from the Brazilian Amazon were analyzed for rostrum and tooth morphology, with a subset analyzed using MicroCT to understand internal structure. This data is supported by trace-element and isotopic chemistry tracking movement across salinity through life and likely habitat associations. Micro-CT results show internal pore structure of rostral teeth is strongly associated with both rostrum length and overall tooth morphology, and point to the utility of rostral tooth morphology as an indicator of basic growth and life-history information. Together, this data indicates that rostral teeth contain morphological information that could inform growth and size-at-age models, as well as containing detailed records of movement and habitat associations.
2586: Many migratory shark species occupy nearshore and offshore waters of the New York Bight (NYB) between late spring and early fall. While these species exhibit spatial overlap during these periods, which may be driven by a high abundance of shared forage fish prey such as Brevoortia tyrannus (Atlantic menhaden), the extent of their foraging habits and trophic overlap warrants further investigation. This is particularly important to reconcile because the NYB is a hotspot of ecological and environmental change due to increasing sea surface temperature and shifting species distributions. To assess species-specific resource use and interspecific overlap, we determined carbon, nitrogen, and sulfur stable isotope values (δ13C, δ15N, δ34S) from blood plasma in 152 individuals comprising 10 shark species from coastal Long Island and New Jersey. Fatty acid (FA) profiles were also determined from 65 individuals comprising eight species. Across all individuals, preliminary δ13C and δ15N values ranged from -26.4 to -14.9‰ and 10.3 to 15.8‰, respectively, suggesting variable habitat association and foraging behaviors among species. Consistent with fecal DNA metabarcoding data, δ13C and δ15N values indicate overlap in the use of basal carbon sources between some species, such as Carcharhinus obscurus and Carcharhinus plumbeus. Further assessments of FA profiles may further improve resolution on the differences in resource use between species. These findings will provide some of the first insight into the functional roles of sharks in coastal New York in an era of accelerated environmental change.
2587: Globally over two-thirds of all chondrichthyan species are threatened with extinction and guitarfish (Rhinobatidae sp.) are among the most threatened families within this group. As benthic mesopredators and potential prey items for large mobile predators such as sharks, guitarfish form an important trophic and energetic link between localized benthic food webs and broader interconnected habitat mosaics. Despite this, the diet and trophic ecology of the Atlantic guitarfish (Pseudobatos lentiginosus), the only Rhinobatid species found in Southeast Florida, has yet to be described and represents a critical gap in our understanding of this Vulnerable species. This project characterizes Atlantic guitarfish trophic ecology and diet using carbon and nitrogen stable isotope analysis (SIA, n=51 muscle, 38 plasma) and DNA metabarcoding of cloacal swabs (n=16). SIA suggested a generalist diet composed of both vertebrate and invertebrate groups, with no significant effect of sex, body size (43-70 cm total length), or season on isotopic niche. Metabarcoding reveals that fish are an important prey group for these rays, with flounder (Bothus sp.), mojarra (Gerres sp.), and striped mullet (Mugil cephalus) among taxa identified. These findings reveal that despite their small size, guitarfish are capable of feeding at higher trophic levels than previously assumed, and thus may play an even larger role linking diverse habitat mosaics than previously assumed. This characterization helps contribute to the informed management and conservation of these threatened rays and the nearshore hardbottom habitats on which they rely.
2588: Blacktip sharks (Carcharhinus limbatus) form large seasonal aggregations numbering in the thousands. These aggregations are typically spotted from the air which makes it impossible to determine the sex and size distribution. We sampled C. limbatus that occur in large aggregations off the coast of southeast Florida. The aggregations were comprised primarily of adult male sharks (95.2%) that were of a similar size (170.8 ± 8.07 SD cm). This provides evidence of both a size and sex segregation for this species during the overwintering phase of their annual migration.
2589: Worldwide, 51-60% of rivers are considered intermittent, periodically drying and refilling. Following a refill, these systems enter states of incomplete recovery. The amount of time to a full recovery is dependent on ecosystem type and the concentrations and/or interactions between abiotic (elements, time of refill, etc.) and biotic factors (vertebrates, invertebrates, primary producers etc.). After refill, elements flush from soil and become available to organisms. This project has two main objectives: (1) expand the emerging field of ionomics, to enhance our understanding of how mineral nutrients and often-overlooked trace elements affect both vertebrates and aquatic systems, and (2) deepen our knowledge of aquatic ecosystem recovery and how amphibians interact with intermittent systems. We will use 64 1000L cattle tanks that will act as mesocosms to replicate grassland pools. Four densities of Lithobates blairi (Plains Leopard Frog) tadpoles (0, 20, 40, 80) will be crossed with four timings of pool refill (fall, early winter, late winter, spring) to create 16 different treatment combinations. We expect as time since refill increases, tadpole survival will decrease while fitness at metamorphosis will increase. Higher tadpole density will likely limit food availability, reducing tadpole growth and size. This effect will be further impacted in the later refill treatments due to the already limited food abundance. As time since refill increases, primary production and periphyton biomass will increase but fluctuate over time. We expect the elemental profiles of the different times since refill to differ, with tadpoles impacting nutrient concentrations, varying in relationship to density.
2590: Frogs from the family Dendrobatidae consume invertebrates that contain alkaloids, which the frogs can sequester. The frogs are then able to secrete these alkaloids as a chemical defense mechanism. The type of alkaloids they sequester are directly dependent on the food that they consume, primarily mites and ants.  In the lab, we can administer these alkaloids to the frogs by dusting fruit flies with an alkaloid-enriched vitamin supplement. During a preliminary study, we compared the metabolic rates of two species, Ranitomeya variabilis and Phyllobates bicolor, with a control group that consumed no alkaloids and a treatment group that consumed fruit flies dusted with a vitamin mixture with 1% decahydroquinoline (DHQ). Importantly, in the wild, these species differ in some of the alkaloids they sequester, with P. bicolor sequestering batrachotoxin, making them potentially lethal to humans. We found that the metabolic rates of the control and treatment groups of P. bicolor did not differ. In contrast, the groups of R. variabilis saw a noted trend of metabolic rate increase in the alkaloid treatment group. These results suggest that the physiological effect of alkaloid sequestration may differ between species.
2591: Smalltooth sawfish (Pristis pectinata) are found primarily in southwest Florida (i.e., current core range) but juveniles have recently been captured in historical portions of the range along both Florida coasts. Long-term sampling in their current core range and, more recently, in their historical range, including Tampa Bay on the west coast and the St. Lucie River on the east coast, has provided DNA from individuals outside the core range. Individuals were genotyped using 15 microsatellite loci and compared to an existing pedigree of 1138 sawfish. We used COLONY to examine the pedigree, which mainly comprises individuals from nurseries in Everglades National Park (ENP) and Charlotte Harbor, and the relatedness within and between members of this group, primarily comparing offspring of individual females across years. Multiple adult females switched areas in which they gave birth, notably moving between ENP and Charlotte Harbor nurseries. We also identified three females that gave birth multiple times in southwest Florida, before later delivering young in Tampa Bay (n = 2) and the St. Lucie River (n = 1). Though gene flow in elasmobranchs has typically been associated with male movements, the results of this study suggest females also contribute to gene flow through pupping in multiple nurseries and along both Florida coasts.
2592: Site fidelity is a behavioral pattern observed in many animals. Biological and ecological reasons for this behavior include increasing foraging efficiency in familiar foraging regions and supporting physiological needs both of which can increase overall fitness. In the western North Atlantic, tracked white sharks (Carcharodon carcharias) have been shown to demonstrate site fidelity in their summer residency region off Massachusetts and Atlantic Canada, with individuals returning to either region over multiple years with minimal overlap between the two areas. While patterns of site fidelity are evident during the overwintering phase, its presence at finer spatial scales within this region remains unclear. Six adult white sharks (Female: n=3; Male: n= 3) were examined using regularized tracks from SPOT (Smart Position and Temperature Transmitting tag) and acoustic geolocations to determine if site fidelity behaviors were exhibited in the overwintering region by characterizing space use from 50% kernel density estimates (KDE). These individuals were selected as they provided consistent geolocations within the overwintering region over a multi-year period. All sharks utilized the coastal to shelf-edge waters from the Outer Banks, North Carolina, to central Florida. However, three areas demonstrated consistent use: (1) the Outer Banks, (2) the shelf edge near the South Carolina–Georgia border, and (3) waters from central to northeastern Florida. Identifying regions where site fidelity is exhibited may provide valuable insight into potential foraging or mating habitats for this population.
2593: The remote island of New Guinea has been long regarded as a biodiversity hotspot, yet remains one of the least explored regions in the world, with little literature present regarding the biology of its herpetofauna. Recent work has uncovered a number of endemic snake species on this island, especially in the cryptic, ground-dwelling genus of Stegonotus. Currently, 26 species of Stegonotus are recognized across Southeast Asia and Australia, with almost half of them occurring in New Guinea. However, due to their largely nondescriptive appearance and secretive nature, Stegonotus, those found in New Guinea in particular, still receive little attention, resulting in the poor understanding of their taxonomic status. This begs for more comprehensive work on the taxonomic revision of Stegonotus, which has great potential to increase their known diversity. Using a combination of genomic and morphometric data collected from specimens sampled across the island, we aim to elucidate the taxonomic status of Stegonotus across New Guinea, which can be a critical step in quantifying New Guinea’s biodiversity and can generate valuable information to guide conservation on this biologically megadiverse land.
2594: Burrow construction is an extremely widespread behavior across non-serpentine Squamata globally. Representative taxa in 36 of the 43 lizard families have been documented to build burrows and species in an additional four families are known to use burrows created by other organisms. Nonetheless, fewer than ten studies exist examining the internal structure of these burrows, none looking at more than a single species each. From these sparse studies we see a wide range of structures, from simple, shallow diagonal tunnels with a solitary chamber to large, multichambered burrows with multiple entrances. This study will, for the first time, compare a wide range of burrows constructed or excavated by lizards in nine families in Southern Africa. A physical representation of burrows created by lizards will be obtained by filling burrows with plaster or aluminum, creating a physical cast which can then be scanned and measured. Burrow casts will be analyzed to determine how burrow structure varies not only within a single species, but across genera and families in the region and in differing natural substrates. The morphometrics of burrowing species will also be investigated to identify trends in burrow morphology that may be reflective of body size or proportion.
2595: Climate change leads to significant changes in ecosystems, including shifts in the habitat ranges of both native and invasive species. For thermophilic reptiles such as Natrix tessellata, global warming may facilitate northward expansion. This process may be further enhanced by the availability of new food resources, such as invasive fish species. Examples include Lepomis gibbosus, and Neogobius melanostomus. Our research, based on the data we collected and SDMs constructed using the MaxEnt and WorldClim, demonstrates that in Ukraine, the ecological niches of these fish species and N. tessellata are quite similar. At the same time, the SDM model of N. tessellata correlates best with the model of L. gibbosus (R²=77.5%) compared to that of N. melanostomus (R²=22%). The primary factor influencing the distribution of N. tessellata and L. gibbosus is the annual mean temperature (bio1), while for N. melanostomus, terrain and bio10 are more significant. Projections for 2050 indicate a potential increase in the range of these species by 1.7 times, confirming the ability of thermophilic species to expand. This is supported by our field observations in Eastern Europe. The study highlights the importance of the trophic interdependence between predators and their prey, which necessitates the conservation of local biodiversity. On one hand, invasive fish promote the adaptation of reptiles, while on the other hand, they pose risks to ecosystem balance by altering food chains and displacing native species. To minimize these impacts, systematic monitoring, control of invasive species, and adaptive ecosystem management under changing climate conditions are required.
2596: Myanmar amber deposits include the most diverse fossil squamate assemblage in the world. From 120 known inclusions in amber from Burma, only one representative each of Agamidae, Gekkota, Xantusiidae, Scincidae, and Anguimorpha, and one squamate of uncertain position have been described. Here, we describe a new gekkotan species, and unlike the first gecko reported in amber — based on a foot, this taxon includes most of the skull, some postcranial elements, and the integument. The new taxon is represented by two specimens, one with many disarticulated bones and another articulated but missing the braincase. Both specimens are placed among geckos based on isodont dentition, tubular dentaries and frontals, posteriorly open orbit, and flat parietal skull table. Derived characters include a unique interlocking mechanism between the frontal and parietal bone, and several features of scalation. There is an indication of a parietal eye and anterior to the cloaca, some scales resemble the escutcheon scales of some geckos. The absence of toepads and large claws may be indicative of  a terrestrial lifestyle. This project follows all the recommendations for ethical sourcing of amber established by the Society of Vertebrate Paleontology.
2597: Specimens are key for providing data to address hypotheses within biological studies. For squamates, specimens play a major role in detailing internal and external anatomy, conducting dietary studies, understanding reproductive biology, and refining geographic distributions. Importantly, these preserved animals are the backbone for species descriptions. However, in certain circumstances the usage of single specimens without additional considerations can confound taxonomy rather than better elucidate it. Here, I highlight cases where the holotype is the only known example for a taxon and where subsequently, using its morphology alone for describing or elevating a species may perpetuate systematic confusion. General considerations for when single individuals are used for species descriptions are discussed.
2598: Anthropogenic pressures are driving elasmobranch populations around the world towards extinction. The islands of Darwin and Wolf in the far north of the Galapagos Marine Reserve are known to harbour an exceptionally large reef fish biomass, mostly composed of sharks, and therefore represent a conservation hotspot of international importance. Due to the dynamic oceanographic setting of the archipelago, the composition of sharks and large predatory fish is likely to change throughout the year. With the aim to investigate these potential changes, the current study combined multiple underwater sampling video techniques to assess the seasonal variation in sharks and large predatory fish assemblages at Darwin and Wolf Islands. The results provided evidence that the biomass and relative abundance of species was significantly higher during the cold season, and that seasonal variation in community composition was driven by large and highly mobile predators, such as the scalloped hammerhead sharks (Sphyrna lewini). As these species are of high conservation and commercial significance, the results on seasonal variation highlight the need for temporal management actions, such as higher restrictions and enforcement  of fisheries at Darwin and Wolf Islands during the cold season.
2599: Phenotypic resemblance between species can arise through various evolutionary mechanisms including convergent evolution and mimicry. Coral snakes (genus Micrurus) and their lookalikes are often cited as representatives of the latter, typically in the form of Batesian mimicry. However, there is a current lack of empirical evidence to fully support this hypothesis. Our study investigates potential geographic and environmental factors that may influence the degree of phenotypic resemblance between species, without assuming an a priori driving force of mimicry. Specifically, our analysis examines the correlation between geographic distance and color pattern similarity between venomous coral snakes and their non-venomous counterparts. Phenotypic characteristics of 10 South American snake species (5 Micrurus and 5 lookalike species across 4 genera: Anilius, Atractus, Erythrolamprus, and Oxyrhopus) were collected and analyzed using multivariate dimensionality reduction techniques. Phenotypic variation and geographic distance between each specimen pair were then determined from pairwise distance analyses. Preliminary mantel tests reveal no significant correlation between geographic distance and phenotypic similarity between these snake populations (P > 0.05). This finding contrasts with the expectation for mimetic species to have increased phenotypic resemblance as sympatric proximity with their model increases. Although these results do not exclude mimicry entirely as a potential driving force, we note that other unexplored mechanisms are likely to contribute to the observed phenotypic resemblance among these snakes. Our research highlights a potential need to broaden the traditional understanding of mimetic system dynamics, particularly regarding the spatial requirements between models and mimics.
2600: "Land-use legacy" refers to the interactive influences of historic and contemporary anthropogenic land-use regimes and ongoing socio-environmental processes in a given area. Such legacies are important to ecology and conservation, broadly, in that they inform biodiversity organization, ecosystem function, and management and conservation, as well as the maintenance of socio-cultural landscapes. More specifically, they are relevant to herpetofauna due to the sensitivity of many of these species to land alteration across multiple scales. Cultivated by the slave-driven alteration of coastal plain wetlands, rice cultivation in South Carolina and throughout the southeast left behind a unique system of racialized land-use legacies. This system has significantly impacted South Carolina coastal wetland environments in terms of soil, hydrology, and vegetation. In this presentation, we present preliminary results from our investigation of the way this history of land use has influenced the composition, structure, arrangement, and habitat relationships of herpetofauna communities. We surveyed herpetofauna and collected environmental data in historic rice fields of South Carolina from April through July 2024 and March through June 2025. Herpetofauna sampling included acoustic recording units, area- and time-constrained visual encounter surveys, aquatic trapping, and PVC and cover board arrays. Environmental sampling of present-day site-level variables involved water quality, hydrology, and vegetation surveys. We perform multivariate statistical analyses to identify relationships between communities and these environmental variables, as well as landscape-level variables and proxies for historic land use. We also analyze microhabitat-use breadth and identify microhabitat-use guilds in herpetofauna communities associated with South Carolina historic rice fields.
2601: The American bullfrog (Lithobates catesbianus) is considered one of the world’s most environmentally damaging invasive species, and is linked to decreases in native species abundance and species extinction by predation, herbivory, and disease transmission. These frogs are naturally found in Minnesota, but only in the “Driftless region” in the state’s SE corner. However, since the 1930s these frogs have increasingly been found elsewhere in the state, from the farmlands of the SW to the lakes country of central Minnesota. Currently, it is unknown whether these populations represent novel introductions from elsewhere in the world or natural range expansion of Minnesota’s native bullfrogs. To address this gap in knowledge, I am collecting environmental DNA (eDNA) samples as well as bullfrog tissue samples from all known populations in the state. These samples will then be compared to each other and to existing bullfrog phylogenies in order to attempt to locate source populations for Minnesota’s bullfrogs. This information will inform land managers and researchers on the origins of novel bullfrog populations and their invasion status, which has relevant implications for conservation actions in the state.
2602: The Trachylepis variegata (Peters, 1870) species complex has long been subject to taxonomic difficulties, and recently the systematics of the Angolan specimens was revised. However, the clade as it exists outside of Angola has not been thoroughly addressed, and specimens long considered as Trachylepis punctulata (Bocage, 1872) may represent a separate species which has been tentatively referred to Trachylepis cf. triebneri (Mertens, 1954). In this study, significant sampling gaps will be filled, and a multi-locus phylogeny of the T. variegata group will be estimated. The phylogeny will be coupled with a population clustering model and morphology to assess the status of T. cf. triebneri as a full species. The timing of divergence between members of the T. variegata group, and the role of the Kunene River and other potential barriers in promoting speciation will be evaluated. Trachylepis cf. triebneri and T. variegata share an extensive range boundary, and information from the time tree and population clustering model will also be used to investigate the nature of a barrier to gene flow between these taxa. Ecological niche modeling using MaxEnt will be used to test the hypothesis that these taxa may segregate ecologically, likely in conjunction with a west-east rainfall gradient in Namibia. The majority of variegata group museum samples will be examined in light of new data, and morphological diagnoses and distributional ranges will be updated for all members of the complex.
2603: Effective biodiversity monitoring is critical to understand marine ecosystems and to inform fisheries resource management and conservation efforts. Environmental DNA (eDNA) is a tool used for accurate, scalable, and non-invasive biodiversity surveys. Amplicon sequencing or “metabarcoding” of eDNA, in which marker genes are amplified with primers targeting organisms of interest and sequenced at large scale, is commonly used to assess community composition. The generation of amplicon sequence variants (ASVs) is recognized as a highly accurate and biologically informative approach to process raw amplicon sequence data. DADA2, a popular open source software program for ASV generation and analysis, uses modeled sequencing error rates to discriminate likely biological variability from spurious sequences. However, the default parameter settings reflect the initial design of this software, which was meant to analyze 16S rRNA microbiome data. Here, we test the effect of changing error rate thresholds, individual vs. pooled sample error modeling, and the addition of “prior” sequences on teleost fish metabarcoding sequence data. We further test different approaches (k-mer based vs alignment based) for taxonomic assignment. We benchmark these results using known mock community data and apply the tests to environmental samples taken from the California Current. These field samples include PCR amplicons that were pooled for sequencing either with or without size selection to remove off-target amplification products. We assess the ecological validity of detected fish species by referencing historical ecosystem survey data and provide a recommended bioinformatic framework for processing MiFish amplicon data for improved accuracy and reliability.
Techniques in Ecology and Evolution / Conservation & Management I
2604: Bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA) is a non-invasive technology that has been widely applied to estimate body composition and key health-related biomarkers in fish, amphibians, and reptiles. This method measures the electrical properties of tissues to assess physiological parameters such as fat content, water distribution, protein density, and overall condition. Unlike traditional methods that require destructive sampling, BIA provides a rapid, repeatable, and non-lethal approach to evaluating physiological status in real-time. In collaboration with the Yukon Delta Fisheries Development Association and the National Marine Fisheries Service, BIA was used to monitor Oncorhynchus spp. out-migrating in the Yukon River, successfully modeling body composition and energy reserves.
