Beyond fish, BIA has been successfully applied to amphibians and reptiles, including Lithobates catesbeianus, Trachemys scripta, and Sceloporus occidentalis, offering insights into hydration status, energy reserves, and health in terrestrial and semi-aquatic environments. The portability and ease of use of BIA make it an accessible tool for researchers, fisheries managers, and citizen science groups. Measurements can be taken in the field and transmitted to a cloud-based data analytics dashboard for real-time monitoring and long-term data tracking. This presentation will provide an overview of how BIA works, its applications in fish and herpetofauna, and how it is being utilized to collect data for conservation and ecological monitoring efforts. By expanding its use beyond fisheries, BIA represents a valuable tool for assessing health and condition across diverse species, enabling more efficient and non-invasive wildlife research and management.
Techniques in Ecology and Evolution / Conservation & Management I
2605: Numerous factors may affect how snakes choose to forage. Piscivorous snakes, such as genus Nerodia, experience restricted foraging spaces that can carry dissolved toxins. Invasive plants commonly grow in riparian areas, with their fruits, leaves, and wood falling into streams throughout the year. Fruits of the chinaberry tree (Melia azedarach), which is invasive in many parts of the world, commonly fall into streams in great numbers. Additionally, these berries carry toxins known to affect a diversity of vertebrates. Using native N. erythrogaster and N. rhombifer from Texas, we tested whether the presence of chinaberry fruits affected snake feeding in lab trials. While these species prefer different relative sizes of fish, their responses to the presence of chinaberries was similar. Unlike animals that are restricted to life in water, snakes may choose to forage in new areas, potentially upsetting predator-prey relationships in contaminated systems.
Techniques in Ecology and Evolution / Conservation & Management I
2606: In 2019, a single Rio Cauca Caecilian (Typhlonectes natans) was captured in a canal in Miami-Dade County, Florida, representing the first record of a wild caecilian in the United States. Many individuals have since been detected throughout the canal system, generating potential for new lines of research concerning the reproductive ecology and impacts of the introduced caecilian population. Here, we 1) characterized the reproductive status of introduced T. natans in south Florida by examining the development of sex organs, 2) calculated the relationship between body condition and reproductive effort in females by counting and assessing the developmental state of ovarian follicles, and lastly, 3) evaluated the potential of T. natans to carry common amphibian pathogens. In total, we necropsied 76 T. natans collected from south Florida, and screened 77 skin swabs to detect the presence and intensity of Ranavirus and Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis using qPCR. We found a positive correlation between female snout-to-vent length and total follicle count. Further, we found that numerous caecilians tested positive for infection with Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis. Our findings provide insight into the ability of T. natans to reproduce in south Florida, as well as their potential role as a vector of emerging pathogens to native amphibians.
Techniques in Ecology and Evolution / Conservation & Management I
2607: Invasive species are top contributors to biodiversity loss and pose major threats to ecosystems. Biological invasions cost billions of dollars annually in damages and control efforts aimed at restoring ecological communities and conserving declining species. However, efforts to reduce invasive species often fail without a comprehensive understanding of how specific actions contribute to sustainable population control and recovery of native species. Predictive models are valuable tools for analyzing invasive species dynamics over time and can evaluate how specific management actions reduce invasive populations to support native species recovery. Channel Catfish (Ictalurus punctatus) have thrived as an invasive species in the San Juan River for decades despite mechanical removal efforts resulting in a need to assess population dynamics and identify new strategies for effective management. We used a catch-at-age model to estimate changes in age-specific Channel Catfish abundance over three decades of removal efforts and to explore the effectiveness of alternative control strategies. Our model revealed substantial variation in catfish abundance throughout the removal period, with a three-fold increase in the first 14 years, followed by a gradual decline when efforts were intensified. Gear selectivity was highest for larger fish, resulting in a shift in age structure. Increased discharge and temperature marginally reduced recruitment. Future projections suggest that removal effort intensity would need to increase by at least 5x to reduce biomass to 15% of the current population within 10 years. Future control projects should consider fitting population models as early as data are available to guide large-scale management efforts.
Techniques in Ecology and Evolution / Conservation & Management I
2608: Environmental DNA (eDNA) sampling often requires a single sample collected at one point in time—a snapshot approach that provides limited information on biodiversity across temporal scales. To address this limitation, water samples were collected over 25 hours from a single site on the Tangipahoa River in Louisiana, utilizing both active and passive sampling methods. Active sampling involved taking water samples from a predefined location every hour for 25 hours, while passive sampling included deploying a stationary sampling device for the same duration. All water samples were filtered using glass microfiber filters, extracted, PCR amplified (12S mtDNA), and sequenced using Illumina technology following a pre-established protocol. The methods used for eDNA detection produced varying species richness metrics, with active sampling identifying 60 species compared to 37 species from passive sampling. On average, active sampling detected fewer species (mean 19, range 2–45) from a single hourly sample than the cumulative findings from passive sampling (totaling 37). Through an analysis of similarities clustering analysis, patterns associated with the time of day—civil twilight (daylight) versus dark (night)—showed significant differences (p=0.018), although the distinction between the clusters was weak (R-stat=0.1779). These findings underscore the importance of considering the timing of active eDNA sample collection and highlight the need for passive eDNA sampling methods when studying fish assemblages. This study illustrates the complexities involved in eDNA-based fish assemblage assessments and emphasizes the necessity of further research to optimize methodologies for accurate biodiversity monitoring.
Techniques in Ecology and Evolution / Conservation & Management I
2609: Fiber tracking algorithms have steadily gained usage in biological sciences to measure muscle architecture in CT data and quantify parameters such as fiber lengths, orientations, and curvature. These methods have increasingly been used to quantity muscle architecture in taxa such as crocodilians, squamates, frogs, and ray finned fish. Two fiber tracking algorithms prominent in biological sciences are Avizo Xfiber and the Goodfibes package for R. Xfiber is an extension of the Avizo 3D imaging analysis platform that has been successfully applied to a variety of taxa, but it has a high initial cost and requires high-end computer hardware to run effectively. Goodfibes is an open-source package for the free and commonly used R environment that can run on consumer hardware. However, it currently has limitations on measuring certain muscle morphologies and natively reports fewer quantitative measures than Xfiber. Most studies comparing muscle architecture measures from DiceCT have used 2 shared datasets. However, two datasets cannot capture the spectrum of morphologies or data quality that researchers are likely to encounter. Here we compare Xfiber and Goodfibes muscle architectural measurements on a variety of DiceCT datasets that are relevant to herpetological and ichthyological morphology. These datasets vary in parameters such as pennation and resolution, including the parallel fibered mPPT of a black ratsnake and jaw muscles of the same individual alligator at different resolutions. We have found that these tools produce similar results for simply structured muscles, such as the mPPT. However, Xfiber is better at tracing strongly curved fibers.
Techniques in Ecology and Evolution / Conservation & Management I
2610: Global disease surveillance shows spikes in disease outbreaks affecting multiple host species and spanning unprecedented geographic distances. This upsurge highlights the need to predict and mediate host-pathogen dynamics across diverse host communities. In addition, co-infection by multiple pathogens and interactions between pathogenic and mutualistic microbial communities can mediate disease outcomes and transmission among hosts. This is especially true in hyper-diverse tropical communities where the biggest knowledge gaps are and where herpetological diversity is most at risk. Consequently, community ecology has become an invaluable framework to investigate complex, multi-species host-pathogen dynamics across multiple scales of biological organization. This symposium will bring together an international group of herpetologists, disease biologists, and quantitative ecologists to create a forum for discussing recent progress in monitoring, forecasting, and managing disease outbreaks across diverse herpetofauna.
Thriving in a changing world: host-pathogen dynamics in hyperdiverse communities of amphibians and reptiles (SSAR)
2611: The fungal pathogen Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (Bd) has caused severe amphibian declines worldwide. These declines peaked in the 1980s, but because Bd was not described until 1998, our understanding of Bd’s panzootic emergence is largely inferred from museum specimens and historical records of amphibian decline. Such a decline was observed between 1979 and 1982 in Brazil’s Atlantic Forest, where Ronald Heyer documented drastic amphibian declines at the Boracéia Biological Station and collected nearly 1,300 frogs now accessioned at the Smithsonian. These specimens span pre- and post-decline periods, offering a unique opportunity to investigate Bd’s role in the decline. Previously, Brazil’s amphibian declines have proven difficult to link to Bd and conflicting studies propose two hypotheses: (1) Bd is a long-term endemic of the Atlantic Forest, or (2) Bd was introduced more recently, coinciding with global amphibian declines. To test these hypotheses, we swabbed 328 museum-preserved frogs collected in Boracéia and used qPCR and histopathology to assess historical Bd infection. Strikingly, no frogs from the pre-decline period were infected, while 58.8% of frogs from the post-decline were infected. Bd prevalence differed between species inferred as decline-positive versus decline-negative. To assess Bd lineage diversity, we applied a SNP-based PCR assay and genome-scale target capture to both museum and modern samples. We detected Bd-GPL and Bd-Brazil lineages in the post-decline specimens, and evidence of coinfection and rampant hybridization in modern samples. Our findings do not support long-term Bd endemism in Boracéia and instead suggest that Bd was introduced around 1979, strongly implicating Bd in the observed decline.
Thriving in a changing world: host-pathogen dynamics in hyperdiverse communities of amphibians and reptiles (SSAR)
2612: Amphibians face one of the most virulent global threats, chytridiomycosis, caused by the fungus Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (Bd). This pathogen drives the decline and extinction of several species worldwide. While commonly associated with aquatic breeding frogs, terrestrial breeding frogs may also play a crucial role in disease spillover, facilitating Bd transmission in tropical forests. This study aims to assess the environmental factors influencing Bd prevalence in multi-host terrestrial breeding frog communities in the mountain forests near Manu National Park in Peru. We evaluated whether environmental factors, including soil pH, C, N, and P concentrations, canopy coverage, herbaceous and moss coverage, and proximity to water bodies, influenced Bd prevalence along 12 forest transects. We hypothesized that pH and humidity would be the principal factors determining changes in Bd prevalence. Our results indicate that Bd infection dynamics are complex, influenced by host species, local habitat characteristics, and various landscape variables at smaller spatial scales. Additionally, Bd prevalence shows a weak negative correlation with the variables N and C. Understanding the environmental factors associated with Bd infections can provide valuable insights to mitigate the spread of the disease. These findings may help inform conservation strategies, particularly for endemic species, and contribute to more effective management plans.
Thriving in a changing world: host-pathogen dynamics in hyperdiverse communities of amphibians and reptiles (SSAR)
2613: The amphibian-killing fungus (Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis [Bd]) has been described as the most devastating wildlife pathogen known to date. Globally, incredible efforts to detect the pathogen and characterize isolates have been carried out by scientists over the past two decades. However, many regions of the world, and the amphibian habitats within them, still lack robust surveillance efforts. Neotropical habitats, such as Ecuadorian forests, support hyperdiverse amphibian assemblages, and thus, are prime targets for community-wide Bd surveillance in a post-invasion scenario. Yet, major factors affecting host sampling efforts include remote field sites, difficult to access habitats (e.g., forest canopies), or technical challenges related to the limited availability of genetic instrumentation. Ongoing sampling across multiple sites in Ecuador demonstrates how leveraging portable genetic instruments can help amphibian biologists more rapidly measure Bd presence/absence and infection intensity. The occurrence of Bd was detected across multiple host taxa and habitat types, suggesting a much wider distribution in Ecuador than previously perceived.
Thriving in a changing world: host-pathogen dynamics in hyperdiverse communities of amphibians and reptiles (SSAR)
2614: Amphibian declines worldwide have been significant in neotropical mountains. The primary causes of these declines include habitat loss, climate change, and wildlife diseases. However, different amphibian communities along climatic gradients may exhibit different extinction causes, risks, and adaptive capacities. One of the most studied altitudinal gradients in the Neotropics is the San Marcos, Guatemala transect. This transect made possible the comparisons of amphibian populations and chytrid presence from 1970 to 2009, which shed light on the enigmatic decline of salamanders. The main cause seems to be related to the synergy between habitat loss and the arrival of the chytrid fungus in the 1980s. After four decades of chytrid fungus presence, we evaluated with a multi-species occupancy model approach the current status of amphibian populations, chytrid infection, and its association with forest canopy, slope, altitude, and water presence along this gradient. As expected, altitude explained amphibian species occupancy in the gradient, whereas canopy cover and slope did not. Low amphibian detection probabilities were associated with higher altitudes in pristine and secondary pine-cypress forests. However, we rediscovered a population of Plectrohyla glandulosa in a secondary pine forest. This species populations were considered extinct in the Pacific volcanic chain region. In general, high prevalence and low infection of the chytrid fungus were detected in cloud forest amphibian species breeding aquatically, showing similar trends to reported amphibians' prevalences. On the other hand, direct-developer salamanders and frogs had lower chytrid prevalence. Habitat loss is still a threat to the upper gradient amphibian populations.
Thriving in a changing world: host-pathogen dynamics in hyperdiverse communities of amphibians and reptiles (SSAR)
2615: Male secondary sexual traits in frogs provide an opportunity for integrating phylogenetic, behavioral, anatomical, genetic, and other tools to study morphological novelties. Here, I will present what is known of the elongate third finger in males of the African frog genera Arthroleptis and Cardioglossa (family Arthroleptidae). Hyperelongation of the third manual digit evolved in the ancestor of these two genera and was both elaborated and reduced multiple times. Males of at least two species are known to use these digits in male-male wrestling, including rapidly vibrating and wiping the fingers across the dorsum of competing males. The elongation of this digit is associated with sexual maturity and is hypothesized to be driven by androgens. Elongation of the distal cartilaginous epiphysis of the phalanges, metacarpal, and radioulna contribute to creating a longer forearm and third finger. This hypertrophy and subsequent ossification create a composite skeletal element that is unique among anurans, and likely co-opts existing developmental mechanisms. I will present preliminary evidence for how these bones experience stress and how their associated muscles differ from other frogs, as well as a hypothesis for why larger bodied species exhibit limited sexual dimorphism in the third finger. An integrated, organismal approach allows us to begin making sense of the evolution and function of novel traits in these poorly studied frogs.
2616: At macroevolutionary scales and across species, levels of sexual dimorphism often covary with body size, generating allometric trends. While such patterns are most evident for sexual size dimorphism, interspecific trends in sexual shape dimorphism remain underexamined. Furthermore, how such patterns are affected by miniaturization is largely unknown. In this study, we evaluated trends in sexual shape dimorphism across 99 gecko species from two families, to determine whether miniaturization was associated with increased shape dimorphism in the group. First, geometric morphometric methods were used to characterize head shape from surface scans of nearly 600 individuals, and levels of sexual shape dimorphism were quantified for each species. Phylogenetic comparative analyses were then used to evaluate evolutionary patterns of shape dimorphism relative to body size across species. We found strong interspecific allometry of sexual shape dimorphism with body size, where smaller bodied species displayed greater levels of head shape dimorphism. Additionally, interspecific patterns differed between the two families, with strong negative allometry observed in Sphaeorodactylidae (a family with many miniaturized species), while in Phyllodactylidae (a family containing few miniaturized species) patterns were more isometric with no discernable trend. Notably, the greater sexual shape dimorphism displayed by miniaturized species corresponded with females exhibiting more robust heads, which was consistent with sex-specific foraging strategies and dietary differences observed in this group. Our study reveals that interspecific allometry in traits other than body size can have a pervasive influence patterns of phenotypic diversity across the tree of life.
2617: Cichlid fishes (Cichlidae) are a celebrated system in evolutionary research with impressive diversity, broad geographic distribution, and well-studied natural history that make them textbook subjects in evolutionary biology. Yet, despite their “iconic” status, cichlid age estimates vary widely, with large uncertainty within and widespread incongruence among studies. A fundamental reason for these disagreements is the lack of a morphological framework within which to phylogenetically interpret and place the cichlid fossil record. Without a robust age estimate for cichlids, we are limited in our ability to discern the patterns of cichlid divergence and understand the underlying processes leading to their extraordinary evolutionary history. We present the first family-wide matrix of cichlid osteology and squamation (145 characters for 113 living and 22 fossil taxa) built from examining specimens of living and fossil cichlids, complemented with coding of fossil descriptions from the literature. Maximum Likelihood (ML) analyses demonstrate the value of this new dataset in enhancing clade diagnosability and fossil placement across cichlids in a total evidence context with genomic data for 299 species of living cichlids. We find that age estimates under ML are highly sensitive to the number of fossils included in the analyses. We also present preliminary results of Bayesian Total Evidence dating using Fossilized Birth Death models that simultaneously integrate phylogenetic analyses and fossil placement into new estimates of cichlid age, quantitatively incorporating time and rate uncertainty into phylogenetic estimates for the family.
2618: Biofluorescence (absorption of high-energy light and reemission at lower energy wavelengths) and bioluminescence (production and emission of light by a living organism) are widespread across the tree of life, and especially prevalent in fishes. These traits evolved numerous times across fishes and play key roles in their diversification. There are few studies that have investigated the intersection of the two, where organisms use their own higher-energy bioluminescent emissions to excite fluorophores, creating fluorescent emissions of lower-energy wavelengths of light. We investigate this phenomenon in the bioluminescent ponyfishes (Leiognathidae); an ideal study system to assess the interaction of bioluminescence and biofluorescence as ponyfishes are abundant, live in near-shore areas of the Indo-Pacific, and have registered bioluminescent wavelength readings. Using blue light in four discrete wavelength categories associated with known bioluminescent light we analyzed 15 of 51 species of fresh ponyfishes. We found one species, Deveximentum ruconius, to be biofluorescent. Emitted light ocured in the wavelengths of 515-520 nm, with a shoulder at 535-550 nm (green). Biofluorescence occurred under excitation light of 460 nm and 482 nm but not under 500 nm or 513 nm. This is in line with the wavelengths emitted by their symbiotic bioluminescent bacteria, which emit at ~480 nm. This is the first evidence of biofluorescence in Leiognathidae and one of only two other instances of possible bioluminescence-induced fluorescence in fishes. These findings continue to add to the important body of work investigating the complexities of signaling and communication in the marine environment.
2619: The Axillary Lymphoid Organ (ALO) is the fleshy lobe immediately above the pectoral fin in the Zebrafish, Danio rerio.  The ALO emerges comparatively late in development and is not found in embryonic or larval Zebrafish. A discrete immune system function for the ALO has recently been described. The ALO is a translucent organ with an outer cortex with immune cells, an inner medulla with a mesh-like network of fibroblastic reticular cells along which immune cells migrate, and a network of lymphatic vessels draining to a large adjacent lymph sac. The ALO is easily removed for analysis or as a source of genetic material and regenerates within two weeks following removal. A survey of museum specimens of an array of teleost taxa revealed a diversity of pectoral lobe morphologies, with some fish species possessing substantially larger or more elaborate structures than the ALO of the Zebrafish. We infer an immune system function for the pectoral lobe in other teleosts, which is open to test. The pectoral lobe is found in basal teleosts such as the Tarpon, Megalops atlanticus, osteoglossiforms, and other ostariophysans. It is absent in higher teleosts such as the Medaka, Oryzias latipes, Fugu, Takifugu rupripes, and the Three-spined stickleback, Gasterosteus aculeatus.  The distribution of the pectoral lobe evokes the distribution of the adipose fin—a somewhat fleshy dorsal fin of unclear function.
2620: Adaptation and modularity are two major features of morphological evolution that are increasingly investigated by modern macroevolutionary biologists. However, many such studies assume that adaptive processes or modularity are constant across species. Evolution of morphology and its modularity both relate to the ecological role of morphological traits. Here, we investigate whether morphological adaptation and modularity vary across families of the Neotropical superfamily Doradoidea, comprising the Aspredinidae (banjo catfishes), Auchenipteridae (driftwood catfishes), and Doradidae (thorny catfishes). We quantified morphological diversity using three-dimensional geometric morphometrics and estimated evolutionary rates, shifts between adaptive regimes, and evolutionary modularity and integration differences among families. We found that doradoids diversified into nine adaptive regimes across morphospace. We also found some significant differences in modularity and integration between families. Major morphological shifts have surprising correspondence to previously or currently recognized taxa within the Doradoidea. We found repeated, parallel evolution of body elongation across adaptive regimes, implying a role for selection in driving parallel evolution across a primary axis of shape diversification. However, modularity and integration do not necessarily shift in correspondence with shifts in morphological adaptive peaks.
2621: Most tetrapods have relatively impermeable skin, sacrificing permeability for protection and water retention. Amphibians occupy the other end of this spectrum, with more permeable skin that allows cutaneous respiration but increases vulnerability to desiccation, physical damage, pollutants, and disease (e.g. fungal susceptibility). However, anuran species show striking variation in many skin features that are hypothesized to affect anuran gas exchange and water loss rates. The importance and variability of amphibian skin texture has long been recognized but is typically categorized into a few groups, such as "smooth," "tuberculated," "granular," "warty," etc. Our study aims to move beyond these categorical descriptions to quantify external skin variation in an efficient and reproducible manner. We are building a global database of skin texture photos and data for hundreds of species using museum specimens. In addition to building this resources, we are use these new skin texture data to test whether skin varies in association with a species’ microhabitat, climate or body size. In total, our study provides a way to measure and compare skin texture among anuran species and studies and begins to test whether amphibian skin has evolved in ways that allow anurans to thrive in a range of climates across the globe.
2622: Information on reproduction in white sharks Carcharodon carcharias is critical for estimating rates of population growth and improving the management and conservation of this globally vulnerable species. However, because of their large size, low abundance, and broad oceanic distribution, it is often difficult to obtain reproductive data from white sharks, especially females, which lack external indicators of sexual maturity and reproductive status. In this study, we used the two nonlethal approaches of blood hormone analysis and transcutaneous ultrasonography to examine sexual maturity and reproductive stage in female white sharks sampled via catch-and-release fishing. Female white sharks ranging in size from 152-501 cm total length were sampled from western North Atlantic waters between Nova Scotia, Canada and Jacksonville, FL, USA from 2012 to 2024. Size measurements, blood sampling, and ultrasonography were performed. Ultrasound images of the reproductive system were used to evaluate ovarian development and pregnancy status, while blood was used to measure plasma concentrations of the gonadal steroid hormone, 17β-estradiol, which is known to increase during sexual maturity and the preovulatory period in female sharks. A significant increase in the variability of plasma estradiol concentrations was observed in individuals ranging in size from 317-379 cm TL, suggesting that this is the period of sexual maturation. Ultrasonography images also show evidence of ovarian growth in females at ~380 cm TL, suggesting that females likely mature between 400-425 cm TL. Data pertaining to male white shark reproductive activity based on measurements of plasma testosterone are also presented.
2623: The southern stingray, Hypanus americanus, is a common coastal ray in the western North Atlantic, ranging from the United States to Brazil, including the Gulf of Mexico and Caribbean Sea, and is an important resource for ecotourism in the Bahamas and Cayman Islands. It is a hardy, long-lived species that commonly reproduces in human care. Though many aspects of its life history have been described from natural and fabricated habitats, the mating system is not well understood. While behavioral polyandry has been documented in southern stingrays, genetic polyandry, or multiple paternity, has not been reported. The goal of this investigation was to document multiple paternity based upon a population of 23 reproductively active southern stingrays at the National Aquarium in 2005 with the data set examined in 2017. Amplicon deep-sequencing using next generation sequencing (NGS) technology was used to determine multiple paternity. The two-step PCR approach combined Illumina’s dual indexing strategy and species-specific primers. Results confirmed multiple paternity, and that two to three potential sires were involved. Since it was documented in this group of rays, it is likely to occur in wild conspecifics given the similar polyandrous mating events. Although the southern stingray is not a species of concern for extinction, it is an important consideration for population management. This investigation provided the first documented case of multiple paternity in a dasyatid ray, and only the second case in a viviparous batoid.
2624: There are national, regional, and local networks that coordinate responses to injured or deceased marine wildlife, mostly marine mammals and turtles. However, in Florida, there is currently no statewide protocol to respond to injured or deceased sharks. The Florida Fish and Wildlife Research Institute manages the Fish Kill Hotline (FKH), a public-facing reporting tool that can alert FWC biologists about shark mortalities, but they often have limited capacity to physically respond to the average 71 reports they receive per year. A shark stranding or mortality event can involve multiple agencies, departments, and officials, causing confusion, resulting in the animal’s disposal before samples can be collected. ASC created the Shark Reporting and Response Network (SRRN) to help build the capacity to respond, collect samples, and disseminate those samples to appropriate facilities for research. We have responded to 36 stranding reports over the past three years along Florida’s southeast coastline, including two pregnant great hammerhead sharks (Sphyrna mokarran), tiger shark (Galeocerdo cuvier), lemon shark (Negaprion brevirostris), blacktip shark (Carcharhinus limbatus), and a small tooth sawfish (Pristis pectinata). We have built a network of turtle surveyors, anglers, ocean rescue personnel, and others to report to the FKH and ASC. The value of building out a coordinated effort in responding to these events allows for the collection of samples that would otherwise require lethal sampling, but can afford critical insights into the individual’s cause of death as well as insights into the growth, diet, reproduction, and habitat use of the species.
2625: Global concern about the conservation status of the white shark, Carcharodon carcharias, has afforded the species a relatively high degree of national and international protection. In the US Atlantic, it has been designated a prohibited species by the federal government and coastal states since 1997. However, white sharks still face numerous and evolving threats including vessel strikes which may represent a previously overlooked source of mortality for the species. Though there is documented evidence of injuries and healed scars from boat strikes on white sharks throughout the species’ range, how they occur is currently not well understood. To characterize the behavioral response of sharks to approaching boats, we conducted a series of experimental approaches and collected drone footage of the shark’s behavior before, during, and after each trial. Sharks were approached from different directions and at different speeds reflective of actual marine traffic conditions to evaluate whether these factors influence their ability to detect and evade approaching boats. Preliminary results from 20 trials conducted off the coast of Cape Cod, Massachusetts, during the summer and fall of 2024 suggest that speed (> 15 kts), rather than direction, may elicit stronger reactions from sharks. Very few individuals exhibited a reaction that would adequately evade an actual oncoming boat, which provides insight into how collisions between boats and white sharks occur.
2626: Largetooth sawfish (Pristis pristis) are an endangered ray with a rostrum containing a large number of teeth. Due to population declines, live fish are difficult to study and track, limiting our understanding of their life history and behavior. Largetooth sawfish use habitat across a range of salinities, including fully fresh water. They are known to pup in freshwater, presumably to avoid predation, however their movement ecology is poorly understood outside of their stronghold in Australia. The Brazilian Amazon coast is considered the last remaining stronghold of largetooth sawfish in the Americas, but very little is known about their distribution, abundance, or movement in this region. Trace element chemistry in fish hard parts has revolutionized our understanding of migration and movement in bony fishes and increasingly in elasmobranchs. Sawfish rostral teeth grow throughout their life, making them a unique hard structure in an elasmobranch that can record chemical changes through time and across salinity. Rostra are often preserved, providing a potential archive of movement that are more accessible to study than live fish. In this study we examined rostral teeth from 121 largetooth sawfish from the Brazilian Amazon coast, for trace-element and isotopic chemistry using LA-ICPMS. Isotopic data shows for the first time the movements of Brazilian sawfish in and out of fresh water using Sr/Ca and Ba/Ca ratios, as well as river 87Sr/86Sr signatures in fresh water. This data also shows indications of habitat associations during early life and the timing of ontogenetic shifts. This data shows for the first time the range of life history exhibited by sub-adult sawfish using the detailed chemical and isotopic data preserved in rostral teeth.
2627: Tropical freshwater fishes frequently encounter hypoxia, driving the evolution of diverse adaptations, including modifications to gill morphology that increase branchial surface area. Yet, the evolutionary basis of these traits remains poorly understood. The Neotropical electric knifefish family Hypopomidae, which inhabits environments spanning a broad range of dissolved oxygen (DO) conditions, provides a valuable model for investigating these patterns. Using phylogenetic comparative methods, we analyzed three gill traits—mean filament length, mean hemibranch length, and total filament number—across 27 hypopomid species. Species specialized to hypoxic habitats exhibited significantly greater mean filament length, even after phylogenetic correction, suggesting an adaptive response to low DO. By contrast, species restricted to normoxic habitats had lower filament length, consistent with potential trade-offs involving developmental costs and structural or physiological constraints. Many hypopomid species are eurytopic, with demes occupying both hypoxic and normoxic systems; hypoxia-tolerant demes also exhibit elevated filament length, suggesting a shared morphological basis for hypoxia tolerance that spans both population-level variation and species-level divergence. Ancestral state reconstructions indicate that species with elevated filament length evolved from normoxia-adapted ancestors and that a major transition in gill morphology and habitat use occurred at the base of the Brachyhypopomus beebei group. This transition, dated to approximately 4 Ma, coincides with the Pliocene expansion of seasonally hypoxic Amazon whitewater floodplains, likely driven by increased Andean sedimentation. Our findings suggest that ancient environmental shifts promoted ecomorphological innovation in hypopomids, shaping respiratory phenotypes and potentially accelerating lineage diversification.
2628: Increasing frequency of heat waves, not just warmer overall environmental temperatures, is a signature feature of ongoing climate change. Heat waves exert adverse impacts on populations, communities, and ecosystems of a variety of biota. In globally-imperiled turtles with temperature-dependent sex determination, warmer temperatures should produce an excess of female offspring, potentially leading to long-term demographic collapse. Yet, temperature spikes in turtle embryonic development could be problematic in more immediate ways. Using experimental manipulation, we show that heat waves during key periods of embryonic development substantially increase the frequency of shell scute abnormalities in slider turtles (Trachemys scripta). Anatomical assays confirm that a considerable fraction of these scute anomalies reflect underlying skeletal malformations. In turn, large-scale field experiments link these abnormalities to reduced survival of neonates during the key life-stage of their journey from nest to water. Moreover, long-term capture-mark-recapture fieldwork further detects that the frequency of slider turtles with scute anomalies declines with age, implying ongoing adverse impacts on survival through maturity and thereafter. In sum, an increase in environmentally-induced frequency of this deleterious trait should reduce population-level fitness in turtles.
2629: Understanding the mechanisms of speciation and adaptation is a fundamental question in biology that also provides an opportunity to uncover new gene functions of clinical relevance. Highly conserved genetic regulatory pathways shared across diverse vertebrate species have been shaped by adaptive evolution to produce spectacular morphological, behavioral, and ecological diversity. Here I review a decade of my lab’s work investigating the rapid evolutionary transition from generalist algae-eating pupfishes to trophic specialists endemic to hypersaline lakes of San Salvador Island in the Bahamas and Laguna Chichancanab, Mexico. We show that colonizing these niches occurred in stages, beginning with selection on standing genetic variation for feeding behavior, then aided by adaptive introgression from diverse sources, and ending with selection on de novo mutations in key craniofacial genes. We discovered that only 157 single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and 87 deletions are fixed between scale-eating and molluscivore specialists despite extensive phenotypic divergence in their craniofacial morphology, metabolism, and behavior. These few differences resulted in major transitions in ecological niches and the colonization of new fitness peaks and novel performance optima for scale-biting. Overall, our work provides a new microevolutionary framework for investigating how major ecological transitions occur in nature and illustrates how both shared and unique genetic variation contributes to diversification and provides a path through complex fitness landscapes for access to novel ecological niches.
2630: Identifying the molecular mechanisms underlying adaptive phenotypic changes is essential for understanding species divergence. The visual system is an ideal model for studying these adaptations due to the well-documented genetic basis of its characters and their adaptive consequences. While many environmental factors shape visual systems, most studies have concentrated solely on the role of light. This leaves critical gaps in understanding how multiple selective forces interact and shape visual systems. In aquatic systems, depth is a strong predictor of visual evolution because light availability decreases rapidly with increased depth. However, depth is also correlated with other factors, such as hydrostatic pressure, that also strongly affect vision but are often overlooked. To evaluate how multiple selective forces shape visual systems, we use 107 genomes from a diverse genus of marine fishes (Rockfish; Sebastes). We analyze sequence and expression-level variation in opsins — the proteins responsible for detecting specific wavelengths of light. We use a phylogenetic comparative approach to (a) test for changes in amino acid sequences and gene expression that tune visual systems to the available light spectrum and (b) examine amino acid sequences that enhance protein stability and reduce protein compressibility under high hydrostatic pressure. We present preliminary findings on how the rod opsin (RH1) and one cone opsin (LWS) respond to these selective forces through changes in amino acid sequence. Understanding how visual systems in rockfish simultaneously respond to different environmental factors will help identify general patterns of opsin, visual system, and species diversification across aquatic taxa.
2631: Catfish species in the genus Ictalurus (family Ictaluridae) are commercially and recreationally important fishes in the United States. Densities of Blue Catfish (I. furcatus) and Channel Catfish (I. punctatus) are high within Lake Maurepas (Louisiana), but there has been little investigation into the population dynamics and structure within the lake. Future plans are to construct a nearby clean energy complex that will utilize carbon capture and sequestration in the production of hydrogen and permanently store the carbon dioxide by-product in bedrock formations miles below Lake Maurepas. Considering the commercial and recreational importance of these catfish species, it is crucial to understand the baseline levels of genetic variability and structure among populations of these fishes. Herein we present the initial baseline genetic assessment using thousands of single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) genotyped from ddRAD sequences. Samples of Blue Catfish (n = 90) and Channel Catfish (n = 85) were collected from Lake Maurepas and the three major rivers that flow into the lake (Tickfaw, Amite, and Blind rivers). We also opportunistically examined levels of natural introgression between species. Blue and Channel catfishes are consistently artificially hybridized in hatcheries to yield traits desirable for food production, but few studies have demonstrated natural hybridization in the wild. Our results provide valuable insights into genetic diversity and structure and levels of introgression for these catfish species and provides a baseline for future studies of gene flow and genetic structure following the implementation of this large industrial project.
Conservation & Management II / Conservation Ecology and Genetics I
2632: Cuatrociénegas, in the Chihuahuan Desert of northern Mexico, is the world’s most biodiverse spring-based wetland and a federally protected area. However, water-level declines linked to largescale regional groundwater extraction, mostly for agriculture, in adjacent valleys that contribute to the valley’s aquifer clearly imminently threaten sustainability. At the same time, the area has transformed into a popular tourism destination, with rapid and massive expansion of the hotel industry and visitation. Two of the primary developers established non-profit foundations with conservation- and community-support objectives and are working together with the Federal Reserve System (CONANP), local conservation groups, regional universities, and the municipal government to assure that development is sustainable and compatible with biodiversity conservation. While aquifer management is clearly a high priority, many unknowns continue to impede develop and implementation of plans to accomplish that. At the same time, much research is still needed to improve knowledge of basic ecology and genetics of its highly endemic, diverse and endangered fish and herpetofaunas, not to mention many invertebrates and plants. There are new initiatives working to support field and laboratory research, as well as establishment of captive breeding programs. There will be opportunities for others to become involved in research and conservation efforts, and the Desert Fishes Council (https://www.desertfishes.org/) meeting in Cuatrociénegas in November of this year will provide opportunities to learn more about that.
Conservation & Management II / Conservation Ecology and Genetics I
2633: Amplified wildfire activity in western U.S. forests threatens biodiversity, yet the impacts of some fuels treatments, including slash piling and burning, have received little attention. Piling of wood from forest thinning activities may create suitable conditions for species that require cool, moist microclimates. Sacramento Mountain Salamanders (Aneides hardii), endemic to the mountains of south-central New Mexico, have been found beneath slash piles, but the extent of their occupancy by salamanders has not yet been evaluated. We quantified slash pile structure and fuel characteristics, compared soil moisture and soil temperature beneath slash piles and under nearby logs, and surveyed for salamanders in slash piles, under nearby logs, and under logs within a 1.4 ha area encompassing all slash piles. We found Sacramento Mountain Salamanders in 50% of surveyed slash piles. Pile characteristics, environmental setting, soil temperature, and soil moisture did not differ between piles occupied by salamanders and piles in which no salamanders were detected. Salamander density was highest in slash piles, nearly 10% lower under logs in the 1.4 ha surrounding the piles, and nearly 23% lower under logs nearby piles. Evidence from this study and detections of this species into mid-October indicate that pile burning is best initiated in late fall, when most salamanders are likely to have retreated below the ground surface. Constructing smaller, pyramidal piles and restricting residence time of piles on the landscape may limit their suitability as habitat, reducing the potential for adverse impacts on salamander populations when piles are burned.
Conservation & Management II / Conservation Ecology and Genetics I
2634: Ecological connectivity is critical to the survival and long-term viability of populations but is often overlooked in regulatory frameworks. We integrated landscape-level processes into a mitigation strategy for impacts to aquatic resources on the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) OakRidge Reservation (ORR) in eastern Tennessee. Wetlands on the ORR, which contain significant breeding populations of the imperiled Four-toed Salamander (Hemidactylium scutatum), will be impacted by construction of an environmental waste disposal facility. We emphasized habitat connectivity through models that prioritized an area’s importance to natural area connectivity and maintenance of population structure for an affected habitat specialist (Four-toed Salamanders). We also emphasized in-kind mitigation through the preservation and enhancement of ecologically similar resources and the translocation and establishment of a new subpopulation of four-toed salamanders elsewhere on the ORR. We translocated dozens of four-toed salamander nests, reared larvae in a unique outdoor mesocosm setup, and we ultimately released over 500 juvenile salamanders that originated from the impacted site into the chosen mitigation wetlands. This study helps show that ecological connectivity and the conservation of species that are not afforded explicit regulatory processes can be effectively and efficiently integrated into environmental decision-making and land use planning.
Conservation & Management II / Conservation Ecology and Genetics I
2635: Eurycea tonkawae (Jollyville Plateau salamander) is a fully aquatic neotenic salamander endemic to springs, spring-fed streams, and groundwater flow paths in the Austin, Texas metropolitan area. Because much of the range of E. tonkawae occurs in a developed urban area, infrastructure projects for stormwater conveyance, flood abatement, water and wastewater transport, transportation, and others have the potential to impact salamander habitat in urban streams. Our goal was to estimate rates of occupancy in tributaries throughout the salamander’s range, including those in highly developed watersheds. We conducted area-constrained surveys across 17 tributaries, with the goal of better delineating the range of the Jollyville Plateau Salamander and identifying important predictors of species occurrence. We fit a Royle-Nichols model to our repeated presence-absence data in order to describe the distribution of salamanders among sites while accounting for the impacts of detection covariates on the observation process. Jollyville Plateau Salamanders were detected at 107 of 311 survey sites included in this study. Based on our results, occupied habitat is likely to coincide with areas near municipal infrastructure that is placed in or near streams, as all surveyed tributaries in developed watersheds have predicted rates of occupancy ranging from 27 to 71%. At the same time, urban cover was negatively correlated with salamander abundance. Our study shows the prevalence of E. tonkawae throughout urban tributaries while indicating there are ample opportunities for conservation. These may serve as mitigation for projects that would otherwise harm salamanders to potentially satisfy regulatory requirements for the Endangered Species Act.
Conservation & Management II / Conservation Ecology and Genetics I
2636: Invasive species can impact native species indirectly by introducing novel pathogens or altering the epidemiology of resident pathogens. However, few studies have explored whether the introduction of amphibians causes shifts in community-wide infection dynamics. Here we assessed spatiotemporal trends in the dynamics of three amphibian pathogens in a recent invasion of Cuban treefrogs, Osteopilus septentrionalis, in Louisiana, USA. We collected toe clips from 555 O. septentrionalis and 266 resident anurans around the greater New Orleans area from September 2017 to August 2023. We attempted to sample 15 O. septentrionalis from the primary invasion range each month, and we concurrently sampled resident anurans across both invaded and non-invaded locations to determine the impact of invasion on the community. We extracted DNA and used pathogen-specific qPCR protocols to determine pathogen presence and intensity for each individual. Overall, 48/821 tested positive for Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (Bd), 204/821 tested positive for Ranavirus (Rv), and 106/821 individuals tested positive for Amphibian Perkinsea (Pr). Across our entire sampling period, we observed no difference in body condition by infection status (p > 0.067) or intensity (p > 0.07) within O. septentrionalis, implying this species likely serves as a pathogen reservoir. We also did not observe any significant differences within resident anurans between invaded and non-invaded sites for Bd, or Pr; however, there is a slight trend (p = 0.059) towards higher Rv prevalence in locations with O. septentrionalis. This study highlights the importance of monitoring pathogen dynamics in both the invader and native community beyond the initial invasion.
Thriving in a changing world: host-pathogen dynamics in hyperdiverse communities of amphibians and reptiles (SSAR)
2637: Pathogens interact with complex microbiomes at host mucosal surfaces, yet little is known about how these microbial communities respond to infection. While pathogen exposure can drive dysbiosis and contribute to disease, an alternative hypothesis suggests that microbiome perturbations may instead reflect selection for a more defensive community enriched with anti-pathogen members. Here, we tested this hypothesis in amphibians by conducting a meta-analysis of over 25 studies examining microbial responses to fungal pathogen infection. Using data from both field surveys and experimental studies with known Batrachochytrium infection status, exposure, and/or infection intensity, we assessed how pathogen presence influences key microbiome characteristics, including alpha diversity, beta diversity, and dispersion. Additionally, we used an updated AmphiBac Database, which includes over 7,000 bacterial cultures from hundreds of amphibian hosts tested for growth-inhibiting function of Batrachochytrium pathogens, allowing us to predict functional microbial responses across datasets. Our analysis revealed that microbiome composition shifts significantly upon Bd exposure, with responses varying based on host life stage and population trajectory—i.e., whether amphibian populations are in decline or remain stable. We also identified microbial taxa that were consistently enriched following pathogen exposure, including Flavobacteriaceae and Weeksellaceae, whereas Burkholderiaceae and Mycoplasmataceae were negatively associated with Bd presence. Understanding how microbiomes respond to pathogens is critical for evaluating their role as a dynamic component of amphibian immunity. By disentangling the drivers of amphibian–Batrachochytrium disease dynamics, our findings provide important insights into host-microbe-pathogen interactions in our changing world.
Thriving in a changing world: host-pathogen dynamics in hyperdiverse communities of amphibians and reptiles (SSAR)
2638: Shifting precipitation regimes driven by global climate change alter vertebrate behavior and host-symbiont relationships, potentially compromising host resistance to pathogen invasion. In Brazil's Atlantic Forest, a biodiversity hotspot, prior research identified drought as a key factor disrupting the skin microbiome, contributing to the die-off of pumpkin toadlets due to the invasive waterborne fungal pathogen Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (Bd). As observational studies often cannot distinguish the direct effect of moisture on Bd growth from increased amphibian activity during wet breeding seasons, we experimentally tested the impact of drought conditions on host behavior, Bd disease dynamics, and the composition and predicted Bd-inhibitory function of cutaneous bacterial communities using field enclosures. Each enclosure housed ecologically realistic densities of Brachycephalus pitanga, a micro-endemic species of pumpkin toadlet. We simulated a short-term drought in half of the enclosures using translucent tarp coverings. To track individual toadlets, we identified their unique markings and collected skin swabs biweekly over three months. Then, we implemented molecular techniques to quantify Bd loads and characterize skin bacterial diversity and composition over time. Our results show that drought suppressed Bd, but an increased host use of wet microenvironments and shifts in the protective skin microbiome partially offset the effect of drying on Bd. This study provides valuable insights into the cascading impacts of climate change on animal behavior, host-symbiont interactions, and disease dynamics. Understanding how changing environmental conditions influence the microbiome’s role in susceptibility to invasive pathogens is crucial for the survival of vulnerable hosts.
Thriving in a changing world: host-pathogen dynamics in hyperdiverse communities of amphibians and reptiles (SSAR)
2639: Amphibians face many challenges to their conservation, including major threats from emerging infectious pathogens. In diverse amphibian communities, where multiple emerging pathogens tend to co-occur, we know little about how the structural partitioning of host specificity among pathogens impacts infection dynamics in the host community. Here, we used field data from diverse amphibian communities in north Florida to investigate host-specific traits influencing the prevalence, intensity, and transmission of three emerging pathogens of amphibians: Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (Bd), Perkinsea (Pr), and Ranavirus (Rv). We found that Bd exhibited specificity for later developmental stages, and that overall infection patterns differed between ephemeral and semi-permanent sites and across seasons. For each pathogen, we identified key hosts that overwhelmingly contributed to community transmission dynamics and found evidence of pathogen interactions that may facilitate Bd-Rv co-infections, and dilution effects of increased host diversity on Pr infection. Our findings confirm that declining species within the region are routinely infected with emerging pathogens. However, the probability of infection relied on differences in habitat characteristics and the composition of the associated host community. Thus, our study emphasizes the importance of identifying key and sensitive hosts that drive or succumb to infections in natural communities before reintroducing amphibians into the wild. This approach can help improve conservation efforts in diverse host communities as successful repatriation of sensitive species can benefit from detailed characterization of the established disease dynamics at the release site.
Thriving in a changing world: host-pathogen dynamics in hyperdiverse communities of amphibians and reptiles (SSAR)
2640: Apicomplexan parasites in the genus Hepatozoon, a relative of the better-known Toxoplasma that infects cats and rats, have a broad host range that includes snakes and lizards. While Hepatozoon has not caused documented die offs in wild reptiles, it can cause clinical disease in captive reptiles. Clinical symptoms generally occur when parasites from an asymptomatic host infect a new host species. If this process occurs in the wild, infection risk to new host species may be correlated with times of high parasite load in the reservoir host species. To understand patterns of potential risk, we quantified Hepatozoon infection load in a population of the Florida banded water snake, Nerodia fasciata, across three seasons. We captured snakes in a shallow seasonal wetland on the campus of Florida Gulf Coast University, in Ft. Myers, Florida, in winter, spring, and summer of 2022. Using Sanger sequencing, we identified infection by a Hepatozoon lineage closely related to H. ophisauri in the population. Using quantitative PCR, we found that pathogen load varied between individuals in winter and summer. In spring, sampled individuals had uniformly high loads. Several processes could explain this pattern, including higher rates feeding of by the snakes (and therefore transmission) during spring, or vulnerability to infection due to the energetic demands of breeding. The prevalence and variability in parasite load of Hepatozoon in Florida water snakes makes it an ideal system for understanding the drivers of infection intensity and transmission risk between individuals and between seasons.
Thriving in a changing world: host-pathogen dynamics in hyperdiverse communities of amphibians and reptiles (SSAR)
2641: Animals host diverse microbiomes essential for their health and ecological roles. Metacommunity theory provides a framework for understanding host-associated microbiome assembly across scales, linking regional environmental processes to local host-microbial processes. We formulated hypotheses based on community ecology theory and tested them using 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing and novel analytical approaches to analyze the microbiomes of three Appalachian salamander species and their corresponding environments: red-backed salamanders (Plethodon cinereus) in forest soils, two-lined salamanders (Eurycea bislineata) in streams, and eastern newts (Notophthalmus viridescens) in ponds. Given prior findings on evolutionary history and Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (Bd) shaping salamander microbiomes, we hypothesized niche-based deterministic processes would be dominant. Our analysis revealed variable levels of deterministic processes: 14% for N. viridescens, 34% for P. cinereus, and 68% for E. bislineata. Environmental microbiomes in forests and ponds were highly structured by deterministic processes (91% and 86%, respectively), while stream microbiomes showed a moderate level (47%). Across all three salamander species, we found that bacterial communities were enriched with rare environmental bacteria. We further hypothesized that patch dynamics, such as competition-colonization trade-offs, would dominate metacommunity processes, given that rare environmental microbes are more likely to colonize amphibian skin. Network analyses supported patch dynamics, revealing competition and colonization processes within salamander skin microbiome networks. We identified bacteria from the genus Pedobacter, which includes Bd-inhibitory taxa, as good colonizers on salamander skin. Our findings suggest that niche-based processes shape microbiome structure at the environmental-host interface and highlight key factors predicting microbiome composition based on environment and host biology.
Thriving in a changing world: host-pathogen dynamics in hyperdiverse communities of amphibians and reptiles (SSAR)
2642: Amphibians are the most threatened group of vertebrates, with their populations continuing to decline at an alarming rate due to factors such as habitat loss, disease, and climate change, making genetic strategies aimed at enhancing resilience more critical than ever. The genomics revolution has created many opportunities to enhance amphibian resilience, increasing the potential for establishing self-sustaining populations. These strategies include identifying populations facing genetic threats such as inbreeding depression, performing genetically informed translocations, and releasing pre-adapted individuals. Genetic intervention is also supported by advances in assisted reproductive technologies, stem cell and gamete cryopreservation, and genetic engineering. I will discuss some of the tools and resources required for genetic management, as well as recent developments in the field of genetic intervention.
Thriving in a changing world: host-pathogen dynamics in hyperdiverse communities of amphibians and reptiles (SSAR)
2643: Local adaptation to parallel environmental pressures offers a powerful natural framework to investigate the genomic basis of phenotypic variation such as disease resistance. However, understanding the phylogenetic and demographic background of populations is essential to place adaptive patterns in the proper evolutionary context. Integrating phylogeographic sampling of natural populations with functional genomic data, allows simultaneous exploration of evolutionary history and the genomic signatures of adaptation. We applied this strategy to investigate population structure, phylogeography, demography, and local adaptation across several North American leopard frog species. Using a genome-wide targeted exon capture approach, we enriched our dataset for loci related to immune function and skin integrity to explore genomic responses to chytridiomycosis. We compared genome-wide variation across multiple populations that span a range of ecological conditions and disease outcomes, including chytrid susceptible, tolerant, and disease-naïve populations. Our findings reveal that populations with reduced genetic diversity exhibited greater disease susceptibility and were more likely to face local extirpation. Interestingly, some susceptible or extirpated populations also harbored unique functional alleles not found in more stable populations, which could indicate the presence of historical local adaptations now potentially at risk. We also observed strong nuclear genetic differentiation among populations in contrast to shallow mitochondrial divergence, consistent with recent population fragmentation and drift. Although genetic structure and drift can obscure conventional outlier-based scans for selection, the use of multiple complementary methods revealed candidate genes potentially involved in local adaptation and disease resistance. This study illustrates how combining functional genomic tools with phylogeographic context can provide valuable insights into both demographic history and adaptive processes in non-model amphibians.
Thriving in a changing world: host-pathogen dynamics in hyperdiverse communities of amphibians and reptiles (SSAR)
2644: With increased research and study, our knowledge of diseases of reptiles and amphibians continues to grow. However, scientists, wildlife health experts, and veterinarians all face a common challenge: a rapidly expanding and changing target. The combination of rapid global movement of people, animals, and goods coupled with growing worldwide demand for reptiles, amphibians, or related products in the private sector has created unprecedented challenges for animal health. While there are a number of well-known and well-studied examples of this concept, such as amphibian chytridiomycosis, sadly the number of emerging disease risks facing herpetofauna is swiftly increasing. Emerging pathogens, including fungi, such as ophidiomycosis in snakes, bacteria, such as enterococcosis in lizards, viruses, such as picornaviruses in snakes, and parasites, such as Raillietiella orientalis in reptiles and amphibians, are all documented to cause disease at the level of individual animals, and have the potential to have population-level impacts. This lecture will detail several emerging diseases affecting reptiles and amphibians and will place particular emphasis on the captive:wild interface to demonstrate the challenges that herpetofauna are likely to continue to face in the future.
Thriving in a changing world: host-pathogen dynamics in hyperdiverse communities of amphibians and reptiles (SSAR)
2645: Chameleons are unique amongst tetrapods for their exceptional suite of anatomical modifications which have allowed them to adapt to and diversify in arboreal environments. Specializations shared amongst this unique lizard lineage include having shortened and compressed bodies, reduced flexibility in the trunk and neck, grasping and cleft hands and feet, a prehensile and non-autotomizing tail, highly developed and independently movable eyes, and ballistic tongues. Here we study the optic nerve of chameleons and compare them with other squamates using diceCT methods. Results from the 3D modeling of the brain and associated structures reveals that chameleons developed a coiled optic nerve, which is unique among tetrapods and might be correlated with lateralized eye movements.
2646: Mastacembelus (Synbranchiformes:Mastacembelidae) is a speciose genus of eel-like fishes that is geographically restricted to the freshwaters of tropical southeast Asia and Africa. Previous studies suggest that mastacembelids originated in Asia during the early Miocene and then subsequently invaded and radiated throughout the Afro-Tropics, where 70% of species within the genus reside. Invading a new geographic region by a clade may trigger an early burst of rapid lineage and morphological diversification as species capitalize on ecological opportunity and subsequently slows as niches become saturated. The ecological diversity of Asian and African mastacembelids differ remarkably. Asian species are restricted to swampy habitats. By contrast African species include lacustrine invades, burrowing riverine taxa, and inhabitants of the dark depths of the lower Congo rapids. Ecological diversity is often coupled with morphological diversity; however, the anatomical disparity of mastacembelids remains unexplored. Here we use micro-computed tomography and geometric morphometrics to capture cranial diversity as well as linear morphometrics to capture overall body shape. We then employed phylogenetic comparative methods to compare the tempo and mode of lineage and morphological diversification of African and Asian mastacembelids. We find that all mastacembelids are characterized by rapid lineage diversification rates and African mastacembelids are more morphologically diverse than their Asian relatives. This work provides insight on how ecologically fragmented river drainages in the Afro-Tropics play a pivotal role in the evolution of tropical freshwater fishes.
2647: Ostariophysi is among the most ecologically and morphologically diverse clades of bony fishes, comprised of five orders and over 10,000 species, which together constitute nearly 70% of freshwater fish diversity. While Ostariophysi includes some of the largest orders of fishes (e.g., Cypriniformes and Siluriformes, represented by over 4,000 and 3,000 species respectively), species richness is unevenly distributed across the clade. An outlier among more speciose kin, Gonorynchiformes is a species-depauperate order, consisting of a mere 37 extant species across seven genera. It is the sister-lineage to all other ostariophysans, and despite relatively low species richness, gonorynchiform fishes exhibit striking morphological diversity. From the hefty marine milkfish to the bizarre hingemouth to the miniaturized shellears, gonorynchiform fishes present an intriguing evolutionary phenomenon in which a small order possesses a degree of morphological disparity that may be on par with lineages that are orders of magnitude more speciose. However, no study to date has sought to quantify this disparity. In this study, we employ a landmark-based geometric morphometric approach to quantify three-dimensional skull shape disparity in gonorynchiform fishes. We characterize patterns of morphospace occupation and identify regions of the skull with the greatest shape variation. We compare the gonorynchiform morphospace with that of cypriniform fishes and test the hypothesis that gonorynchiforms have evolved as much morphological diversity as other ostariophysan orders in the absence of a large species radiation.
2648: Colubrids have a near-global distribution and comprise 50% of snakes worldwide. Morphological variation has revealed mechanistic features associated with prey preference. Skeletal modifications of mollusk specialists have been studied extensively, particularly within the genus Pareas, which exhibit a shorter, more compressed snout and, in some, mandibular asymmetry. However, little attention has been paid to those that specialize on slugs (limaxivores). Unlike the snail-eating members of the Pareidae and Dipsadini, limaxivores lack the morphological traits associated with the extraction of snails from their shells. Instead, they often possess elongated, needle-like teeth, which have been hypothesized to assist with the consumption of soft-bodied prey. We used microCT imagery to examine the morphological basis for limaxivory in the two species of Contia. Their skeletal and soft-tissue morphology was compared to that of Carphophis amoenus and Diadophis punctatus. Although not always considered to be sister-taxa of Contia, Carphophis and Diadophis are members of the basal cluster of New World dipsadids to which Contia belongs (sometimes recognized as the Carphophiinae), and they appear to afford the most appropriate comparisons for distinguishing limaxivorous adaptations in Contia. We observed substantial cranial differences between taxa with respect to their trophic structures, presumable reflecting differences in both feeding and locomotor behavior. Diet appears to be the largest determinant of variation in dentition. A more extensive investigation into the prey handling exhibited by limaxivorous snakes should inform the functional interpretation of their morphological features.
2649:
We present here our preliminary findings using DiceCT imaging to visualize the cranial anatomy of front-fanged and rear-fanged snakes collected near Kindia, Guinea. Medically relevant front-fanged species included here were Dendroaspis viridis (Elapidae) with a proteroglyph dentition, and Atractaspis aterrima (Lamprophiidae; Atractaspidinae) and Causus maculatus (Viperidae) with (convergent) solenoglyph dentitions. Medically non-relevant, rear-fanged species included here were Psammophis phillipsii and P. elegans (Lamprophiidae; Psammophiinae) and Toxicodryas blandingi (Colubridae; Colubrinae) all with opisthoglyph dentitions. Highlights of our findings are as follows: The elongate venom glands of C. maculatus were expected but nevertheless impressive to see imaged in this way for the first time; The nasal glands of the lamprophiids were enlarged relative to those of the other snakes, which we speculate may be related to the role of gland secretions in their social lives.

Nous présentons ici nos résultats préliminaires utilisant l'imagerie DiceCT pour visualiser l'anatomie crânienne de serpents à crochets antérieurs et à crochets postérieurs collectés près de Kindia, en Guinée. Les espèces à crochets antérieurs d’importance médicale incluses ici étaient Dendroaspis viridis (Elapidae) avec une dentition protéroglyphe, et Atractaspis aterrima (Lamprophiidae ; Atractaspidinae) et Causus maculatus (Viperidae) avec des dentitions solénoglyphes (convergentes). Les espèces à crochets postérieurs, sans importance médicale, incluses ici étaient Psammophis phillipsii et P. elegans (Lamprophiidae ; Psammophiinae) et Toxicodryas blandingi (Colubridae ; Colubrinae) tous avec des dentitions opisthoglyphes. Les points saillants de nos résultats sont les suivants : Les glandes à venin allongées de C. maculatus étaient attendues mais néanmoins impressionnantes de voir imagées de cette façon pour la première fois ; Les glandes nasales des lamprophiidés étaient plus grandes que celles des autres serpents, ce qui, selon nous, pourrait être lié au rôle des sécrétions glandulaires dans leur vie sociale.
2650: Several studies have documented associations between the relative size of brain regions among fishes, such as chondrichthyan and cichlid fishes, and their habitats. The cerebellum and telencephalon, for example, tend to be relatively larger in species that inhabit more spatially complex environments, such as coral or rocky reefs as compared to simple benthic substrates or up in the water column. These relationships have not yet been examined in Neotropical electric fishes (Gymnotiformes), that sense self-generated electric fields. Here, we compare patterns of diversity in brain anatomy with ecological traits using principal components analysis to explore correlations between the relative size of brain regions with environmental features associated with river size (small, large, or both) and mesohabitat (small lotic, large river margins, pelagic in large rivers, benthic in large rivers, and multiple environments). We find gymnotiform species that inhabit more spatially complex environments have relatively larger telencephalic lobes as compared with species that inhabit spatially simple habitats. These analyses support the hypothesis that in Gymnotiformes, relative size of the telencephalon is correlated and perhaps influenced by environmental adaptations, as reported in other fish taxa. However, unlike other fishes, cerebellum size in gymnotiforms is not correlated with habitat complexity. The exceptionally large size of the cerebellum in gymnotiforms, used in active electroreception, may mask brain size patterns observed in other fish groups.
2651: Within Microhylidae, only two genera putatively develop keratinized feeding structures during the tadpole stage: Scaphiophryne of Madagascar and Otophryne of northern South America. Based on our current understanding of the microhylid phylogeny, it is possible that these two lineages independently regained keratinized mouthparts after the common ancestor of microhylids lost these structures. To evaluate this hypothesis, we generated histological sections of Scaphiophryne and Otophryne tadpoles and reconstructed the evolutionary history of tadpole keratinized mouthparts across the frog tree of life. We confirm that the cellular microanatomy of the keratinized jaw sheaths in Scaphiophryne and Otophryne is comparable to that of other tadpoles, composed of basal keratinocytes that proliferate into a stacked column of cone cells and supporting sheath cells. The inferred ancestral larval state in crown-group frogs is a tadpole with keratinized mouthparts, and these specialized larval structures were subsequently lost in more than 15 anuran lineages. Tadpole keratinized mouthparts were lost in the most recent common ancestor of Microylidae and independently regained in the ancestors of Scaphiophryne and Otophryne. Our findings provide new insights into the constraints and flexibility of tadpole mouthpart evolution, and we add microhylid tadpole keratinized mouthparts to the growing list of complex traits that have been evolutionarily lost and regained in violation of Dollo’s law of irreversibility.
2652: Mormyridae, a family of weakly electric fishes native to African lakes and rivers, display remarkable diversity in their craniofacial morphologies from brachiocephalic to dolichocephalic.  Despite their ecological importance, the functional morphology of these fishes remain largely understudied. The goal of this study is to investigate the functional implications of face elongation on the mechanical leverage of the lower jaw, an important proxy of force transmission in the jaws of teleost fishes. Initially, we hypothesized that mormyrids with longer snouts (i.e., the distance from orbit to end of the rostrum) would have lower mechanical advantages due to the assumed jaw elongation. We assessed the mechanical properties of the jaw lever-linkage system using simple lever mechanics measured from high resolution microCT scans. Preliminary results show that some species with extreme craniofacial phenotypes and elongated snouts exhibit lower mechanical advantages. However, this pattern is not necessarily attributed to jaw length alone. In some species with elongated snouts and lower mechanical advantages, their skeletal jaws are relatively short, which conflicts with the general assumption that mormyrids with shorter jaws would have a greater bite force. In our preliminary dataset, we see different configurations of face elongation (e.g., long faces but relatively short jaws versus long faces with relatively long jaws) and this leads to various functional outcomes from relatively weak to strong jaws.
2653: Overlap between marine megafauna and maritime activities is a topic of global concern. Basking sharks (Cetorhinus maximus; CM) are listed as Globally Endangered under the IUCN, though reported sightings appear to be increasing in Ireland. While such trends in the region are welcome, increasing spatiotemporal overlap between CM and numerous water users poses an increased risk of boat strikes to the animals.
