Our findings suggest that precipitation can induce changes in thermal quality which can indirectly limit species ranges, and that the seasonal timing of these changes is important.
2709: Nonnative species have large and varied impacts in ecosystems they invade. To determine if a novel nonnative species may become invasive, the species’ capacity to negatively affect the native ecological systems and spread over significant distances from its original introduction site should be assessed. Typhlonectes natans, an aquatic amphibian native to South America, was first discovered in the water system of Miami-Dade in 2019, designating it as the first introduced caecilian species in the United States. As the current distribution of this species is unknown, this study aims to determine its range in the canal system of Miami-Dade, throughout urban areas and extending into the Everglades, utilizing environmental DNA (eDNA). eDNA is a non-invasive, sensitive method that can detect species in aquatic environments, where traditional sampling methods may be more difficult to implement. The goal of this study will provide the first comprehensive map of T. natans distribution in the region and establish a baseline for determining future range expansions. We hypothesize that we can use eDNA to determine if T. natans has spread from its original site of discovery in the C-4 (Tamiami) Canal near the airport to areas approaching, or potentially within, the Everglades. Since the potential ecological impact of T. natans is not well understood, accurately assessing its range and dispersal capacity is crucial for evaluating its potential negative effects on native species.
2710: International liver oil trade is a major driver of targeted fisheries and retention of bycatch for deepwater sharks. Sharks are targeted for the squalene content in their liver oil, which is used for cosmetic and human health applications. The unique properties of shark liver oil make it a sought-after commodity, contributing to targeted fisheries and incentivizing fishers to retain bycatch. However, the trade's sustainability is questionable due to a lack of management and the precarious status of many shark species. Liver oil fisheries are understudied and overshadowed by more visible global trades of other shark and ray products but are presumed to not be sustainable. The global liver oil trade is also difficult to measure because of its complexity with the mixed end-product making it hard to identify and quantify species. This presentation will discuss efforts currently underway to extract DNA from liver oil products to identify shark species within. Various methodologies are being explored with the aim to establish a robust molecular monitoring tool for improved traceability and management of liver oil fisheries globally.
2712: Understanding the behavioral ecology of marine species is crucial for conservation and management, but has lagged in the study of elasmobranchs. Using Unoccupied Aircraft Systems (UAS, or drones) to observe sharks minimizes disturbance, reduces costs, and increases efficiency. This study examines the efficacy of fine-scale tracking, quantification, and analysis of near-shore shark behaviors through drone observations and a deep learning pose estimation tool. Surveys were conducted in the Rachel Carson Reserve in North Carolina, a coastal estuarine habitat with a multi-species assemblage of juvenile and adult sharks. The DJI Mavic 3 Classic and Enterprise, equipped with 20-megapixel cameras, captured videos at altitudes of 20 to 25 meters. These surveys produced stationary nadir aerial footage of 1-4 sharks per video, with durations ranging from 20 seconds to 2 minutes. Additional videos from the eastern Mediterranean were collected by project partners using a DJI Phantom 3 equipped with a 12.4 megapixel camera at altitudes of 40 to 60 meters. Behavioral assessments of in-video shark activity were conducted with Social LEAP Estimates Animal Poses (SLEAP), a deep learning based framework for multi-animal pose estimation. SLEAP outputs were used to calculate velocity, orientation, tail beat frequency, and more to understand individual shark movement. Further analysis quantifies behavioral patterns of multiple sharks, including hierarchical clustering that can drive comparisons of vectors amongst larger aggregations. The resulting transfer model and methodology provide a standardized approach for further characterization and quantification of the behavior of nearshore sharks in isolation and aggregation using drones and video-based behavioral analysis.
2713: Estimating the distributions of cryptic species is essential for conservation, yet understanding distributions is hampered by animal behavior and imperfect detection. We developed and implemented a multi-scale occupancy survey protocol to estimate the probability of occurrence, probability of being active on the surface, and detection probability of two range-restricted terrestrial salamanders, Scott Bar (Plethodon asupak) and Siskiyou Mountains salamanders (P. stormi), in interior northern California. We established survey sites near locations of historical occurrence of these salamanders and surveyed each site on 1–6 visits in the late fall of 2023 and spring of 2024. We used WAIC to compare models with different environmental variables for predicting salamander occurrence and surface activity. Much model selection uncertainty in the effects of covariates existed, but the model with most support indicated that Plethodon salamanders in interior northern California were more likely to occur at sites near recent historical occurrences that were warmer, at lower elevations, and had north-northeast aspects. Plethodon salamander surface activity was higher at night than during the day, and was highest when substrates were cool and moist. Our survey protocol was successful for quantifying the effects of site and visit characteristics on Plethodon salamander occurrence and availability; minor modifications will likely improve its utility for providing unbiased inference about salamander occurrence and surface activity.
2714: Circadian rhythms are innate responses to cyclic daily changes in the environment allowing physiological and behavioural processes such as feeding or resting to occur at the most suitable times. Circadian rhythms are thought to be an adaptive response to prevailing conditions, raising the question of whether globally distributed species display adaptative routines in response to local conditions. Here, we tested if the activity rhythm of the white shark, Carcharodon carcharias, a circumglobally distributed marine predator, features conserved circadian properties in four distinct populations, across eight aggregation sites in three of the world’s oceans. We derived the diel activity of white sharks by attaching motion-sensitive biologgers to 104 free-swimming sharks, estimating tail beat frequencies over 2,500 hours of data. Overall, we found that activity rhythms were consistently diurnal across all populations and documented only minor site-specific variations, with the activity of some populations peaking in the morning and others in the afternoon. Our results show that despite populations diverging over hundreds of thousands of years and foraging in diverse habitats, consistent diurnality occurs in white shark activity globally. We suggest that the maintenance of diurnality is a result of a conserved circadian rhythm supporting sensory specialisation in this visual predator, while the minor variations of the timing of activity may be an adaptive response to the availability and behaviour of prey.
2715: As part of a larger research program on the role of the forest in maintaining the local ichthyofauna of the Congo Basin, a study focused on the diets of Alestidae, a family of many represented fishes in the Boumba and Kadei rivers in eastern Cameroon. Indeed know the diet of savage specie fish can help to make their conservation. A total of 106 fish specimens including five species in the Boumba (Alestes macrophthalmus, Brycinus macrolepidotus, Brycinus longipinnis, Bryconaethiops spp. and Hydrocynus vittatus) and four species in the Kadei (Alestes macrophthalmus, Brycinus macrolepidotus, Brycinus imberi and Hydrocynus vittatus) were collected monthly from December 2018 to May 2019. Qualitative and quantitative analysis of all of these stomach contents reveals that the diet of fish hovers around four food categories: prey fish, macroinvertebrates, macrophytes and other unidentifiable particles, and according to each fraction ate by different species, Alestidae family fish of Boumba and Kadei is divided into herbivorous, carnivorous and omnivorous. Furthermore, it is obvious that the forests of the Congo Basin constitute an essential source of food (leaves, fruits and insects) for the ichthyofauna of the rivers they shelter and mainly contribute to maintaining the diet balance of fish community of each water course. Consequently, deforestation would negatively impact certain taxa of fish such as the Alestidae which depend on them and would inevitably lead to their loss.
2716: Wildlife trade, a multibillion-dollar industry involving over 100 million plants and animals annually, has emerged as a major driver of species decline globally. However, the lack of comprehensive assessments for many taxa limits our understanding of the global scale and patterns of wildlife trade. In this study, we investigated the global online trade dynamics of pythons (family Pythonidae), which are popular worldwide as pets, trophies and status symbols. We conducted extensive web searches on Google Chrome, using the phrase ‘python for sale’ in different languages, to compile a list of websites involved in the python species trade and the selling price of each python species. We identified websites from different countries in the world, involved in buying and selling python species. The required data was manually extracted from each website and added to spreadsheets, and analyzed in R Studio (4.4.1). We provided a framework for analyzing online python trade, which can be adapted for other taxonomic groups. Our results emphasize the need for improved monitoring to assess the origin (captive-bred or wild-sourced) and legality of the trade. Immediate conservation actions, including population monitoring, are crucial to ensure that the wildlife trade does not threaten the survival of python populations in the wild. We also suggested monitoring traded pythons to ensure they do not become established as the invasive species.
2717: Tonic immobility is a commonly used method during the handling of elasmobranchs, however, the biological processes by which it occurs, and the physiological effects, are all poorly understood.  Nine juvenile lemon sharks (Negaprion brevirostris; 6 M, 3 F; mean TL = 80.34 cm, ± 4.5 SE) were each subject to three 30 min trials: tonic immobility with and without ventilation, and normal orientation (15 mins) into tonic immobility (15 mins) both with ventilation.  Blood samples were taken at 0, 5, 10, 15, 22.5, and 30 mins.  Collected blood was processed on an iStat machine for stress indicators including lactate, glucose, pH, bicarbonate (HCO3), partial pressure of oxygen (pO2), partial pressure of carbon dioxide (pCO2), and sulfur dioxide (SO2).  Lactate and glucose steadily increased throughout each trial and showed similar trends and values between treatments.  Blood pH dropped from 0 - 10 mins then stabilized while in normal orientation.   For the tonic immobility treatments, pH continued to drop until the 15 min mark, then was buffered by bicarbonate which it helped it to raise and stabilize.  Interestingly, the largest disparity in trends over the course of the 30 mins, between the tonic immobility and normal treatments, was observed in the blood gas parameters (pO2, pCO2, and SO2).  These were considerably more stable during the normal orientation treatment, indicating potential disruption to blood gas exchange at the gills while inverted.
2718:
This study investigates the phylogenetic relationships within the Acanthodactylus genus in its easternmost range, particularly Pakistan. Using a concatenated dataset of mitochondrial (16S, COI, cyt b) and nuclear (Rag1) genes, we reconstructed the phylogenetic relationships constructed by two tree methods that consistently revealed four, strongly supported major clades (A-D). These clades exhibit significant genetic differentiation, with level of uncorrected p distances highlighting deep divergences among them. Clade A, consisting of a single sequence identified as A. micropholis, is the sister group to the remaining clades. Clades B and C, both identified as A. blanfordii from the Helmand Basin in northwestern Balochistan, are geographically separated by the Chagai Hills and show moderate genetic differentiation. Clade D, identified as A. cantoris, is the most divergent and widespread, yet it shows shallow intraspecific genetic variation through the Indus Valley. Additional analysis of 178 cyt b sequences, including data from GenBank, supported the division into the four main clades identified from the concatenated dataset. Notably, Clades B and C are newly identified in this study and represent novel phylogenetic entities within Acanthodactylus. Our research enhances our understanding of the evolutionary relationships and geographic distributions of Acanthodactylus lizards in the eastern edge of its wide distribution and providing a robust phylogenetic framework for further taxonomic and conservation studies.

Keywords

Afghanistan, endemism, Balochistan, remote areas, speciation, taxonomy.
2719: Everglades conservation is critical to both the well-being of Everglades biodiversity and the communities surrounding this unique ecosystem. The management of water resources, agriculture impacts, and invasive species all affect the viability of the Everglades. The success of invasive species can often be attributed to their ability to outcompete the native species in their niches. To investigate the success of invasive cichlid fishes in the Everglades and their ecological impact on native centrarchid fishes, bite force and suction pressure were investigated over ontogeny using biomechanical modeling. Invasive Mayan cichlids Mayaheros urophthalmus (14 - 29 cm TL) had an oral jaw mechanical advantage of 0.36, bite force of 5.3 N, epaxial mechanical advantage of 0.24, and suction pressure of 1.9 kPa. Invasive Nile tilapia Oreochromis niloticus (12 - 26 cm TL) had an oral jaw mechanical advantage of 0.42, bite force of 1.6 N, epaxial mechanical advantage of 0.19, and suction pressure of 0.9 kPa. Native bluegill sunfish Lepomis macrochirus (10 - 15 cm TL) had an oral jaw mechanical advantage of 0.37, bite force of 0.7 N, epaxial mechanical advantage of 0.31, and suction pressure of 2.7 kPa. Preliminary analyses suggest that bluegill have lower bite forces but higher suction pressures, suggesting that any extent to which the bluegill is being outcompeted by these invasive cichlids may not be attributable to deficits in feeding performance. Future analyses will examine scaling patterns of feeding biomechanics and add sampling of additional native redear sunfish Lepomis microlophus and spotted sunfish Lepomis punctatus.
2720: The ecological theory of adaptive radiation posits that available niche space drives diversification, with new species evolving to occupy unfilled gaps. Thus, theory suggests that older or species-rich faunas will tend to “fill out” community-wide niche space more than younger or species-depauperate faunas. However, it is also possible that young, species-depauperate faunas can fill available niche space to a similar extent, with each component species occupying a larger breadth in the absence of competitors. Therefore, it remains unclear whether the filling of community niche space is primarily driven by faunal age and diversity, or whether idiosyncrasies related to geography or taxa are more important. Here we investigate the importance of island size in shaping the structural niche space occupied by individual species and whole communities of reptiles and amphibians across the vertical profile of forest habitats on Puerto Rico, Jamaica, Hispaniola, and Madagascar. On each island we collected data from three distinct landscape types (warm dry, warm wet, and cool wet forest) for a total of 37 unique vertical tree-climbing transects. Our results suggest that reptiles tend to fill vertical niche space more readily than amphibians, regardless of island size. We also demonstrate that terrestrial abundances of both groups are inversely related to island size, but that in the canopy this pattern only holds for reptiles. Ultimately, our findings show that reptiles consistently take advantage of ecological opportunity in vertical niche space, while amphibians often fall short.
2721: Aquifers exert strong selective pressures on the subterranean organisms that inhabit them. Several salamander species have independently colonized aquifers and, alongside teleosts, are the only known vertebrates to occupy groundwater environments. Previous studies have shown that groundwater organisms have convergently evolved traits such as reduced eye development, enhanced olfaction and mechanoreception, altered circadian rhythms, slowed metabolism, and elongated limbs. However, the genetic basis of these adaptations in salamanders remains poorly understood, especially in comparison to other subterranean taxa. Thus far, our research has found that the DNA-binding paired box domain of pax6, a transcription factor involved in eye development, shows mixed evidence of positive selection. Additionally, strc, a protein essential for hearing and mechanoreception, displays strong evidence of positive selection within an unannotated extracellular domain. These preliminary results suggest that the genetic mechanisms underlying groundwater adaptation are diverse, encompassing both changes in gene regulation and potential structural modifications to gene products. We anticipate that our findings will lay the groundwork for future research into the structural and functional roles of genomic elements in subterranean species. Moreover, a deeper understanding of these species’ evolutionary histories will aid conservation efforts, particularly as amphibians face increasing anthropogenic threats.
2722: Cave environments exert strong selective pressures on the subterranean organisms that inhabit them. Several salamander species have independently colonized subterranean karst aquifers and, alongside teleost fish, are the only known vertebrates to inhabit groundwater environments. Previous studies have shown that groundwater organisms have convergently evolved traits such as reduced eyes, enhanced olfaction and mechanoreception, altered circadian rhythms, slowed metabolism, and elongated limbs. However, the genetic basis of these adaptations in salamanders remains poorly understood. We assembled transcriptomes of 16 surface- and 8 cave-dwelling salamanders representing 20 species of the genus Eurycea. We found that the DNA-binding paired box domain of pax6, a gene encoding a transcription factor involved in eye development, shows weak evidence of positive selection. Additionally, strc, a gene encoding a protein essential for hearing and mechanoreception, displays strong evidence of positive selection within an unannotated extracellular domain. These preliminary results suggest that the genetic mechanisms underlying groundwater adaptation are diverse, encompassing both changes in gene regulation and potential structural modifications to gene products. Our findings will lay the groundwork for future research into the structural and functional roles of genomic elements in subterranean species. Moreover, a deeper understanding of these species’ evolutionary histories will aid conservation efforts, particularly as amphibians face increasing anthropogenic threats.
2723: The study of human attitudes towards animals has many implications, conservation ones. Snakes are the most polarizing of animals, eliciting human feelings of fear and disgust, but also awe and respect, due to their religious symbolism. Although attitudes towards snakes seem to be shifting to more positive, residues of negative attitudes remain. Venomous snakes in particular are widely recognized for being extremely dangerous. However, there are people who deliberately seek them out—a subgroup of herpetoculturists. Snake keepers represent an ideal model system to explore human-snake interactions. Colloquially known as “hots,” these snakes are illegal to own in many states, yet many keep them anyway. I conducted an ethnographic study of reptile keepers to tease out the characteristics of venomous snake ownership. While aesthetics is a primary reason many keep such snake species, others are drawn to them for their dangerous appeal and “coolness” factor, thus lending social capital to the keeper. Demographically, the vast majority of venomous snakes keepers are young males. Venomous snake keeping is definitely implicated in constructions of masculinity. Ethnoherpetological studies provide critical insight into human attitudes towards reptiles and can contextualize ecological studies.
2724:
Abstract

The tropical areas of Africa are home to some of the global biodiversity hotspots. In Kenya we have three key biodiversity hotspots, namely Coastal forests of Eastern Africa, Eastern Afromontane and Horn of Africa hotspots. These hotspots harbor a unique diversity of reptile and amphibian species, some of them being endemic or having a restricted range. Consequently, some of the species are threatened and listed in the IUCN Red list of threatened species in high threat categories such as Critically Endangered, Endangered, Vulnerable and Near-Threatened. Some few are listed in the CITES Appendix I and II due to threat from international pet trade. The rich Kenya herpetology consists of about 110 amphibians and 280 reptiles. In addition, new species continue to be described with about 25 new species described in the last 10 years. The major threat to Kenya herpetofauna is habitat loss and to some few species by international pet trade. Fortunately, majority of the key biodiversity areas occur within formal wildlife protected areas particularly wildlife and forest parks and reserves.  Some of these herpetofauna have not been recorded for decades and/or a century and are known from the type material. Therefore, the search of these ‘lost species” continues so as to better understand their conservation status and ultimately help in developing new conservation action pans or enrich existing ones.
2725: Micro-CT scanning has become ubiquitous with biological research, expanding the types and sizes of specimens that can be scanned. The University of Michigan Museum of Zoology houses over 170,000 reptiles, of which most are candidates for micro-CT scanning. This morphological variety requires new innovations to reduce movement and optimize the position in packing of specimens. Micro-CT scanners can be equipped to scan a broad range of sizes of specimens. Utilizing the transmission target of our Nikon XTH 225 ST scanner we can scan specimens down to a 1 micron pixel size, allowing us to scan the skulls of very small lizards (such as Sphaerodactylus sp.) with a 2mm head length. At this high resolution, the specimens must be very close to the x-ray source and must not move or dry out, so we developed a method to pack specimens in the tips of syringes. On the other hand, the reflection target on our scanner allows us to scan specimens or regions of interest (ROIs) between 2 cm and 30 cm. The largest specimens we scan using the reflection target include large fluid-preserved snakes such as a king cobra (Ophiophagus hannah) longer than 2 meters. These require different innovations for fitting the specimen or ROI within the field of view and reducing movement. In the microCT lab at the UMMZ, we have developed several solutions for packaging challenging reptile specimens and additional packing methods for optimizing our scans.
2726: Pharmaceutical pollution in marine environments is an emerging concern, yet its effects on higher trophic levels remain poorly understood. Our preliminary study investigates the presence of pharmaceutical compounds in nurse sharks (Ginglymostoma cirratum). Using non-lethal sampling methods, we detected multiple human pharmaceuticals—including Ibuprofen (anti-inflammatory), Levetiracetam (antiepileptic), Venlafaxine (antidepressant), and Quinidine (antiarrhythmic/antimalarial)—in nurse shark plasma. These findings suggest bioaccumulation through direct environmental exposure and possible trophic transfer from contaminated prey. With lifespans exceeding 25 years and slow metabolic rates, nurse sharks may experience chronic exposure to these substances, raising concerns about sublethal effects on physiology, behavior, and reproductive success. Wastewater effluent is the primary source of pharmaceuticals in marine ecosystems, yet remains largely unregulated. Compounding the issue over 80% of pharmaceutical compounds lack toxicity data for marine species. This study confirms pharmaceuticals in nurse sharks and underscores the urgent need for further research. Understanding how these compounds affect apex and mesopredators is essential for developing informed conservation strategies and effective wastewater management policies. Our findings highlight a significant and understudied threat to marine biodiversity and call for integrated approaches to mitigate pharmaceutical pollution in coastal ecosystems.
2727: Cave environments exert strong selective pressures on the subterranean organisms that inhabit them. Several salamander species have independently colonized subterranean karst aquifers and, alongside teleost fish, are the only known vertebrates to inhabit groundwater environments. Previous studies have shown that groundwater organisms have convergently evolved traits such as reduced eyes, enhanced olfaction and mechanoreception, altered circadian rhythms, slowed metabolism, and elongated limbs. However, the genetic basis of these adaptations in salamanders remains poorly understood. We assembled transcriptomes of 16 surface- and 8 cave-dwelling salamanders representing 20 species of the genus Eurycea. We found that the DNA-binding paired box domain of pax6, a gene encoding a transcription factor involved in eye development, shows weak evidence of positive selection. Additionally, strc, a gene encoding a protein essential for hearing and mechanoreception, displays strong evidence of positive selection within an unannotated extracellular domain. These preliminary results suggest that the genetic mechanisms underlying groundwater adaptation are diverse, encompassing both changes in gene regulation and potential structural modifications to gene products. Our findings will lay the groundwork for future research into the structural and functional roles of genomic elements in subterranean species. 2728: Jefferson salamanders (Ambystoma jeffersonianum) represent a unique and ecologically significant species whose populations face mounting challenges due to habitat loss, climate change, and a lack of data on their distribution and abundance. This thesis research investigated how Jefferson salamander abundance in Virginia has changed, identified the extent and location of suitable habitats, and determined potential areas within those habitats for future vernal pool creation. Species Distribution Models (SDMs) and Habitat Suitability Models (HSMs) were employed to predict and assess their distribution and to identify critical habitats, using occurrence data from sources such as the Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF) and iNaturalist, alongside environmental variables key to both salamander and overall amphibian biology and ecology. Analyses revealed that the Appalachian and Blue Ridge regions offer the most suitable habitats for Jefferson salamanders. However, historical data comparisons reveal a decline in salamander occurrences, which correlates with habitat degradation. Citizen science data from the Virginia Master Naturalist program further supported the study, revealing species-specific preferences within vernal pool ecosystems and highlighting co-occurrence patterns with other amphibians. Findings underscored the necessity of conserving vernal pools and surrounding forest habitats to ensure the species' survival. This research provided actionable insights for habitat restoration and vernal pool creation, supporting the conservation of Jefferson salamanders and broader amphibian biodiversity. Field validation is recommended to refine models and gain a deeper understanding of the species distribution. Ultimately, this study helps bridge knowledge gaps and informs efforts to preserve these ecological indicator species and their unique habitats.
2729: Asymmetric species diversity is one of the key observations that allows us to examine factors promoting adaptive radiation. Adaptive radiation is often initiated by ecological opportunity, which is the availability of ecologically accessible resources that may be evolutionarily exploited. Ecological opportunity can be presented by colonization to a new region or the appearance of a key innovation. When a lineage enters a new region, they are often exposed to previously foreign pathogens and forced to adapt to these newer pathogens. The ability for a lineage to adequately adapt to foreign pathogens could be a potential innovation of lineages that are best able to exploit ecological opportunity and subsequently diversify. While there have been numerous comparative genomics studies examining genomic response to infectious disease in birds and mammals, it has been underexplored in squamates. We harness squamate genomics and a comparative phylogenetic methods framework to clarify macroevolutionary patterns of genes associated with infectious disease response. We identify squamate clades that exhibit higher levels of pervasive positive selection of genes associated with immune response compared to other clades. We also clarify correlations with immune response genes undergoing pervasive positive selection with spatial patterns, including differences between temperate/tropical and island/continental taxa. Here, we present the genomics of immunological response as a potential field to explore to better understand the underlying mechanisms that allow lineages to take advantage of ecological opportunity and diversify.
2730: Climate change poses significant selective pressure for organisms to respond to shifting temperature and precipitation regimes. For dispersal-limited organisms, like many salamander species, responses to climate change are limited to “in situ” mechanisms such as adaptation through standing genetic variation, plasticity, or thermoregulatory behaviors. Linking variation in thermal phenotypes, such as thermal limits and color variation, with environmental variation provides a starting point to explore the adaptive potential and climatic vulnerability within a given species. Here, we investigate populations of the ensatina salamander (Ensatina eschscholtzii) in a portion of California to explore the links between thermal trait variation, such as critical thermal maximum, dorsal hue, and dorsal brightness with environmental variation. To characterize relevant environmental conditions, we built a fine-scale model of mean soil temperature across California as well as estimated soil temperature variation over the past 20 years. We also documented the microhabitat at the site-of-capture for each individual and characterized the macrohabitat through remote sensing products. Although we do not find a clear environmental driver of critical thermal maximum, we do find preliminary links between color variation and environmental conditions, suggesting potential heat-associated risks tied to dorsal coloration. We present these findings amid future work to increase sampling across the entire California ensatina distribution and plan to examine mechanistic links between phenotype, genotype, and environment in the context of environmental change.
2731: Amphibians, particularly anurans, secrete a diverse array of bioactive compounds that serve crucial ecological, defensive, and physiological roles. These secretions have gained attention for their antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, and pharmacological potential. However, there is limited research on the ecological drivers influencing metabolite expression and their broader implications for biodiversity and human health. My study employs an integrative eco-metabolomics approach to investigate the biochemical diversity of Hylarana erythraea skin secretions, linking metabolomics and peptidomics to ecological and biomedical applications. Utilizing advanced analytical techniques such as high-performance liquid chromatography–quadrupole time-of-flight mass spectrometry (HPLC-QTOF MS), data-dependent acquisition (DDA), and in-silico screening, this research aims to characterize bioactive peptides and metabolites with pharmaceutical relevance. The study also evaluates the influence of environmental factors, habitat conditions, and seasonal variations on metabolite production, offering insights into the dynamic interplay between amphibians and their ecosystems. By integrating eco-metabolomics with conservation bioacoustics and ecological assessments, this research not only enhances our understanding of amphibian chemical defenses but also contributes to conservation strategies for H. erythraea and other threatened species. Moreover, this work aligns with the One Health framework by emphasizing the interconnections between environmental health, species survival, and biomedical innovation. The findings could pave the way for novel bioactive compound discovery while advocating for amphibian conservation in Southeast Asia. This research represents a unique interdisciplinary effort that bridges amphibian ecology, biochemical research, and human health applications, highlighting the untapped potential of amphibians in ecological resilience and biomedicine.
2732: Most of Malaysian’s anuran species are nocturnally active, including Pulchrana glandulosa. However, all the studies on the description of this species’ call were done during nocturnal surveys in Sarawak, Borneo. Here we report the diurnal call of this frog from Langkawi Island, Kedah, Peninsular Malaysia. This male frog exhibits two types of calls: repetitive one-note advertisement calls and multiple-note response calls. Anuran bioacoustics can use to monitor the well being of the environment they occupy. This information is very informative for the conservation management authority and decision-making for conservation purposes. The diurnal call of this frog is a rare discovery and was not yet described in previous records. This research shows us that this frog calls diurnally and nocturnally because its skin secretion has a high toxicity level. Besides that, this frog is well known for its loud “WAHK” call at night. However, the diurnal call is not as rare as one thinks; we need to know the specific spot at a specific time of occurrence. Furthermore, these surveys also need to be done diurnally to minimise the undetected species behaviour as in this study, which is essential for our scientific community.
2733: Recent surveys in the Mae Klong River basin in western Thailand have greatly increased the number of species of fishes known to occur there (~250) and revealed previously unknown biogeographic patterns. Explaining these patterns requires accurate taxonomic, phylogenetic, and distributional information for the fishes, and knowledge of the geological history of the region. Extant fish communities in the basin reflect dispersal and vicariance, i.e., historic connections with the Chao Phraya, Salween, and Tenasserim River basins, as well as with rivers in the northern Malay Peninsula; evolutionary diversification within the Mae Klong basin, including Tenasserim Hills endemism; and environmental constraints, primarily lowlands vs. uplands. These factors have resulted in four primary communities of fishes in the Mae Klong basin: 1) lowlands with species shared with river basins in the northern Malay Peninsula; 2) upper Khwae Yai with affinities to the Salween basin to the north; 3) upper Khwae Noi, with Tenasserim Hills endemics and species shared with rivers to the west; and 4) widespread species, many shared with the Chao Phraya basin to the east. The assemblage of fishes in the upper Khwae Yai suggests the river previously was connected to the Moei River and flowed north to the Salween River basin.
2734: Embryonic survival of aquatic and semi-aquatic amphibians is difficult to estimate in situ, thus recruitment data are often lacking despite being critical for understanding life history. As effects of localized habitat degradation become increasingly exacerbated by climate change, amphibian recruitment may be more susceptible to factors like desiccation and pollution. These factors are especially consequential at the edge of a species range. Peripheral populations are more susceptible to declines, as habitat modifications at the range edge push them beyond their environmental tolerance. Streamside salamanders (Ambystoma barbouri) reproduce in first- and second-order ephemeral streams, mostly using large, flat rocks for egg deposition. West Virginia represents the eastern limit of the species’ range, with only two extant populations remaining. Streamside salamander’s mode of egg deposition in conjunction with a lack of suitable nesting material in West Virginia makes these populations well suited to examine recruitment. We used artificial cover objects that provided large, flat surfaces for egg deposition to monitor Streamside salamander nesting phenology and estimate embryonic survival.  We sampled coverboards weekly between January and April 2024 to photograph eggs and nest substrate. We then georectified images in ArcPro, and used spatial and environmental covariates as predictors of embryonic survival.
2735: Morphological differences in the peripheral (sensory) and central (brain) nervous system have been predicted to confer functional variation in elasmobranchs across taxa and throughout ontogeny. Additionally, the nervous system of fishes grows continually throughout life and may be highly plastic in relation to environmental change. Over the last century, sea surface temperatures have increased over 0.5˚C and are predicted to rise 1–4˚ by 2100, potentially affecting species’ physiological performance. Therefore, assessing effects of temperature on changes in size and organization of the nervous system may have implications for brain function in future ocean conditions. Effects of increased rearing temperature on nervous system development were studied in the little skate (Leucoraja erinacea), epaulette shark (Hemiscyllium ocellatum), and Port Jackson shark (Heterodontus portusjacksoni). Egg cases from each species were collected and placed into either ambient or 3–5˚ above ambient seawater conditions through hatching, for up to five months. Using histological analyses, relative volume of the olfactory rosette, total brain, and major brain regions were compared between treatment groups. Results indicate significant, species-specific differences in both total brain volume and size of major brain regions, possibly indicating sensory or motor impairment at elevated temperatures. While studies on acute responses to environmental conditions cannot inform true adaptation across broad timescales, understanding effects of increased temperature on neural phenotype can aid in predicting consequences of environmental perturbations in elasmobranchs.
2736: Atlantic guitarfish (Pseudobatos lentiginosus) are a vulnerable batoid species found in the Western Atlantic, with populations declining due to bycatch in commercial fisheries and habitat loss. Despite their Vulnerable status, limited information exists on their biology and ecology. This study evaluated the effectiveness of using individual spot patterns for individual photo-identification of wild Atlantic guitarfish to support minimally-invasive monitoring of their movements and habitat use. Photographs of the rostrum were taken during field surveys in Palm Beach County, Florida, and processed using I³S Spot software to generate a database of unique individuals (n=200). The software demonstrated high accuracy, with a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve showing an area under the curve (AUC) value of 0.93, indicating strong sensitivity and specificity. This method provides a cost-effective and minimally invasive alternative to traditional tagging techniques for studying guitarfish movement patterns. Initial resighting data revealed evidence of site fidelity and local movements, with several individuals documented at multiple study site locations. The successful implementation of photo-identification could enhance long-term monitoring efforts, inform management, and allow the incorporation of citizen science into the study of Atlantic guitarfish
2737: In 2023 the Minnesota Department of Natural Resources identified Shortnose Gar (Lepisosteus platostomus) and Longnose Gar (L. osseus) as priority native species lacking accurate life history (age, growth, recruitment) and ecological data (e.g. habitat use and diet) critical for effective management. To address these knowledge gaps, we initiated a pilot study to collect age, growth, and ecological data from three major river systems (Minnesota, Saint Croix, and Mississippi Rivers) and select inland lakes. Sampling methods included boat electrofishing and nearshore netting, with additional samples acquired from anglers. To investigate potential latitudinal variation in growth rates of Longnose and Shortnose Gars, we compared age-growth models (von Bertalanffy, ANCOVA) between northern (Minnesota) and southern (Mississippi) populations. Preliminary results indicated significant differences in growth rates between sexes for northern Longnose Gar, but not for northern Shortnose Gar. Conversely, growth of southern Longnose Gars did not differ between sexes, however, growth between sexes in southern Shortnose Gars was different. Our study directly addresses priority native fish knowledge gaps identified by the Minnesota Department of Natural Resources, and as directed by the Minnesota state legislature. These strategies will also be adapted for other native non-game species, helping to improve native fish conservation and management in Minnesota, and better understand latitudinal variation among populations.
2738: Declines in Blanchard's cricket frog (Acris blanchardi) along its northern range edge were well documented in the upper Midwest during the late 1990’s and early 2000’s. However, its status since then is poorly known. We surveyed 743 sites in apparently suitable habitat in the 2000s in southern Minnesota and Wisconsin and northern Iowa and Illinois, using nighttime call surveys to assess the status of this species at that time. In 2024, we resurveyed 340 of these sites to compare current distributions to known locations from the past. Each site was visited multiple times throughout the year by different observers, using both naked ear and parabolic microphones. We detected Blanchard’s cricket frog at 63 sites in 2024 at which we did not detect it in the early 2000s, and these sites are widely spread across northern Iowa and southern Wisconsin, north of most of our earlier records. This species also continues to inhabit most locations at which we found it two decades ago. This indicates that Blanchard’s cricket frog has likely expanded in recent years through its zone of previous decline along its northern range boundary. These findings highlight the importance of ongoing monitoring and conservation efforts to support this species in a changing landscape.
2739: Two processes that all life forms must face are the joint effects of shifting thermal regimes and ecological stoichiometry. Temperature impacts various biological activities, such as metabolic and developmental rates, while ecological stoichiometry mediates the balance of nutrients for reproductive, growth, and developmental purposes. Organisms inhabiting intermittent waters must navigate different times of system refill, higher temperatures, and elementally complex environments. However, there is a lack of studies investigating the ecological impacts of dynamic wetland ionomes on ecosystem function and organismal fitness. This research aims to uncover how changes in wetland ionomes from different times of system refill, temperature regimes, and the nutritional quality of periphyton interact to influence the growth and development rates of larval anurans (Lithobates blairi) across life stages. We use a factorial design crossing two times of system refill (fall vs. spring) with a thermal gradient of seven temperatures (16, 18, 20, 22, 24, 26, 28℃), yielding 140 replicate tadpoles. Measurements of body mass, snout-vent length (SVL), growth rate, and development rate for individuals will be collected across ontogeny (egg to metamorphosis), while ionomes will be collected at the end of the experiment. We also include elemental analyses of housing water and the primary food source—periphyton. By investigating how environmental and dietary nutrient fluctuations shape the thermal tolerance of L. blairi, this study provides insights into organismal fitness in dynamic wetlands and characterizes ionomic changes across trophic systems.
2740: Out of the 13 flathead toad species in Southeast Asia, three are endemic to the Philippines: P. albotaeniata, P. brevipes, and P. lighti. Eight species are endemic to the island of Borneo: P. api, P. guentheri, P. linanitensis, P. murudensis, P. penrissenensis, P. rhopophilius, and P. saravacensis, while the remaining two species, P. ingeri and P. signata, are considered to be present on the island of Sumatra in Indonesia. However, there has been no extensive research conducted on the Sumatran Pelophryne population to assess their taxonomic and systematic status. In this study, we sequenced fragments of the mitochondrial 12S and 16S rRNA genes, as well as the nuclear ncx1 gene, to address this gap. We also incorporated available GenBank sequences in our analysis. Our findings reveal that all Sumatran populations are unique, and there are at least three candidate species on the island. These candidate species exhibit sufficient genetic divergence (>2.4%) to warrant classification as new species; for instance, a 2.4% divergence exists between P. penrissenensis and P. signata. This study highlights the conservation implications for the Sumatran Pelophryne populations as well.
2741: Invasive Red lionfish (Pterois volitans) are responsible for the heavy destruction of reefs, including a decline in biodiversity. Their success in their non-native range is attributed to their lack of predators in their invasive range. Parasites are often overlooked as predators but low parasitic loads make for a more biologically fit individual, allowing for higher invasion success. For this reason, it is hypothesized that lionfish carry a lower parasitic load in their invasive range. This project aims to assess the parasite abundance in lionfish collected from along the entire reef slope in Curaçao in 2019 and 2022 by the Tornabene Lab. Using these fish I am conducting dissections examining various parts of the fish under a dissection microscope and carefully looking for parasites. The parts that are examined are the skin, body cavity, buccal cavity, fins, gonad, liver, spleen, eye, heart, intestine, filet, and gills. Using data collected from dissections, I am performing descriptive analyses to summarize parasite presence and quantity by species and body site where they were found. It is most likely that there is a low abundance of parasites within these lionfish, suggesting that parasites could play a major role in regulating populations. The absence of which could contribute to a population's success. Additionally, understanding the role that predation plays in invasive species can help us develop strategies to control their spread and prevent further ecological damage.
2742: Southeastern crowned snakes (Colubridae: Tantilla) are a group of morphologically conserved, centipede-eating snakes native to the southeastern United States. Three species are currently recognized: Tantilla coronata (southeastern crowned snake), T. oolitica (rim rock crowned snake), and T. relicta (Florida crowned snake), with the latter containing three subspecies. All taxa were originally described by Sam Telford (1966) based solely on morphological data, with some taxa described from a very limited sample size. As a result, his study may not reflect the full extent of variation within and between taxa. Furthermore, recent preliminary mitochondrial sequence data suggest significant discordance between these historical classifications and genetic clades. Some populations of T. relicta may be relegated to the wrong subspecies, and others may be relegated to the wrong species altogether. In addition to this, these preliminary data suggest that some of these taxa may be paraphyletic. We seek to address these discrepancies between Telford’s taxonomy and mtDNA clades through a comprehensive morphological and molecular analysis of the species group.
2743: The early life environment is a major driver of variation in organismal performance, health, and fitness. While phenotypic responses to early life conditions can occur immediately, effects of early environments can also persist into or emerge during later life stages. Despite the well-established role of early life conditions in shaping long-term phenotypic and performance outcomes, the developmental mechanisms underpinning these “carry-over effects” remain largely unknown. My work has been investigating the mechanistic basis of carry-over effects in desert-dwelling species of the spadefoot toad genus Spea. At the larval stage, Spea exhibit the ability to develop on two qualitatively distinct diet types: an ancestral detritus-based diet (i.e., dead or decaying plant and animal matter) or a more novel carnivorous diet of live shrimp prey. While the shrimp diet can promote faster larval growth and increase the likelihood of reaching metamorphosis before ephemeral ponds dry, developing on this alternate resource type can also alter phenotypic and performance outcomes in post-metamorphic frogs. In this symposium seminar, I will present my recent work investigating the developmental basis of diet-induced carry-over effects. Specifically, I will discuss (1) the lasting effects of early life diet on biomarkers of long-term somatic health and resilience, and (2) how these carry-over effects are shaped by hormonal and genetic mechanisms. Altogether, this work highlights the spadefoot toad as an emerging system for studying the role of diet in the evolutionary and developmental origins of health and disease.
Stress and Welfare in Organisms throughout Lifetime (HL)
2744: Bonnethead sharks (Sphyrna tiburo) form aggregations, yet the ecological and reproductive significance of this behavior remains unclear. This study examined aggregation patterns, habitat use, and reproductive behavior in Biscayne Bay, Florida, over 12 months using drone monitoring and hormone analysis. Drone surveys across 82 days recorded 1,751 bonnethead sightings, with aggregations of five or more sharks occurring on 56 days. The largest aggregation of 117 sharks was observed in August, coinciding with pupping season. Behavioral observations revealed social interactions and documented mating attempts from October to mid-November. Plasma samples from 91 female bonnetheads collected in 2019-2024 were analyzed for 17β-estradiol, progesterone, and testosterone, supporting expected reproductive timelines. Testosterone and estradiol levels were elevated from November through February, while progesterone remained high throughout all recorded aggregations, aligning with reproductive cycles such as mating, sperm storage, ovulation, gestation, and parturition. Environmental factors influencing aggregation events were analyzed, revealing that water temperature and human density significantly affected aggregation probability. Temperature, human density, and lunar illumination influenced the number of sharks in an aggregation. These findings provide insights into bonnethead reproductive ecology and habitat use, documenting high aggregation densities, mating attempts, and reproductive timelines. Understanding aggregations' environmental and biological drivers is crucial for effective species management, particularly in urban coastal habitats undergoing ecological change.
2745: Southern California provides critical nursery habitat for juvenile white sharks (Carcharodon carcharias), with historically shifting aggregation sites. In recent years, multiple aggregations have formed simultaneously at different locations, notably one near San Diego and another near Santa Barbara. These sites share key habitat features, including sandy flats, nearby estuaries, and rocky reef patches, but differ significantly in water temperature and oceanographic conditions. From 2019 to 2024, we tagged 199 unique juvenile white sharks (JWS) across both sites, yielding over 14 million detections, with many individuals carrying sensor tags recording temperature, depth, and acceleration. Generalized Additive Mixed Models (GAMMs) revealed significant differences in hourly depth use and activity levels between sites despite sharks remaining within a similar temperature range throughout the day. Notably, there was little to no mixing between sites; sharks tagged near Santa Barbara remained in the north, while those tagged near San Diego primarily stayed in the south. However, nine sharks with sensor tags were detected at both locations, with preliminary analyses suggesting behavioral switching in individuals that moved north. While northern-tagged sharks maintained shallow-water use at both sites, southern-tagged sharks, which utilized deeper waters in San Diego, adopted a shallower depth profile upon moving north. The colder temperatures and steeper thermoclines characteristic of the northern site may drive this shift. Future research will focus on the ecological and physiological drivers of these behavioral differences and the mechanisms underlying site fidelity and movement patterns in JWS.
2746: Pollution is a major driver of biodiversity loss in marine ecosystems, especially in coastal waters which serve as critical feeding and nursery grounds. As apex predators and keystone species, sharks are vulnerable to contaminant bioaccumulation, but to what degree may depend on life history and habitat urbanization. This study investigates how habitat use and feeding strategies influence contaminant bioaccumulation in sharks. We examined (1) broadnose sevengill sharks (Notorynchus cepedianus) from an urbanized (San Francisco Bay, CA (SFB)) versus a non-urbanized (Willapa Bay, WA (WB)) estuary and (2) specialist (finetooth shark, Carcharhinus isodon) versus generalist (sandbar shark, Carcharhinus plumbeus) feeders in South Carolina’s coastal waters. We hypothesized that (1) sharks in SFB will have higher contaminant concentrations than sharks in WB and (2) generalist feeders would exhibit higher contaminant burdens than specialists that consume mainly Atlantic menhaden. We quantified total mercury (Hg) using thermal decomposition, amalgamation, and atomic absorption spectrophotometry. Preliminary results indicate no significant differences in blood Hg across ontogeny in SFB, but significantly higher muscle Hg in subadult sevengill sharks compared to juveniles and neonates. In WB, total Hg concentrations differed significantly between adult and subadult sharks. Finally, subadults from SFB had significantly higher Hg concentrations compared to subadults from WB. Ongoing research includes analyzing 24 per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) via liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry, and stable isotope analysis (δ13C, δ15N) of shark muscle and prey to evaluate trophic transfer. Findings will advance ecotoxicology, inform conservation, and support pollution mitigation strategies to protect marine biodiversity and ecosystem health.
2747: Climate warming can induce a cost-of-living “squeeze” in ectotherms by increasing energetic expenditures while reducing foraging gains. We used biophysical models (validated by 2685 field observations) to test this hypothesis for 10 ecologically diverse lizards in African and Australian deserts. Historical warming (1950–2020) has been more intense in Africa than in Australia, translating to an energetic squeeze for African diurnal species. Although no net impact on Australian diurnal species was observed, warming generated an energetic “relief” (by increasing foraging time) for nocturnal species. Future warming impacts will be more severe in Africa than in Australia, requiring increased rates of food intake (+10% per hour active for diurnal species). The effects of climate warming on desert lizard energy budgets will thus be species-specific but potentially predictable.
2748: Sawfishes are emblematic of many of the current challenges faced in marine conservation. Despite comprehensive protection measures across various levels in Australia, populations remain under threat from bycatch and illegal take for their rostra. While commonly available in collections, trophy rostra often have little associated location data, limiting their use in distribution analyses critical for effective conservation strategies. This study evaluates the use of trace elemental analysis via Induction Coupled Plasma Mass Spectrometry (ICPMS) of rostral teeth to identify capture location and origin estuary for narrow (Anoxypristis cuspidata), green (Pristis zijsron) and freshwater (Pristis pristis) sawfishes along the Queensland coast. We also analysed transects along the growth axis of adult teeth aiming to reconstruct life-histories movements, providing much needed insights on endangered elasmobranchs predominately represented in literature by juveniles. Preliminary spot results from 146 teeth across 16 estuaries show promise to pinpoint rostra origin at the regional level, reducing uncertainty by several hundred kilometres. This analysis not only bridges a knowledge gap in sawfish ecology, but also suggests that rostral teeth can serve as a non-lethal solution in obtaining life history data, continuing to build on the structures that can be used as tools in conservation and marine spatial planning.

2749: Species distributions are strongly impacted by habitat availability and dispersal abilities. Dispersal in the marine environment, is influenced not only by physical barriers but also variation in habitat (i.e., temperature, depth, salinity), species biology, reproduction, and historical biogeography. While there is a large body of information relating to the distributions of many larger, wide-ranging sharks, there is limited information available for smaller bodied, cryptic species. Walking sharks (Hemiscyllium) are small, benthic dwelling sharks endemic to northern Australia and New Guinea. They are currently described as having restricted, nonoverlapping distributions. Here we present a novel finding of a mosaic of overlapping but not co-occurring distributions of two walking shark species from Milne Bay, Papua New Guinea that challenges the current understanding of walking shark distribution. We discuss these findings with response to their unique biology and biogeography.

2750: Marine protected areas (MPAs) are a widely used tool in the conservation and protection of threatened marine species. When MPAs include a species’ essential habitat into its design, they provide refuge and opportunity for recovery from exploitative pressures. This is crucial for species like elasmobranchs (sharks and rays) that are facing global declines. Using Visual Observational Transects (VOT) and Baited Remote Underwater Videos (BRUV), we assessed species richness, relative abundance, and community composition of subtropical rays to identify essential habitats within a long-standing MPA and identify current and potential conservation benefits of MPAs for rays. Surveys conducted over four years in Moreton Bay Marine Park, Queensland, Australia, observed 1195 rays of 13 species across intertidal mangrove, diverse sand flat, seagrass, and inshore reef habitats. High species richness and relative abundance were recorded at five locations where intertidal mangrove and diverse-sandflat habitats occurred adjacently and appeared to be interconnected. The high diversity and density of rays, including threatened species, using these areas for vital life history functions including reproduction, feeding, or resting, supports the identification of these as an Important Shark and Ray Area. No-take areas of Marine National Park within the Moreton Bay Marine Park overlapped with just 25% of the key habitat areas essential to rays, signifying a limitation of this MPA to contribute to ray conservation. This study underscores the need for the recognition of ray habitats into adaptive management of MPAs to ensure effective protection of rays, ultimately contributing to their persistence and to conservation of threatened species. Future research that identifies essential ray habitats should focus on long-term monitoring and the application of advanced tracking technologies along with observational data. This will further refine and more adequately apply spatial conservation measures for rays.

2751: Understanding drivers of reef manta ray (Mobula alfredi) movement and foraging is crucial for effective conservation. However, assessing their food environment, particularly the availability of zooplankton their primary food source, is challenging due to its ephemeral nature and limitations of traditional proxies such as chlorophyll-a. This study investigates environmental factors influencing M. alfredi regional movement patterns in Baa Atoll, the Maldives, using a long-term (2007-2023) dataset of 57,000 sightings, including 43,000 within the Hanifaru Marine Protected Area (MPA). Mobula alfredi sightings were analysed alongside remote environmental variables. Results indicate a significant decline in M. alfredi sightings across Baa Atoll, but a significant increase within the Hanifaru MPA, highlighting its critical role as a shallow-water foraging site. Current research focuses on identifying environmental drivers of zooplankton concentrations that trigger mass feeding aggregation events and the site affinity of M. alfredi. A zooplankton visual density index from the logbook data has been validated against in situ zooplankton biomass samples; this will be invaluable for assessing how the food environment has driven M. alfredi feeding events over the past 17 years. This research provides insights into the environmental dynamics influencing M. alfredi behaviour, essential for targeted conservation strategies.

2752: Essential habitats support ecological functions critical for species’ survival. For highly mobile and elusive marine species, aggregations in these habitats provide rare opportunities to study their ecology. This study developed a dynamic species distribution model (SDM) to predict essential habitats for migratory species, tested on whale sharks (Rhincodon typus). With ~30 documented aggregations globally, a major knowledge gap exists in the southwest Pacific (SWP). High-resolution SDMs assessed key environmental drivers and predicted seasonal habitat suitability using satellite telemetry and sightings data. An ensemble modelling approach combined regression and machine learning algorithms to reduce uncertainty and enhance reliability. Predictions indicate high suitability in the northern Great Barrier Reef during the monsoon season (Nov–Apr), shifting eastward into the Coral Sea in the dry season (May–Oct). Bathymetric variables were key drivers, alongside dynamic variables like sea surface temperature and currents. Variation across data sources and algorithms highlights the benefits of integrating diverse occurrence data sources. This first habitat suitability prediction for whale sharks in the SWP provides a framework for improving population assessments and guiding conservation strategies. The approach is broadly applicable, facilitating essential habitat identification, research prioritisation in data-limited regions, and targeted conservation in dynamic environments.

2753: Conservation of marine species is challenging, especially for threatened species that are data deficient, to inform accurate trends and condition of marine populations. The scalloped hammerhead shark (Sphyrna lewini) is classified critically endangered (IUCN), with little to no information on the habitat use and marine park protection of juvenile hammerheads in Queensland. To address this knowledge gap, we used sightings and recreational catch information and environmental variables to model (Maxent) the suitable habitat distribution of juvenile scalloped hammerhead sharks across ~11,330 km2 of the Queensland coastline. The study area included three major marine parks (Great Barrier Reef, Great Sandy and Moreton Bay Marine Parks). We used low-level protection (multiuse zones) and high-level protection (“no-take” zones) for suitable habitats within MPAs. Modelling results showed highly suitable habitats accounted for 15.75% of the study area, occurring in nearshore coastal and wetland areas and urban centres. Only 11% of these occurred in no-take MPA zones, while the majority of high suitable habitats occurred in multi-use zones (41.93 %) or outside MPAs (46.98 %). Our results showed most suitable habitats for juvenile scalloped hammerhead sharks do not fall within protected zones in Queensland waters, exposing juvenile sharks to higher anthropogenic pressures, potentially further endangering this species.

2754: Climate change driven warming of ocean temperatures is having major impacts on marine ecosystems. However, it remains poorly understood how behavioural variability within species shapes climate change responses. We utilise long-term acoustic telemetry data across 17 species of elasmobranchs to investigate climate change impacts on different movement strategies (“migrants”, “residents”, “irruptors”, and “occasionals”) across species. Using cluster-analysis and remotely-sensed temperature we find that species that employ diverse movement strategies will be less exposed to suboptimal temperatures under future climate change scenarios compared to species with less movement strategies (e.g., only residents). To illustrate possible future outcomes on distribution and migration patterns, we present a case study on bull sharks (Carcharhinus leucas). Based on 15 years of tracking data we found that sharks have delayed departure from their temperate summering grounds off Sydney, Australia by an average of 1 day per year over the study period, while also for the first time recording arrival times in October rather than November, as previously published. As a result, sharks are increasing residency duration, shifting the timing of migrations back to tropical latitudes. Since we found an average warming of 0.67 °C in the region, increased presence of bull sharks in temperate areas has the potential to impact local ecosystems through intensified predation while increasing overlap with people.

2755: The Global FinPrint Project began in 2015 with the goal of assessing the factors that influence shark and ray abundance, diversity, and distribution on the world’s coral reefs. We surveyed 391 coral reefs in 67 nations and territories using 22,756 baited remote underwater video systems (BRUVS). Analyses revealed the functional extinction of sharks on ~16% of sampled reefs and we failed to detect several key species at up to 50% of surveyed reefs. Remote reefs and nations where shark fishing is prohibited had abundant and diverse shark assemblages, elsewhere there was a shift of the shark and ray community towards ray dominated assemblages in areas lacking effective shark management. A positive effect of some forms of fisheries management (catch limits, gear restrictions) and large marine protected areas (MPAs) on shark abundances was observed, particularly when combined. Now, a nearly decade later, we are resampling sites with paired MPA, non-MPA reefs to determine the long-term effectiveness of spatial management. Preliminary results will be discussed, with an emphasis on Southeast Asian sites.

2756: Tun Mustapha Park (TMP), Sabah’s second-largest Marine Protected Area, supports over 80,000 coastal residents reliant on small-scale fisheries. Sharks and rays, often caught as bycatch, are retained for food security and economic reasons by communities in TMP. Fisher interviews suggest declining populations, with reduced catch frequencies compared to historical levels, highlighting the need for bycatch mitigation measures. Structured interviews with 49 fishers in TMP identified live release as the most feasible and accepted bycatch reduction strategy. A pilot trial was agreed to be conducted from August to December 2024 in two villages with voluntary, experienced fishers to evaluate its effectiveness. Fishers were given safe release practices and are encouraged to release all small or juvenile sharks and rays. Over three months, enumerators recorded all captured sharks and rays, whether released alive or retained dead, using standardized data sheets and video documentation of safe releases where possible. This study assesses the feasibility of live release for selected species and explores how non-financial incentives—such as safety equipment and social recognition—can encourage pro-conservation behavior. Findings will inform potential long term integration of live release practices into TMP’s small-scale fisheries management.

2757: Many threatened chondrichthyans rely on critical habitats which facilitate functions essential to their ongoing persistence. This includes areas which are required for use as corridors where species can move freely between sites utilised to fulfil life history requirements. Effective management of these areas requires understanding of how and when they are utilised by species. Developments in underwater camera technologies have improved the capacity of citizen scientists to collect quality data, allowing for broadscale monitoring of species site use at locations which are frequently visited by divers. Wolf Rock, Queensland, Australia is a critical habitat for the east Australian population of the critically endangered grey nurse shark (Carcharias taurus), serving as the only known gestation site for the species. The site also supports a variety of other threatened chondrichthyans, though, the importance of Wolf Rock to these species remains unknown. Wolf Rock is frequented by recreational divers, but is difficult to survey with traditional methods due to its location and ecological significance to C. taurus. Currently, only a handful of studies have been conducted at the site, all focusing on C. taurus, and none assessing species behaviour. Here we partner with a local dive tourism operator to conduct roaming diver surveys to assess seasonal richness, abundance and behavioural patterns of chondrichthyans at Wolf Rock.

2758: Leopard sharks (Stegostoma tigrinum) seasonally aggregate in Southeast Queensland, yet their behaviours and habitat use in coastal areas remain unclear. Acoustic telemetry confirms their presence at key aggregation sites, such as North Stradbroke Island, but their activities in these areas remain poorly understood. This study leverages drone footage from the Queensland SharkSmart drone trial alongside acoustic telemetry data (2019–2024) to examine their behaviours in coastal environments. \Our objectives are to (1) characterise observed behaviours such as surface swimming, milling, and resting, (2) assess the potential biological functions of these areas, including mating, social interaction, and thermoregulation, and (3) evaluate the alignment between drone-based observations and telemetry data in tracking movement. By comparing telemetry detections with behavioural observations from drone footage, we aim to better understand how leopard sharks interact with these environments while aggregating. Coastal areas may serve critical functions such as reproduction, social behaviours, or environmental regulation, yet their specific role in leopard shark ecology remains uncertain. While drones provide valuable insights into surface activity, their inability to capture submerged behaviours highlights the need for complementary methods. Findings will enhance knowledge of essential habitats, and improve understanding of coastal environments’ importance for leopard sharks in Australia.

2759: Urogymnus dalyensis, the freshwater whipray, was initially separated from Himantura chaophraya, the Asian giant freshwater whipray, in 2008, leaving many critical aspects of its biology, such as distribution, size, and salinity range, ambiguously documented, primarily due to the limited data availability. Previously categorised within the Himantura genus, both species were reassigned to the Urogymnus genus in 2016, which now comprises five species. For a long time, U. dalyensis was considered to be restricted to freshwater environments, but both morphological assessment of its sensory organs and acoustic telemetry data indicate that the species is likely to inhabit higher salinity habitats as well. The species is currently only known from selected rivers in Northern Australia (from Western Australia to the Gulf of Carpentaria), and southern New Guinea. The combination of fieldwork, citizen science data, and Aboriginal rock art provides insights into the biology of U. dalyensis that have not been described to date. Citizen science data indicates that this species also inhabits the east coast of Australia, from the tip of Cape York to the Cooktown region, with specimens documented in upstream freshwater habitats as well as coastal and reef environments. A juvenile ray, likely young of the year, was captured and released in Rinyirru (Lakefield) National Park CYPAL, with a disk width of 38 cm. Large female rays up to 150 cm disk width have been documented through ecological surveys in the Mitchell River and Port Musgave, increasing the known size of the species. East coast rays were genetically sampled, and confirmed to be U. dalyensis through genetic barcoding. Large rays are also present in the documented rock art from the Laura Region, indicating that the presence of this species on the east coast is not a recent range expansion.

2760: While we know that many adults fear sharks, little is known about how children perceive sharks, particularly at younger ages. This study explored children’s perceptions of sharks through utilising a parent-mediated survey where we collected qualitative responses from children (N = 374) aged 2–12 years predominantly from Australia, the United States, and the United Kingdom. We found that children often described sharks by referencing physical attributes (e.g., teeth, fins, size) and behaviours (e.g., swimming, eating). Twothirds of the children expressed liking sharks, citing their perceived “coolness” and visual appeal, while dislike of sharks was frequently linked to fear of harm or perceptions of sharks as being scary. Notably, 39% of children associated sharks with fear or danger, with these associations peaking at ages 4 and 11. Fear associations were less prevalent among children who visited the ocean weekly, suggesting that familiarity with marine environments may mitigate fear. Parental fear of sharks showed a slight influence, as children of highly fearful parents were more likely to associate sharks with danger. We also explore where children obtain their experiences of sharks, aside from through their parents. Our findings underscore the importance of educational initiatives and balanced media representations that emphasize the ecological diversity of sharks, aiming to foster nuanced and less fear-driven perceptions among children.

2761: Intertidal reef flats serve as communal nurseries for juvenile stingrays, where they perform important roles as mesopredators and ecosystem engineers; however, contributions to ecosystem processes can vary among species. We investigated the foraging behaviours of three stingrays: the cowtail stingray (Pastinachus ater), mangrove whipray (Urogymnus granulatus), and pink whipray (Pateobatis fai) at Pioneer Bay, Orpheus Island. Individual rays were followed using drones for 7-18 minutes (mean = 13.5) at heights of 3-5 m, and details were recorded for each feeding event. Analysis of 96 behavioural tracks revealed distinct foraging tactics among the three species. Cowtail stingrays and mangrove whiprays fed more frequently at low tides than high tides, which may reflect changes in prey availability across the tidal gradient or increased predation risk with depth. Cowtail stingrays and pink whiprays preferred foraging on smooth sand using nondisruptive feeding behaviours, although cowtail stingrays also used intense excavation feeding more often than other species. In contrast, mangrove whiprays showed greater preferences for coral rubble substrates and alternated between surface and suction feeding. Although findings support resource partitioning and species-specific functional roles, further works are needed to effectively link diets, prey distributions, and specific foraging behaviours, and to quantify functional outputs at the species level.

2762: Coastal systems are a vital resource to marine biodiversity, facilitating many essential ecological functions. However, proximity to human populations exposes aquatic animals in these systems to substantial levels of anthropogenic pressures. An understanding of the environmental factors influencing how species use coastal resources can help managers reduce the impact of human stressors on these coastal species. Southern eagle rays (Myliobatis tenuicaudatus) are distributed broadly across southern Australia and are highly resident to Gulf St Vincent, Adelaide, South Australia. We used standardised, repeated drone surveys at two locations on the Adelaide coastline (Christies Beach n = 70; Seacliff Beach n = 71) to assess the influence of environmental factors and backyard feeding (i.e., non-regulated provisioning of food) on the abundance, habitat selectivity, behaviour, and distribution of southern eagle rays. Southern eagle rays were observed 503 times and were more frequent off Seacliff Beach where backyard feeding occurs. Ray abundance was driven by water temperature at both sites, by time of day at Christies Beach, and by tidal phase at Seacliff Beach. Southern eagle rays at Christies Beach selected for macroalgal reef over sand, while the opposite was observed at Seacliff Beach. Behaviour at Christies Beach was influenced by environmental variables, but by human presence at Seacliff Beach. This study provided insight into southern eagle rays on a localised scale which can be used to inform managers and reduce the possible influence of backyard feeding on ray abundance, habitat use, and behaviour.
