2763: The marine park waters surrounding Lord Howe Island are a World Heritage Listed site that hosts the world’s most southerly coral reef, and support an abundance of marine life, including numerous endemic species and healthy fish populations. Yet, the most common shark species (the Galapagos shark, Carcharhinus galapagensis) regularly interact with fishing vessels through depredation of target fish. These fisher-shark interactions impact not only local commercial and recreational fisheries (through the loss of catch and gear) but also sharks (through bycatch injury and retaliatory actions). This human-wildlife conflict poses a threat to a range of social, economic and environmental values for the marine parks. An ongoing shark research program was established in 2018 to better understand the dynamics of negative interactions at this location and develop solutions to mitigate them. We use a co-designing approach that combines acoustic telemetry and vessel tracking to assess overlap between fishing effort and fish movements; social surveys to investigate community perceptions towards sharks; logbook reports to estimate depredation rates and financial loss; testing of deterrent devices to assess their effectiveness at reducing depredation; genetic analyses of population structure; and a citizen science project to photo-identify sharks. Here, we present data identifying optimal strategies to promote co-existence and benefit sharks, the local community and broader marine ecosystem.

2764: Fishes utilise an array of undulatory swimming modes during steady locomotion, characterised by variation in the length, amplitude, and frequency of propulsive waves across the body. Several disparate aquatic lineages (including sturgeon, eels, lamprey, and sharks) have been shown to use a double oscillation system, in which head yaw (lateral movement of the head) is decoupled from tailbeat frequency. Double oscillation systems consequently result in the propagation of multiple wavelengths across the body and have been hypothesised to convey sensory benefits. Despite this, our understanding of how morphology or body form may influence use of a double oscillation system is limited. Here, we use drone videography to study the volitional swimming kinematics of the giant shovelnose ray (Glaucostegus typus) at Lucinda Beach, North Queensland, Australia. As a rhinopristiform batoid, G. typus utilises body caudal fin locomotion but exhibits substantial dorsoventral flattening and fusion of the pectoral fins, head, and anterior body into a pectoral ‘disc’. This study aims to quantify the double oscillation system during steady swimming which we hypothesize will be constrained in a species with morphological specialisation and reduced anterior body flexibility.

2765: Identifying essential habitats across life stages is crucial for effective conservation. The great hammerhead shark (Sphyrna mokarran), one of the most endangered shark species globally, experienced steep population declines throughout much of its distribution. Despite its conservation importance, knowledge about its habitat requirements remains limited. Research is hindered by ecological challenges such as the species' naturally low population densities and frequent misidentification of neonates and juveniles due to morphological similarities with other hammerhead species. Adding to these difficulties are significant language barriers in scientific communication, with valuable information often remaining isolated in non-English literature. These challenges have created significant knowledge gaps compared to better-studied congeners like the scallop and smooth hammerheads. In this study, we conducted a comprehensive synthesis of great hammerhead habitat use patterns by expanding beyond English-language publications. By including Portuguese, Spanish, and French literature—languages spoken in many tropical and subtropical countries within the species' distribution range—we uncovered valuable information from theses, fisheries reports, and scientific publications, that had remained invisible in the English-language scientific literature. This approach revealed previously overlooked data from regions that represent critical parts of the species' distribution. Our findings demonstrate that breaking language barriers is essential for uncovering the full picture of habitat requirements for widely distributed species.

2766: Artificial intelligence (AI) can recognise species in photographs and videos, can extract species occurrence from video processing, and can re-identify known animals. AI substantially improved researchers’ productivity, reducing the bottleneck of data processing, and expanding the possibilities of non-invasively tracking individual animals through time and space. Photographic identification (photo ID) is used to identify individuals via their skin patterns, and AI allows researchers to process large dataset. This study combines the most novel AI solutions to improve animal re-identification for several species of elasmobranchs. The final model uses convolutional neural networks to identify individual animals from whale sharks, tiger sharks, epaulette sharks, leopard sharks, oceanic whitetips. Methods such as semi-supervised and unsupervised learning, and similarity learning networks are used to streamline learning and improve the flexibility of the model when tackling different tasks. For instance, the same fundamental structure is used to recognise individuals of leopard shark, from juvenile to adult stages, identifying and tracking areas of pattern stability during morphological ontogenetic changes. Overall, this approach has the potential to address challenges associated with long-term datasets and provide an open access tool for researchers to flexibly use AI for their photo ID research.

2767: The Philippines is a marine biodiversity hotspot, home to a vast array of shark and ray species, many of which face population declines. However, effective conservation strategies require a deeper understanding of the cultural significance and local perceptions surrounding the ecological, economic and spiritual roles of these animals. This study explores the values, beliefs, and attitudes of coastal communities in the province of Palawan toward sharks and rays. Fieldwork was conducted through 60 semi-structured interviews with fishers, tourism operators, and key community members across four sites in Palawan. Findings indicate that while sharks and rays are not considered deities, traditional beliefs permeate contemporary perceptions – such as the use of stingray tails for protection against malevolent supernatural beings. Sharks and rays also hold culinary importance, particularly in dishes like ginataan or kinunot, where their meat is cooked in coconut milk. Despite their cultural and practical uses, sharks tended to be perceived negatively, with many respondents expressing fear or strong dislike. This study highlights the complex and multifaceted relationships between coastal communities and sharks and rays. These animals are seen through a lens shaped by tradition, fear, and utility – from their role in folklore to their place in local cuisine. In Palawan, where some respondents continue consuming sharks and rays despite existing restrictions, integrating cultural perspectives into conservation efforts could lead to more sustainable harvesting practices. A culturally informed approach may bridge the gap between tradition and conservation, fostering stronger community support for marine protection efforts.

2768: Since the 1990s, intense fishing bycatch has driven a steady decline in Mediterranean shark and ray populations, while limited data and low public engagement hinder conservation efforts. iNaturalist, arguably the worlds’ largest citizen science platform for mapping biodiversity, offers a potential data source for studying their diversity and distribution. This study evaluates the benefits and potential limitations of using iNaturalist for its purpose. Shark and ray records from four identified Mediterranean regions were retrieved and mapped for observation patterns, species diversity, and distribution. Each image was scored for image quality, and the species identification given for the record verified by two independent checkers. Key findings reveal that 67% of images were of good quality, 95% of records were identifiable to species level, and 71% were correctly classified. Observations were concentrated in Greece (30%), France (26%), and Spain (15%), with 51% of records from unnatural settings. The most frequently reported species included Hexanchus griseus, Scyliorhinus canicula, Prionace glauca, and Mustelus mustelus among sharks, while Torpedo and Raja species dominated among rays. While iNaturalist is valuable for documenting elasmobranch presence and human interactions, its use in scientific research requires consideration. The platform provides a way to collect information that would otherwise remain unknown or unavailable but requires independent verification for scientific use. Strengthening community engagement, improving photography guidelines, and enhancing internal verification could increase data reliability to inform conservation and management strategies for Mediterranean elasmobranch species.

2769: The diet of Chondrichthyes is often the focus of trophic ecology studies, but few of them have addressed the processes that facilitate coexistence of sympatric predators, such as resource competition or partitioning. Understanding resource use requires quantifying species’ trophic niche widths and their overlap to infer generalist or specialist feeding, and potential competition for preys. This study used stable isotope and multivariate fatty acid datasets to assess habitat and diet, estimate niche widths, and predict overlap of 14 sympatric chondrichthyan mesopredators from coastal southern Australia. Stable isotopes clustered species into pelagic and sandy/seagrass-associated groups, while fatty acids showed two clusters with higher levels of overlap among species. This suggests complex resource partitioning, such as nutritional niche segregation or distinct habitat use, to facilitate coexistence. Mobile species like southern eagle rays (Myliobatis tenuicaudatus) and bronze whalers (Carcharhinus brachyurus) were identified to be the most generalist in both their habitat and nutritional resource use, determined from their isotopic and fatty acid niche width, respectively. Less mobile and smaller species like southern sawsharks (Pristiophorus nudipinnis) and elephant fish (Callorhinchus milii) exhibited specialist traits in both habitat and nutritional resource use. Overlap occurred both within taxa groups and between specialists and generalists. This underscores the need for diverse marine environments to support prey species and minimise competition. Given threats like tropicalisation and trawling that are occurring in southern Australia, understanding trophic interactions and resource use in these mesopredatory chondrichthyans is critical.

2770: White sharks (Carcharodon carcharias) have been shown to expand their diet and foraging strategies as they grow. As they approach ~ 3.5 m, they move from consuming inshore teleost and chondrichthyan prey to a mixed diet also including marine mammals and pelagic cephalopods. White shark diet has yet to be investigated in Australia, where ongoing tagging studies have revealed that they rarely travel off the continental shelf. This contrasts the eastern pacific white shark population where large sharks frequently migrate off the continental shelf. We assessed diet using signature fatty acid profiling from 145 individuals ranging from 1.6– 5.5 m, collected from South Australia. Unlike the ontogenetic diet shifts observed in the eastern Pacific and off the coast of South Africa, white sharks in Australia show no sizerelated differences in diet or increase in pelagic foraging, with fatty acids indicating marine mammal consumption (22:5w3, 20:5w3 or 16:1w7) or pelagic foraging (22:6w3, 16:0, 18:0) remaining similar across all sizes. Instead of specialised apex predators, the South Australian white sharks of all sizes are generalist predators with less reliance on pinnipeds and a wider diet breadth than previously thought. This parallels their coastal habitat use, which affords them a wide variety of coastal prey items.

2771: Port Phillip Bay (PPB) is extensively used for commercial and recreational purposes, including fishing, shipping, and ecotourism. Sharks and rays are abundant throughout PPB, yet despite their high ecological, cultural and economic importance, our understanding of how sharks and rays move throughout PPB is limited. The Southern Fiddler Ray (Trygonorrhina dumerilii) is a common coastal species of elasmobranch, endemic to southern Australian waters, that has been identified by traditional owners as culturally significant. Swan Bay is a small shallow embayment located inside PPB. Almost the entire Swan Bay is a marine national park. Here, I use acoustic telemetry to describe both finescale and larger-scale patterns of space use and activity of Southern Fiddler Rays across varying life stages, within Swan Bay. I will discuss these findings to date, and how understanding these movement patterns enables effective management of these culturally important species in PPB, as it is increasingly impacted by expanding human activity.

2772: Deep-sea skates are among the primary bycatch species in Southern Ocean demersal fisheries yet many aspects of their behaviour and space use are unknown. This knowledge gap is particularly significant given that post-release survival rates for skates in deep-set fisheries can be relatively low. A better understanding of activity patterns may help mitigate fisheries mortality by improving bycatch avoidance and management. Here we investigate free-ranging activity patterns of Kerguelen sandpaper skates (n=6), Bathyraja irrasa, caught in the Heard Island and McDonald Island Patagonian toothfish longline fishery using popup satellite archival tags (PSAT). One tag retrieved by chance provided high frequency data indicating the skate was repeatedly alternating phases of activity with short periods of rest, most often 1 to 2 min long, and likely stayed within 10 m of the bottom. Skates underwent extensive vertical migrations (up to 300 m daily) following bathymetric contours 800-1600 m deep. We modelled horizontal movement patterns based on vertical movements and bathymetric contours using Hidden Markov models. Minimum distance travelled was 2 km/day on average and up to 8 km/day for a skate that travelled 140 km from its release point over 30 days. There was no indication of diel vertical migration, but tidal currents may influence behaviour. These movement patterns will inform Southern Ocean bycatch management measures currently based on limited empirical data.

2773: Satellite tagging of whale sharks (Rhincodon typus) at Ningaloo Reef has previously focused on juvenile males which dominate this aggregation site, with tracking durations averaging 120 days. We present a dataset of 39 whale sharks (Total Length = 3.8 – 9.3 m) satellite tagged at Ningaloo Reef, with comparable numbers of males (n = 20) and females (n = 18) and one shark of unknown sex. Tracks of whale sharks averaged 3009 ± 432 km in length and 67.6% of tracks exceeded 1000 km, with deployment spans ranging from 9 – 340 days. Depth records of whale sharks showed they spent > 90% of time in epipelagic waters ≤ 200 m and dived to a maximum depth of 1906 m. Long-term movements of whale sharks were revealed using state-space models, kernel utilisation distributions and generalised additive models. Horizontal movements indicated diverse migration strategies throughout the eastern Indian Ocean. Vertical movements varied between males and females, both seasonally and across coastal and oceanic phases. Depth use was seasonally influenced by Sea Surface Temperature (SST) with males selecting warmer SSTs in some months, while females inhabited more variable SSTs. The results provide previously undescribed evidence of sex-specific patterns in both horizontal and vertical habitat use of whale sharks over broad spatio-temporal scales. This extends understanding of the movement ecology of this species, particularly for females, whose movements and distribution are poorly understood throughout their range. Knowledge of intraspecific movement patterns is critical for developing effective spatial management tools for migratory species like whale sharks.

2774: Movement patterns of bull sharks along the east coast of Australia are complex, varying according to size and sex and across space and time. Drivers of such behavioural variability have been linked to differences in seasonal prey aggregations and water temperature changes across latitudes. There is some evidence that females demonstrate philopatry to natal rivers on a bi-annual cycle, and juveniles reside within these systems for their first 3 5 years. Here we used a novel approach combining genetics and animal tracking to link wide-roaming individuals to potential natal regions spanning tropical to temperate latitudes and assess how these locations may influence individual movement patterns. Between 2015 and 2023, 95 adult bull sharks were acoustically tagged in New South Wales (NSW; n = 42) and Queensland (QLD; n = 44) and movements monitored from Western Cape York in northern QLD to southern NSW. Movement patterns of adult bull sharks were mapped and individuals with common patterns grouped. Tissue samples from the tagged bull sharks and 374 juveniles sampled from 28 rivers were collected for genetic SNP analysis. Adult females, with comparable movement patterns had similar relatedness values to juveniles from certain nursery regions. Overall, females that made large-scale movements across most of the east coast shared relatedness to juveniles from rivers in NSW and SE QLD, while females that were largely resident across central and northern QLD were more related to juveniles from those northern regions. The pattern for males was less clear. These findings highlight that philopatry and place of birth are a driver for movement patterns in bull sharks, shaping unique movement strategies. ─

2775: Fine-scale movements and the drivers of space-use within restricted riverine habitats by bull sharks (Carcharhinus leucas) are not well understood. From juvenile to sub-adulthood, predator avoidance, competition for space and prey resources, and driving environmental influences all determine how bull sharks are stratified across a system. This project aims to correlate movements of acoustically tagged bull sharks by size and sex with environmental data to elucidate fluctuations in abundance in four neighbouring river systems off the Sunshine Coast, Queensland. Ten bull sharks were tagged as part of a pilot study (2018– 2021), with a further 84 tagged in the full program (2023–2025). Preliminary detection data indicates a significant overlap of juvenile (1-1.5m total length (TL)) and sub-adult (1.5-2m TL) habitat use, while young-of-year (YOY; <1m TL)) used the same habitats, but at different times of the day. YOY initially tagged upriver were prevalent in the lower reaches only in summer after rainfall, when turbidity was higher – areas usually maintained by subadults. Older sub-adult bull sharks exhibit site fidelity, leaving and returning regularly to both their birth rivers, but also neighbouring rivers – demonstrating strong connectivity in the regional systems as they slowly expand their home ranges. The purpose of visitation to the estuarine ‘refuges’ is still being explored. Due to several recent human-shark encounters in southeast Queensland, management of bull sharks is under critical review. These data will assist managers in understanding coastal movement drivers better, and facilitate informed shark smart information for waterway users in the region.

2776: Animal behaviour is influenced by a complex interplay of internal and external factors. However, identifying primary drivers of behaviour is often a challenge, particularly in marine environments where direct observation is difficult. This is especially acute for large marine predators like sharks, which travel long distances horizontally and vertically and do not need to surface to breathe. We combined high-resolution biologging data from 20 white sharks (Carcharodon carcharias) with environmental variables (e.g. temperature, depth, currents, habitat type) to identify key drivers of foraging behaviour. Using a hierarchical Hidden Markov Model, we classified four distinct behaviours, area-restricted searching (ARS), travelling, resting, and bursting, based on pitch angles, vector of dynamic body acceleration (VeDBA), step lengths, and pseudo-track tortuosity. The influence of abiotic factors on behavioural states was assessed using Generalised Additive Mixed Models and identified that foraging behaviour (ARS) was primarily driven by habitat type, time of day, and individual variation. Additionally, ARS typically occurred on the seabed or at the surface, during the day. Resting was the dominant behaviour and consisted of both linear and circular swimming. Circling behaviour may indicate uni-hemispheric sleep in white sharks. Our study is among the first to examine the fine-scale behaviour of immature white sharks in a nearshore environment and over extended periods (> 4 days)

2777: The need for a comprehensive understanding of species movement has become increasingly evident for the world’s animals. This knowledge is essential for developing effective policy and management strategies. Apex predators play a crucial role in their environments due to their disproportionately large influence on ecosystems and have become a focal point for fisheries because of seemingly increasing anthropogenic interactions. Understanding their distribution is vital, as they often cover vast ranges and contribute to complex trophic cascades, increasingly influenced by and influencing human activity. Along the east coast of Australia, tiger sharks (Galeocerdo cuvier) are a top predator who have been the subject of tracking studies across their geographic range, especially more recently from associations with negative human- shark interactions. Tracking studies conducted along east coast Australia have lacked sampling mature male tiger sharks. To quantify the movements of this segment of the population, we satellite tagged ten mature male tiger sharks and assessed the horizontal and vertical characteristics of these tracks to determine if any sex- and size-based shifts in dispersal or distribution are evident. Our findings will provide critical knowledge towards appropriate species’ assessments and management, especially in regard to anthropogenic ocean activities such as game fishing and bather protection programs).

2778: Human coastal populations and water-based recreation are growing, increasing potential for interactions with sharks in coastal waters near popular beaches. However, lethal means of mitigating shark bite risks may have ecological effects, while non-lethal relocation of sharks could result in recurrent risks to beachgoers. Tiger sharks (Galeocerdo cuvier) are one of three species involved in most unprovoked shark bites globally. Under the Queensland Shark Control Program, tiger sharks caught on drumlines and catch alert drumlines at beaches in the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park are tagged and relocated away from the beach. Using the IMOS acoustic tracking network off eastern Australia, we compared movements of 51 tiger sharks relocated from beaches with 82 tagged at other locations in the marine park over more than two years. We discuss whether relocated tiger sharks are more likely to visit beaches than conspecifics from locations further offshore. We also compare the broad-scale movement ecology of both groups using network analyses and assess trends in visitation and residency at beaches among sex and maturity classes. Insights from this study will help assess the risks and benefits of relocating tiger sharks away from popular beaches.

2779: The great hammerhead (Sphyrna mokarran) is listed as Critically Endangered (IUCN, 2019) due to overfishing and significant population declines across its range. Despite growing conservation concerns, its movement patterns and functional habitats in the Pacific remain poorly understood. In the western Tuamotu Archipelago of French Polynesia, this species is frequently observed around the atolls of Rangiroa and Tikehau. Sightings reported by citizen science groups suggest that the Rangiroa lagoon may serve as a key feeding, breeding, or nursery ground, prompting the establishment of the largest acoustic receiver network in the Central Pacific (58 receivers in the Rangiroa lagoon, 23 in the atoll passes, and 4 in the Tikehau pass). We acoustically tagged 27 female great hammerheads (22 in Rangiroa, 5 in Tikehau) to investigate movement patterns and connectivity between these atolls. Preliminary findings reveal individual variability in space use and distinct habitat utilisation between the two atolls. Sharks tagged in Tikehau exhibited consistent residency to the pass year-round (RI: 0.23 - 0.79), with occasional and brief visits to specific areas of the Rangiroa lagoon in winter and summer months. In contrast, sharks tagged in Rangiroa were not detected in Tikehau but displayed residency to the Tiputa pass during the austral summer (RI: 0.46 ± 0.06), likely driven by abundant prey availability, leaving the pass area the rest of the year (RI: 0.11 ± 0.05), with one shark spending seven straight month in the lagoon. Sharks also showed evidence of diel habitat use, being found in passes primarily during the day. 2780: Mobile predators often exhibit resident behaviour, whereby they remain in restricted geographic areas for extended periods (Chapman et al., 2015). Despite their broad distribution across neritic and pelagic ecosystems, white sharks (Carcharodon carcharias) show residency to specific sites likely due to prey availability and environmental conditions. The white sharks at Neptune Islands Group, South Australia, have a high abundance of white sharks, in part due to the abundant prey from local pinniped colonies. Australia’s only cage-diving site is located at the Neptune Islands, providing tourists from around the world with the unique opportunity to view white sharks in the wild. The effects and regulations of cage-diving on white sharks are well documented at the Neptune Islands. However, there has been limited investigation on biological and environmental factors affecting the visitation patterns of white sharks. Changes in white shark presence and residency have been observed over the years, highlighting the need to monitor movement in the area and determine what factors may influence this behaviour. Our research aims to identify the drivers of white shark residency at the Neptune Islands by analysing long term acoustic telemetry data from 187 individuals tracked over an 11-year period. We present our findings, including sex and size-class composition of white sharks at the Neptune Islands, residency trends across years, and the influence of environmental factors on residency patterns.

2781: Sharks often modify their behaviour in response to human activities. Food provisioning, where animals obtain food from humans either directly or indirectly, can lead to disrupted resource use patterns and altered interactions within and between shark species. At Norfolk Island, a remote small island in the Pacific Ocean, sharks aggregate at two piers where fish are cleaned and discards are thrown into the water. We used acoustic telemetry and dietary biomarkers (fatty acids and stable isotopes) to quantify dusky (Carcharhinus obscurus; n = 18) and Galapagos (C. galapagensis; n = 16) shark associations with the piers. Specifically, we evaluated the frequency and timing of visitations to piers across diel periods, patterns of co-occurrence, and contribution of discards to the diet of both species. Individuals visited the piers, on average, once every four days (~3 hours daily), with dusky sharks usually arriving in the early afternoon and staying until dusk while Galapagos sharks arrived at dusk and left in the early morning. Despite this temporal partitioning, the diets of both species were indistinguishable from each other and showed only limited contribution of discarded fish. The findings of this study indicate that food provisioning at the piers has not markedly altered foraging behaviour and that regular visits to the piers only serve to supplement diet. Understanding how sharks use the piers in response to human activities will help assess current waste disposal practices at Norfolk Island and ongoing monitoring needs.

2782: Spatio-temporal niche partitioning is a crucial component of ecosystem dynamics. For elasmobranchs, niche partitioning can reduce intraguild competition and predation, subsequently underpinning the function and structure of these predator communities. Despite the ecological importance of niche partitioning, for many coastal shark communities we lack a detailed understanding of how they may partition in space and time. Hence, the objective of this study was to investigate whether niche partitioning allows apex and mesopredator sharks to coincide at an inshore island group on the Great Barrier Reef. We utilised acoustic tracking data to assess whether four functional groups; reef sharks, small whalers, large whalers, or top order sharks used spatio-temporal separation. Although spatial partitioning was low in the Whitsunday Islands, the timing of activity varied for all groups, where reef sharks had the greatest probability of detection at night, small whalers during the morning, top order sharks around midday, and large whalers in the afternoon. Furthermore, shark groups appeared to use Cid Harbour at different temporal scales, where reef sharks and small whalers had longer visit durations, while top order and large whaler sharks were only active in the harbour for short durations. Overall, these findings highlight that in the absence of spatial partitioning, diel partitioning may serve as an important driver of coexistence among intraguild predators.

2783: Natural mortality can be used as a measure of a species’ resilience and is widely used in the management of fish species. Natural mortality can be calculated using life history parameters, however this can be difficult in data poor species. Acoustic telemetry provides an accurate alternative to estimate natural mortality based on relocations over time. Northern Australia’s river sharks, the Northern River Shark (Glyphis garricki) and Speartooth Shark (G. glyphis), are two rare and threatened species occurring in rivers, estuaries, and inshore marine waters. This study aimed to use acoustic telemetry to estimate natural mortality across a range of size classes and explore the effect of size class, season, and location on mortality rates. An array acoustic receiver was deployed in rivers of Van Diemen Gulf, Northern Territory, Australia. Detections from 185 sharks between 2013 and 2024 were converted into capture histories which were used to calculate yearly and monthly estimates of mortality. Data demonstrate that river sharks experience extremely high rates of mortality. Younger individuals had significantly higher rates of mortality, with G. glyphis and G. garricki neonates experiencing average yearly mortality rates of 0.898 and 0.731, respectively, compared with 0.120 and 0.233 in subadults. Although mortality was highly variable temporally, over months and years, there were no significant differences between seasons, years or location, and there was no significant difference between species. Results indicate that river sharks in Van Diemen Gulf likely have very limited capacity to recover from population decline and are therefore vulnerable to environmental change and anthropogenic threats. Population monitoring and habitat management is critical to ensure the persistence of river sharks into the future.

2784: Fishing activities are the primary threat to deepwater chondrichthyans (sharks, rays, and chimaeras). These species are highly susceptible to overexploitation but are frequently captured as bycatch in deepwater fisheries. While international interest in understanding and reducing fishing mortality on chondrichthyans is growing, limited research has been conducted on deepwater species. Leafscale Gulper Shark (Centrophorus squamosus) are being tagged with Wildlife Computer survivorship tags (sPATs) as part of a study to understand their post-release survival in offshore fisheries in New Zealand and the wider Pacific region. To date, nine individuals have been tagged in bottom longline fisheries and five in bottom trawl fisheries. Preliminary survival estimates are about 60% and 40% in longline and trawl gear, respectively. Three tags have been recovered, and tag data showed sharks engaged in regular diel movement patterns with preferred temperature and depth ranges. Survival in the longline fisheries is comparable with a study in the Northeast Atlantic, but to the author’s knowledge, this is the first attempt to tag trawl-caught sharks. While these preliminary survivorship estimates are promising, depth profiles suggest the species spends most of its vertical distribution within the reach of current fishing effort, with limited refuge at depth.

2785: The IUCN Species Survival Commission (SSC) Shark Specialist Group (SSG) was established in 1991 in response to growing concerns about the severe impact of fisheries on sharks, rays, and chimaeras (chondrichthyans). Since then, the SSG has played a critical role in the global conservation of chondrichthyans and has significantly contributed to guiding research and informing policy at local, regional, and international scales. As a network of volunteers, the SSG fosters connections with experts globally and provides access to cutting-edge research, training, and collaborative opportunities to advance the conservation of chondrichthyans. This presentation highlights some key SSG initiatives including (1) ongoing efforts to assess and monitor the conservation status of chondrichthyans and maintain the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species for these species; (2) identifying critical habitats for chondrichthyans through the Important Shark and Ray Areas (ISRAs) project; 3) informing multilateral environmental agreements to promote the introduction and implementation of effective and evidence-based policies; and (4) our recent global synthesis on the status of chondrichthyans that includes Oceania´s regionspecific threats and priority conservation actions. By integrating science with conservation planning, the SSG aims to ensure that knowledge translates into meaningful interventions for chondrichthyan species worldwide.
2786: We introduce the IUCN SSC Shark Specialist Group’s report on the Global Status of Sharks, Rays, and Chimaeras, which provides a comprehensive update on the state of these species two decades after the first report in 2005. Over the past 20 years, significant changes have occurred in the understanding and conservation of these species, marked by an expanded scope of research and the recognition of emerging threats. The global focus on sharks, rays, and chimaeras has grown substantially, with increased attention in policy, fisheries management, and conservation efforts. The report highlights the accelerating global changes to aquatic ecosystems and the critical need to address these threats. This presentation will highlight the chapters covering the Oceania region, including Australia, New Zealand, Melanesia, Micronesia, and Polynesia.

2787: The International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List of Threatened Species is the world’s most comprehensive inventory of the global conservation status of animal, fungi, and plant species. In response to the growing awareness and concern of fisheries impacts on chondrichthyans (sharks, rays, and chimaeras), the IUCN Species Survival Commission Shark Specialist Group (SSG) was established in 1991 and is now recognized as the leading authority on the status of chondrichthyans. All 1200+ species of sharks, rays, and chimaeras have now undergone at least one round of the Red List assessment (RLA) process. RLAs are living documents and are updated every ten years. Some species are now being globally reassessed for the third time, shedding light on the increasing extinction risk of this group over recent decades. Over the course of this process, RLAs have been designed to provide updated and evidence-based data on the global status of each species. Continued advancements in knowledge and expertise needs to be gathered from the SSG and wider global research community to update assessments. This can lead to conservation action for priority threatened species groups. Despite progress in our knowledge of chondrichthyan biology, population trends, and threats, crucial speciesspecific knowledge gaps still exist. Here, the most needed and useful information often missing for RLAs will be provided to guide future research efforts.

2788: Chondrichthyans face a high risk of extinction, with an estimated 37% of species threatened with extinction. Immediate action is required to halt population declines and allow for species recovery. The Important Shark and Ray Areas (ISRA) approach was developed to put sharks on the map. The ISRA approach delineates ‘discrete, threedimensional portions of habitat, important for one or more shark, ray, or chimaera species, that have the potential to be managed for conservation’. A set of four science-based criteria, incorporating seven sub-criteria, was developed. Criteria are applied to delineate areas based on species vulnerability, range restriction, life history (reproduction, feeding, resting, movement, undefined aggregations), and special attributes (distinctiveness, diversity). The ISRA Criteria can be applied to all environments where chondrichthyans occur (marine, estuarine, and freshwater). The project was launched in 2022, and ISRAs have been delineated in eight (Central and South American Pacific, Mediterranean and Black Seas, Western Indian Ocean, Asia, Polar Waters, New Zealand and Pacific Islands, South American Atlantic, and South American Inland Waters) of 13 global regions, with the European Atlantic region currently under examination. The assessment of the remaining four regions (North America and Caribbean Atlantic, African Atlantic, Australia and Southeast Indian Ocean, and North American Pacific) is intended for completion by 2027. ISRA findings provide the foundation to include chondrichthyans in decision-making processes when designing protected areas, and for marine spatial planning. This can help governments and policymakers advance chondrichthyan conservation and meet global biodiversity and conservation targets.

2789: Establishing baseline information on migratory connectivity is important to identify regions of conservation focus. Despite efforts to track migratory sharks and rays, information on transboundary movements is limited and often inaccessible to managers and policymakers. Here, we synthesised multimethod movement data for migratory Australian sharks and ray species, investigating which species require international engagement to support their population recovery. Based on data from a systematic literature review, we built connectivity networks from telemetry and mark-recapture studies that provide a first baseline for transboundary migratory connectivity for Australian sharks and rays. Of the 31 shark and ray species reviewed, we identified 6 species that link the Australian Exclusive Economic Zone to other national jurisdictions via multispecies migratory connections through the Tasman Sea to New Zealand, through the Tasman and Coral Sea to New Caledonia, and north across the Timor Sea and Torres Strait. White sharks (Carcharhinus carcharias) and whale sharks (Rhincodon typus) were the most data rich, whereas 14 shark and ray species had no movement information. Of note is the grave deficiency in available information for endangered or critically endangered migratory shark and ray populations, for which 76% had only one or no published studies. This work supports future conservation strategies for migratory sharks that require robust international collaboration.

2790: We assessed the vulnerability risk to climate change stressors of 64 species of elasmobranchs with ≥10% of their distribution within a hotspot area named Tamiahua in the state of Veracruz in the Gulf of Mexico. Tamiahua is one of the most important fishing areas in the northern region, and it has been identified as the most vulnerable to climate change based on projections of sea surface temperature. To assess the vulnerability, we combined three components of vulnerability risk to climate change: exposure, sensitivity and adaptive capacity. We grouped the species into ecological groups to several climate change stressors, particularly changes in sea surface temperature. A workshop was conducted to integrate the empirical knowledge of local fishermen, including their historical observations of environmental changes. These insights were then compared with projected emission scenarios (high, medium, and low). The most important fishing areas for local fishermen are the reef zones. A total of 47 species of sharks and 17 rays were registered. Ten taxonomic orders were evaluated, with the order Carcharhiniformes having the highest number of species and being one the highly vulnerable order under the high-emission scenarios. For rays, the most vulnerable orders were Myliobatiformes and Torpediniformes. A total of 12 fishermen from Tamiahua were interviewed. Their ages ranged from 31 to 67 years, with weekly fishing hours varying between 7 and 84 hours and fishing experience spanning from 6 to 40 years. Priority was given to managing species identified as highly vulnerable, while alternative species with lower vulnerability were proposed as potential options for sustainable fishing.

2791: International liver oil trade is a major driver of targeted fisheries and retention of bycatch for deepwater sharks. Sharks are targeted for the squalene content in their liver oil, which is used for cosmetic and human health applications. The unique properties of shark liver oil make it a sought-after commodity, contributing to targeted fisheries and incentivizing fishers to retain bycatch. However, the trade's sustainability is questionable due to a lack of management and the precarious status of many shark species. Liver oil fisheries are understudied and overshadowed by more visible global trades of other shark and ray products but are presumed to not be sustainable. The global liver oil trade is also difficult to measure because of its complexity with the mixed end-product making it hard to identify and quantify species. This presentation will discuss efforts currently underway to extract DNA from liver oil products to identify shark species within. Various methodologies are being explored with the aim to establish a robust molecular monitoring tool for improved traceability and management of liver oil fisheries globally.

2792: As climate change accelerates, ocean warming and deoxygenation are placing increasing pressure on marine ecosystems worldwide, especially vulnerable habitats such as coral reefs. Understanding how these ecosystems, and the species they support, will be affected under future climate scenarios is critical for conservation efforts. Epaulette sharks (Hemiscyllium ocellatum), renowned for their remarkable hypoxia tolerance, are endemic to the Great Barrier Reef—a region that has experienced intense warming over the past few decades. While much research has been devoted to adult epaulette sharks, little is known about how early life stages cope with environmental stressors. This study aims to fill this gap by investigating the physiological and metabolic responses of early juvenile epaulette sharks to elevated water temperatures and reduced oxygen levels, conditions representative of their natural habitats. By employing respirometry, key metabolic proxies were measured, including maximum metabolic rate (MMR), standard metabolic rate (SMR), and critical oxygen tension (O2crit), a proxy for hypoxia tolerance, to assess the sharks' response to water temperatures of 27°C and 31°C and declining oxygen levels. In addition, blood sampling immediately following hypoxic exposure, and again one week later, was conducted to examine changes in haematological parameters such as haematocrit, haemoglobin, and mean corpuscular haemoglobin concentration as well as glucose and lactate concentrations. This approach allowed for a comprehensive evaluation of both the immediate and short-term physiological responses to thermal and hypoxic stress.

2793: Sharks and rays (elasmobranchs) play important ecological roles in marine ecosystems, yet their populations are increasingly impacted by anthropogenic threats. The Mariana Islands, in the remote western Pacific Ocean, host a diverse assemblage of elasmobranch species that experience mixed levels of management and conservation efforts. This study synthesizes current knowledge on the distribution, ecology, and conservation status of sharks and rays in the region, highlighting threats and current management. Fisheries regulations differ across the Pacific, with varying degrees of enforcement and speciesspecific protections. Highly migratory species, including pelagic sharks, face challenges from industrial fishing fleets operating beyond national waters, whereas coastal species encounter localized stressors, including habitat degradation and subsistence fishing. Despite regional conservation initiatives, limited data on population trends and species interactions complicate efforts to develop effective management strategies. Appropriate enforcement, increased research on population dynamics, and international cooperation are necessary to ensure the long-term persistence of elasmobranchs in the Mariana Islands. This review underscores the need for adaptive management approaches that account for ecological connectivity and socio-economic factors influencing conservation outcomes specific to these mostly threatened animals.
2794: Stock assessments in wild capture fisheries are a valuable tool used to determine the biological status and productivity of fish populations. In Sri Lanka, these fisheries play a major role in the livelihood of millions and the economy. However, the data needed to conduct such stock assessments is scarce. This project aims to determine which data is required to conduct an effective stock analysis in data-deficient fisheries. The first phase of the project will be focused on analysing elasmobranch catch data collected from landing sites around Sri Lanka over a period of 8 years. Using results from the first phase, the next objective will be to integrate a data collection template with the essential data requirements for stock assessments onto an online application, which can be accessed globally.

2795: The coastal region of the Karajarri Indigenous Protected Area (IPA) on Western Australia’s northern coastline is a macrotidal environment characterised by expansive intertidal sand, mudflat, and mangrove ecosystems. Gillnet surveys carried out between 2020 and 2024 in two embayments revealed that these habitats support a high abundance and diversity of elasmobranchs and function as a nursery area for dwarf sawfish (Pristis clavata) and green sawfish (Pristis zijsron). Here we present a preliminary description of this nursery area and report on its high social, cultural, and conservation values. Subsequent, Karajarri-led research on these species seeks to better understand sawfish ecology and inform management targets for the Karajarri IPA. This has included satellite telemetry and the installation of an intertidal acoustic monitoring array. Here we discuss preliminary results and the potential for culturally-informed research to contribute to meeting shared objectives relating to biodiversity conservation and aquatic resource management.

2796: Fisheries independent surveys can be used to identify long term abundance trends in sharks and rays. For many species globally abundance data is lacking. Long-term ecosystem sampling regimes, using unbaited gear, allow analysis of species populations, identifying species-specific interactions, and determining environmental impacts upon study species over extended periods of time. The north-western Cape York region is a unique environment, and its elasmobranch species composition is not well understood. From 2016 to 2024, gillnet surveys for sharks and rays were conducted in the waterways of Mapoon (Port Musgrave, Ducie River, Wenlock River) and Weipa (Albatross Bay, Hey River, Embley River), in the Gulf of Carpentaria, north-western Cape York, Queensland. A total of 916 elasmobranchs belonging to 37 species were captured. Factors that affect capture rates and distributions of elasmobranchs were analysed for the five most abundant species in the data set; ocellate eagle ray Aetobatus ocellatus, bullshark Carcharhinus leucas, winghead shark Eusphyra blochii, sicklefin lemon shark Negaprion acudentis and graceful shark Carcharhinus amblyrhynchoides). Environmental (depth, visibility, salinity, temperature, tidal state, time of day) and geographic factors’ influence upon species capture rates are examined using generalized linear mixed models, along with yearly abundance estimates based on CPUE, sampling methods and juvenile-to-adult ratios examined for the five study species. The implications of using these methods to examine the influence of the Queensland gillnet ban in 2027 are presented.

2797: This research examines the sustainability of fishing operations and marine fauna conservation in the Mexican Pacific. A comparison was conducted using commercial nets of the same size and design, equipped with the "Super Shooter" Turtle Exclusion Device (TED) and the "fisheye" Fish Escape Device (FED) in the Gulf of California. Fifteen hauls were performed, with the control net using both TED and FED, while the experimental net had a modified FED. A 40 kg random sample was collected per haul. The six most frequent elasmobranch species were Narcine vermiculata, Pseudobatos glaucostigmus, Urobatis halleri, Urobatis maculatus, Hypanus dipterurus, and Rhinobatos steindachneri, with U. halleri being the most abundant. In the control net, N. vermiculata ranged from 17.2–28.8 cm in total length (TL) for females and 16.9–23.9 cm for males, while P. glaucostigmus ranged from 16–75 cm TL for females and 15.4–60.5 cm for males. The experimental net showed similar ranges. Round ray disc width (DW) varied: U. halleri (7.3–27.2 cm control, 7.2–28.2 cm experimental), U. maculatus (6–15 cm control, 6–12.8 cm experimental), R. steindachneri (34–65 cm control, 38.5–70 cm experimental), and H. dipterurus (15.2–64 cm control, 24.5–56 cm experimental). No significant size differences were found except for U. halleri (U=9166.5, p=0.03), which was more frequently captured in the control net. We expect the presence of bycatch reduction devices (BRDs) to affect the size-frequency distributions of these species both in the catch and the population. Although ignored by most studies, the size selectivity of the fishing gear, including the bycatch escape devices, may have profound effects on the size-frequency distributions.

2798: Depredation of catch by sharks is an emerging issue facing recreational, commercial and charter fishers worldwide involving the interplay of a complex array of environmental, behavioural and operational factors. Since 2021, applied research using a multi-modal approach has been undertaken in Queensland fisheries to determine the significance of shark depredation and identify influencing factors. The multi-modal approach that involved genetic analysis, underwater observation and citizen science allowed the frequency of depredation events to be determined, actual depredation events and shark behaviour to be visualised, responsible depredating species to be identified and influencing factors to be analysed. To address rising sustainability concerns regarding the future of fisheries in Queensland, strategies to mitigate catch depredation were also investigated, such as the effectiveness and practicality of shark repellents during actual fishing operations. The findings of this research will aid in informing future policy and management methods to ensure sustainable fisheries into the future.

2799: Shark depredation is a high-priority issue affecting many fisheries globally, including in Australia. It leads to higher fish mortality, socio-economic impacts on fishers, and loss of support for shark conservation. Building on 10 years of research in Australia, this national project conducted a comprehensive global review of all mitigation methods that have been tested around the world to reduce shark depredation. Methods were assessed through a semi-quantitative ranking process, using seven criteria (effectiveness, suitability across fishing sectors, cost to implement, impacts on target species, depredating sharks, nontarget animals, and the environment). Ninety mitigation methods were identified and ranked and these were classified into four categories: 1) changes to fishing gear; 2) modifications to fishing methods; 3) fisheries management strategies; 4) shark deterrents. This generated a shortlist of the most promising methods for future testing in Australian line fisheries. Ten stakeholder workshops were run across WA, NT, QLD, and NSW to hear from local stakeholders about the impacts of shark depredation on their fishing, determine the key drivers influencing its occurrence, and provide practical feedback on the shortlisted methods. This has been further complemented by a national online survey. Overall, this project has created an important base for guiding future collaborative testing of suitable mitigation methods to reduce shark depredation.

2800: An understanding of how life-history traits, such as growth and attainment of maturity, vary among geographically disparate populations of a species is useful for populationspecific management. We developed a novel hierarchical Bayesian generative classifier model to estimate the length at which a species transition between life-history stages, such as length-at-maturity, at the species and population level. We applied this model to a dataset of lengths and life history characteristics we complied from six populations of school sharks around the world to estimate the length at which male school sharks attained maturity at the species level and for each of the six school shark populations. The species level length-at-maturity for male school sharks was estimated at 1273 mm, total length (fresh total length with tail in a natural position, TL), and population-specific estimates ranged between 1238 and 1306 mm, TL. Most populations, on average, differed in length-at-maturity by at least 19 mm, TL. However, estimates were similar for the New Zealand and South African, and for the Northeast Atlantic and Southwest Atlantic populations. As a result, we consider population-specific length-at-maturity estimates for male school sharks are necessary for the ongoing management of school shark populations.

2801: Anthropogenic noise is an increasingly relevant marine pollutant for which impacts on chimaeras have not been described. The Australian ghost shark, Callorhinchus milii, migrates to lay their eggs in bays off Australia and New Zealand, and may be affected by increased levels of anthropogenic noise in these areas. Specialised hair cells in the inner ear of C. milii are essential to auditory perception. Past evidence in bony fish has shown that these hair cells can be damaged due to anthropogenic noise pollution, impacting their survival. The aim of this study was to examine the effects of anthropogenic noise in the inner ear of C. milii. Captive embryos were exposed throughout development to two acoustic conditions: an ambient soundscape or boat noise. Embryos and hatchlings were then euthanised, stained and scanned using microCT for volumetric analysis and comparison of the inner ear labyrinths between treatments. The results showed that the inner ears of embryos raised in boat noise conditions were larger in volume than those raised in ambient soundscapes. Phalloidin staining and confocal microscopy were then used to quantify the number and distribution of hair cells in the maculae. Variations in inner ear size and hair cell populations between treatment groups highlighted the potential risk that anthropogenic noise pollution poses to embryonic/juvenile C. milii. These results are discussed in the context of conservation and represent the first investigation of the effect of noise on the development of a chondrichthyan.

2802: Since the origin of the Oceania Chondrichthyan Society (OCS), chondrichthyan reproductive research has undergone a significant transformation over the past two decades. This shift has moved from reliance on lethal sampling to innovative non-lethal approaches, improving ethical standards while enabling a more comprehensive understanding of reproductive physiology. Additionally, advancements in understanding the hypothalamus-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axis—which integrates environmental, physiological, and hormonal signals to regulate gonadal activity—have provided valuable insights into endocrine system evolution and adaptation to environmental pressures. These advancements support effective conservation strategies, helping managers assess reproductive potential, inform sustainable practices, and develop species-specific plans. This presentation will highlight key findings from two decades of research and the challenges that remain in fully elucidating the reproductive physiology of chondrichthyans. As global environmental changes and anthropogenic pressures continue to threaten aquatic biodiversity, a comprehensive understanding of reproduction will remain essential for the effective conservation and management of chondrichthyan populations and, more broadly, for the study of vertebrate reproduction.

2803: In light of Karimunjawa National Park (KJNP), Indonesia, being a potential pupping and nursery grounds for rhinorays while considering small-scale fisheries’ potential in unselectively bycatching them, it is crucial to understand their ecology better to design effective management. A market survey was conducted in two villages in KJNP and one village in Jepara Region (access to KJNP) from August 2023 to August 2024, to assess the growth model, reproduction, and diet of three rhinorays species, bottlenose wedgefish (Rhynchobatus australiae, n=984), broadnose wedgefish (R. springeri, n=88), and giant guitarfish (Glaucostegus typus, n=120). The growth model for all three species suggested females may grow bigger than the males of the same age. Subsequently, the length at maturity model showed females to mature at a longer standard total length (STL). The reproduction stages and pregnancy observed could suggest biennial reproduction with 410 pups per litter for the wedgefish species (samples were not available for G. typus). The three species shared similar diet characteristics of a specialized predator with a small variety of prey, mainly consisted of small crabs, shrimps, and fishes, with high overlap between sexes and life stages. The information collected provides a critical baseline for understanding potential habitat use by different groups and life stages of rhinorays species in KJNP and to inform conservation managers on future management plans.

2804: Accurate life history data are crucial for assessing the population status and vulnerability of species, but obtaining such data can be challenging for highly mobile megafauna in marine environments. This is true for the reef manta ray, Mobula alfredi, suspected to have one of the lowest reproductive potentials among elasmobranchs. This study uses 15 years of photo-identification data (2007–2021) to investigate the reproductive ecology of M. alfredi on Australia’s East Coast. A total of 1,281 individuals were identified from 7,900 sightings across the Capricorn Bunker Group to the Solitary Islands, comprising 660 females and 574 males. A quarter of the female population was observed pregnant at least once during the study period, with 249 pregnancies recorded among 169 females. Pregnancies occurred year-round, with late-term pregnancies (10–12 months) peaking at Lady Elliot Island during austral winter and at North Stradbroke Island in spring. This suggests a partially defined annual reproductive cycle with two seasonal peaks. Fecundity and cyclicity varied significantly among individuals. Forty-nine females had multiple pregnancies, with a maximum of five. In contrast, 119 females were pregnant once or had extended interbirth intervals of up to eight years. The average reproductive cyclicity ranged from 5.8 to 8.8 years. These findings suggest M. alfredi may have lower fecundity than previously assessed, even in populations with low anthropogenic pressures.

2805: Effective conservation of elasmobranchs requires robust age and growth estimates, yet data for the critically endangered Winghead Shark (Eusphyra blochii) remain limited. This study assessed the age and growth of Winghead Sharks from Papua New Guinea using traditional vertebral band pair counts and elemental analysis. Traditional band pair counts were difficult due to poor readability, common with hammerhead species. Elemental transects, conducted by laser ablation inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (LAICP-MS) revealed that copper and zinc periodicity was discernible, however questions remain on the seasonal cyclicity and inclusion of such elements. We applied a statistical model to age the sharks based on traditional band pair counts and elemental peaks. Further, elemental relationships were investigated between maternal mothers and embryonic neonates. These results provide the most comprehensive age and growth estimates for Winghead Sharks to date and highlight the potential to improve age accuracy using geochemical tracers as a proxy. Additionally, the first insights into preferential partitioning processes of trace metal elements during the prenatal growth stages are revealed. These findings contribute to critical life history data to inform conservation strategies and fisheries management for this highly vulnerable species.

2806: Body size and temperature set metabolic rates and the pace of life, but the energetics of large fishes is uncertain, especially for the warm-bodied mesotherms, many of which heavily influence the structure of oceanic food webs. We developed a novel approach to estimate metabolic heat production in fishes, enabling tests of how routine energy expenditure scales with size and temperature from tiny 10-mg larvae up to three-tonne mega-planktivorous sharks. We found mesothermic fish use ~ 5 times more energy than similarly sized ectotherms, and uncovered a scaling mismatch whereby large fish produce heat at a faster rate than they lose it, becoming increasingly warm bodied. This heat imbalance creates an overheating predicament for large mesotherms, helping explain their common reliance on cooler ocean habitats. High fuel demands and overheating risks will challenge contemporary mesotherms such as lamnid sharks, and likely contributed to their disproportionate demise during prior oceanic regime shifts
2807: Wedgefish (Family Rhinidae) are caught in many fisheries for their valuable fins and secondary products. Lack of adequate management in many countries has resulted in their global status as ‘critically endangered’, highlighting the need for an improved understanding of wedgefish biology to support future management practices. This study provides diet information for wedgefish species bottlenose wedgefish (Rhynchobatus australiae), smoothnose wedgefish (Rhynchobatus laevis), broadnose wedgefish (Rhynchobatus springeri) and bowmouth guitarfish (Rhina ancylostoma) for the first time in three elasmobranch fisheries hotspots in Indonesia. Results indicate that wedgefish prey preferences include small fishes, crustaceans, bivalves and cephalopods. Crustaceans were dominant prey, with 79.4 %IRIID in all species and prawns were recorded to have >30% IRIID in three of four species. In bottlenose wedgefish, there was no significant difference between sexes in overall prey preference; however, differences were found between size group, region and seasonality. By understanding prey preference, fisheries managers can better decide appropriate measures, especially in protecting important coastal habitats which support wedgefish prey

2808: Understanding life history parameters is key to assessing demography, biological productivity, and extinction risk of fishes. Age-and-growth analyses in chondrichthyans (sharks, rays, and ghost sharks) is primarily undertaken through counting vertebral band pairs. For rare, threatened, and protected species such as river sharks (Carcharhinidae; Glyphis), obtaining sufficient samples of vertebrae may not be possible. Here we use a very small sample size, selective size-class sampling, back-calculation techniques, and a Bayesian hierarchical model that accounts for repeated measures to provide age-andgrowth information for the Speartooth Shark Glyphis glyphis from which comprehensive sampling is not possible. Ten individuals were selectively sampled from the Adelaide River, Northern Territory, Australia. Bayesian length-at-age models using a combination of informative and uninformative priors in a multi-model framework were applied to the observed and back-calculated data with the sexes combined. Band pair counts produced age estimates of 0–11 years and suggest an age-at-maturity of >12 years. Most model parameter estimates for length-at-birth (L0) and asymptotic length (L∞) were biologically plausible. The Gompertz growth function, applied through a Bayesian hierarchical approach to back-calculated data, provided the best fitting and most biologically appropriate length-at-age parameters: L∞ = 229.5 cm TL ± (14.6 SE), gGom = 0.16 yr-1 ± (0.01 SE), and L0 = 58.2 cm TL ± (1.4 SE). Since samples were restricted to juveniles and sub-adults, this analysis should be considered as a partial growth curve. The results presented here are the first study to apply Bayesian methods to back-calculated lengthat-age data while accounting for repeated measures.

2809: Diet estimation with fatty acids and stable isotopes can provide quantitative estimates of a consumer’s diet using mixing models. These models require species- and tissue-specific factors accounting for biomarker metabolism between consumer and prey, achieved with captive diet studies. Isotopic factors are scarce and fatty acid factors non-existent for elasmobranchs, limiting efforts to quantify diets of these complex predators. We present isotopic diet-tissue discrimination factors and fatty acid calibration coefficients for six elasmobranch species and investigate suitable tissue types and sample preparation for accurate biochemical diet estimation. Isotopes and fatty acids provided accurate diet estimates, but fatty acid mixing models gave estimates closer to true diets, likely due to more tracers identified in fatty acid analysis that can explain diet variation. Both isotopes and fatty acids of plasma and muscle performed well, with close estimates to true diets and commonly identifying the correct order of multiple prey items, and red blood cells closely followed but results were tissue- and species-specific. We also investigated diet estimation with non-species-specific and tissue-specific factors, as difficulties keeping many elasmobranchs in captivity prevents calculation of these factors for most species. Non-tissue- and species-specific factors identified top prey items in most scenarios, likely influenced by similarities between the species and tissues being investigated and those for which factors were calculated. While quantitative diet estimation has remaining limitations, we demonstrate the valuable information determined with these techniques and provide ecologists with the tools necessary to quantitatively estimate diet.

2810: The bottlenose wedgefish, Rhynchobatus australiae, and congeners (family Rhinidae) has been listed as critically endangered due to life history characteristics and shallow coastal habitat association that render them highly vulnerable to high fishing pressure. The IndoWest Pacific region, including Malaysia, is known for high wedgefish diversity but conservation efforts are hampered due to lack of basic knowledge on the taxon. A sevenyear survey across Malaysia yielded a total of 85 Rhynchobatus samples that were identified using both morphological and molecular methods. The widely distributed R. australiae made up 87% of the sample composition, followed by R. palpebratus (11%) and a single R. springeri individual. Accurate species assignment for ambiguous looking specimens was challenging without molecular verification. The discovery of the eyebrow wedgefish R. palpebratus is a new species record for Malaysia and indicates a wider distribution for the species than previously thought. Population genetic analysis revealed moderate levels of genetic diversity and fine-scale structuring for R. australiae within the narrow, shallow Strait of Malacca. Collectively these results improve our understanding of wedgefish species diversity and highlight the importance to better protect and manage these threatened species in Malaysian waters.

2811: A comprehensive understanding of key ecological characteristics such as population structure, resource use, and life history are essential for designing management practices, particularly for threatened predators that play a vital role in regulating food webs. The white shark (Carcharodon carcharias) is a highly mobile predator that has experienced systematic population declines, although certain geographically distinct populations are thought to be recovering. We used high resolution stable isotope profiles (δ15N and δ13C) from 74 vertebrae to create retrospective ontogenetic trophic-habitat fingerprints as a method to differentiate population structure, ecological role and as a novel method for estimating age in Australian white sharks. Our results provide evidence to support an ecological two-population model for juvenile and subadult sharks sampled east and southwest of Bass Strait, with strong oscillatory trends across both regions, likely related to seasonal movements. Age estimates for immature white sharks in eastern Australia based on isotopically inferred annual movements from Corner Inlet, Victoria to southern Queensland ranged from less than one (191.4 ± 27.5 TL (cm); n=12) to seven (430 TL (cm); n=1) and were similar to those derived from traditional band counts, contrasting slower growth obtained from bomb radiocarbon studies. Understanding the ecological role of marine predators in addition to obtaining reliable life history demographics are critical for informing management strategies for conservation.

2812: Elasmobranchs play critical roles in maintaining biodiversity across marine ecosystems. However, their physiological resilience to climate change remains poorly understood. The epaulette shark (Hemiscyllium ocellatum) relies on specialized adaptations to persist in the highly variable environments it inhabits. Understanding how populations of epaulette sharks may cope with projected ocean warming is key to understanding the resilience of tropical, benthic elasmobranchs to warming. This study provides a comprehensive, multipopulation assessment of this species, integrating haematological, enzymatic, and respiratory biomarkers across three genetically distinct populations along a latitudinal gradient. Sharks were tested at current summer averages (28.5⁰C) and two future warming scenarios (30.5⁰C, 32⁰C). Haemoglobin concentration varied significantly by population, with the lowest latitude sharks exhibiting the highest haemoglobin concentrations among the three populations examined. Whole-blood glucose concentrations increased with temperature, while lactate showed an acclimatory response – elevated at 30.5°C before returning to control levels at 32°C. Standard metabolic rate significantly increased (Q10 = 2.9), suggesting greater energetic demand under warming, yet CTmax remained unchanged, indicating limitations at the level of upper thermal tolerance limits. These results reveal conserved physiological responses to warming across populations, balancing energetic costs but highlights metabolic trade-offs. Given the increasing frequency of marine heatwaves, these insights are critical for predicting species vulnerability and informing conservation strategies in a rapidly changing ocean.

2813: Shark fisheries and conservation assessments are often constrained by the quality of biological information available, especially regarding reproduction. Current methods for estimating reproductive parameters are logistically challenging and reflect single time points, limiting our ability to effectively manage these iconic species. Thus, innovative approaches are needed to address these shortcomings. Here we developed a method to extract and quantify reproductive hormones from the time-resolved growth increments in shark vertebrae, aiming to reconstruct reproductive life histories. Focusing on gummy shark Mustelus antarcticus, we extracted and quantified oestradiol and progesterone from female, and testosterone from male vertebrae. We found that oestradiol, progesterone and testosterone were all detectable in vertebrae samples and that hormone concentrations increased with maturity profiles. These results demonstrate the potential of shark vertebrae for detailed reconstructions of reproductive histories which could improve the accuracy of life history assumptions, aiding shark conservation and management efforts.

2814: Seafood is an important protein and economic resource globally, however, long and complex supply chains create an opportunity for seafood fraud including mislabelling to occur. This is especially common in the sale of shark products, where varying regulations around the species sold and labelling requirements can increase the risk for mislabelling or species substitutions. As sharks are processed at sea, they can be difficult to identify when landed and near impossible to identify visually when filleted. We investigated the use of Raman spectroscopy as a tool for species identification in shark products. We focus on samples collected throughout Southeastern Australia, with fillets sourced across South Australia and Victoria. Raman spectroscopy was used to create a library of speciesspecific signals, with all species identifications confirmed a priori using DNA barcoding. A suite of classification models were created showing promise for correctly classifying a variety of shark species. This technique has potential to be used as a rapid tool to assist with authentication and regulatory checks in a non-destructive manner. 2815: Ocean warming is redistributing marine biodiversity globally. Assessing shifts in species distributions is particularly interesting for large, highly mobile marine predators as their movement ecology increases their propensity to respond to changing environments and move to more suitable habitats. We built multi-variable and temperature-only habitat suitability models for white sharks (Carcharodon carcharias) under historic and future climate scenarios throughout south-eastern Australian bioregions. Models used satellite tag data from 41 white sharks over 5 years (2015–2020) and associated environmental variables. Future model projections were applied using downscaled sea surface temperature to quantify changes in suitable habitat based on temperature between 2024– 2080 under moderate (SSP2-4.5) and high (SSP5-8.5) climate scenarios. Suitable thermal habitat for white sharks will likely shift poleward during Austral winter and spring and equatorward in summer and autumn. By 2080, equatorial bioregions may become unsuitable year-round, while some poleward regions will likely increase in suitability by 27– 38 % in autumn, winter, and spring. Shifts in thermal suitability will likely alter the timing and extent of seasonal-temperature-triggered equatorial migrations. Shifts in thermal suitability may alter trophic dynamics and human-shark interactions. Our findings will help regional management prepare for ecological and safety implications of changing white shark distribution.

2816: Maternal transfer, defined here as the process where inorganic or organic contaminants that are stored in a mother’s tissues are mobilised during vitellogenesis, gestation, and/or lactation and passed onto the developing follicles, embryos, and young, respectively, is often thought to be the process responsible for the initial exposure of contaminants to developing elasmobranchs. Yet, there is a lack of evidence to support maternal transfer being the process responsible. By examining how and when school sharks (Galeorhinus galeus) provide their young with nutrients and associations of several essential and nonessential elements between maternal and embryonic tissues, we evaluate the extent to which school sharks from the New Zealand population transfer elements to their young. It is likely that developing school sharks are provided with the majority of their nutrients by those assimilated from the mother’s diet during vitellogenesis. Coupled with the lack of evidence of associations between maternal and embryonic element tissue concentrations, we found no evidence to support maternal transfer being the process responsible for the initial exposure of selected elements in school sharks from the New Zealand population. Instead, elements assimilated from the mother’s diet at the time of vitellogenesis is the more likely process. However, further work under controlled conditions is needed to confirm the patterns observed in this study.
